#6623. November’s Bake Club Is a Triple Feature of Holiday Pies

We’re Jesse and Shilpa, senior editors and the resident bakers of the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen. We love to bake—some might even call us obsessive—and we love to talk about all the hows and whys and what-didn’t-works that come with it.

Think of the Bon Appétit Bake Club as a book club, but for baking. Each month we share a brand-new meticulously tested recipe. Bake along with us, share your wins (or your fails—we’ve all been there), post pictures, ask us your pressing questions. We’re creating a community of confident, curious bakers who find just as much joy in the process of baking as the final results.

First, and most important, save each month’s recipe and bake it! You’ll find all of them below.

Join the Bon Appétit Bake Club chat on Substack and we’ll take you behind the scenes of our recipe development process.

Post and share photos of your beautiful bakes on Instagram using the hashtag #BABakeClub.

Share feedback and ask us questions in the Recipe Notes section of the recipe page in the Epicurious app. We read every comment and look forward to talking with you about butter, sugar, and more.

Send your baking questions to [email protected] for a chance to be featured on our podcast. Each recipe’s episode goes live at the start of the following month on the Bon Appétit podcast feed.

To celebrate pie, the iconic food of this American holiday (move over, turkey), we’re bringing back our trusty flaky-as-a-croissant crust that debuted in 2022. It has since become the only pie dough we use in the Test Kitchen—and in a room full of pro cooks, that’s a ringing endorsement. This year it’s the base of two recipes: a single-crust Cranberry Meringue Pie that will teach you all about blind baking and impress your loved ones with its towering slices, and a lattice-topped Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie whose double crust shows off all those buttery layers encasing lightly boozy caramel-draped fruit. Want homemade pie without making your own dough? We didn’t forget about you! Our Salted Coffee Custard Pie has a press-in oatmeal crust and a silky custard filling gilded with an airy layer of mascarpone-whipped cream.

Imagine a Parker House roll having a tryst with Asian-style milk bread and a classic French croissant—that’s the essence of salt bread, a.k.a. shio pan in Japan and sogeum-ppang in Korea. Each soft bun holds a rich secret: a nub of salted butter bundled within the shaped dough. The little pat of fat melts in the oven, pooling on the baking sheet to effectively fry the bottom crust, yielding a crisp, savory shell akin to something you’d find in a patisserie. I like to tear it in half to revel in the buttery, hollow center, then unravel each flaky layer, just like a croissant. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

Is it even fall if you haven’t been apple picking? And have you even been apple picking if you didn’t end the day racing to the farm stand selling still-warm cinnamon-sugar doughnuts? Our latest recipe is designed to recreate that experience—apple-studded dough, a hint of grease, a jolt of sugar and spice—without waiting for yeast to rise.

For those unfamiliar with karpatka, a.k.a. Carpathian Mountain Cake, let us enlighten you. Traditionally, two disks of tender, airy pâte à choux house a layer of pastry cream lightened with whipped cream or crème mousseline. This version ditches the classic filling for a no-bake cheesecake (!) ribboned with homemade plum jam. It’s make-ahead-friendly and endlessly fun; just the thing to keep the summer vibes going a little longer.

This sunflower yellow cake with an alluring bounce is Bake Club’s midsummer stunner. Fresh (or frozen! I don’t mind) corn blended with a can of sweetened condensed milk and our defining ingredient, sweet rice flour, makes up the bulk of the batter. The end result is a textural masterpiece with gentle resistance and slight elasticity that tastes like buttered corn, toasty coconut, and nutty caramel all at once.

If a tomato sandwich, pizza, and flaky pastry started a band, these tomato galettes would be their first hit single. Start by making a black-pepper-spiked pie dough, which needs no specialty equipment to bake up crisp and layered. Each little round is filled with a dollop of garlicky Parmesan and herb mayo, which acts as a barrier between each little galette’s juicy tomato slice and delicate pleated crust. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

Lemons are a powerful ingredient. So why miss out on their full potential by only using their juice and zest? That was the thesis behind these bars. By blitzing up two whole lemons into the curd, then straining out the pulpy bits, we keep lemon’s most exciting qualities: the bitterness of the pith, the essential oils of the skin, and of course, the acidity of the juice. Think Lemonhead candy. It’s everything I love about classic lemon bars with the volume turned up to a reckless decibel level.

Last year, for deputy food editor Hana Asbrink’s birthday, I made a strawberry roll cake filled with whipped cream and tiny jewel-red strawberries. It was an immediate hit and we decided right then that it belonged in Bon Appétit Bake Club. With fluffy cake, vanilla-bean-flecked cream, and juicy berries, it’s a dream dessert, tailored for this joyful season filled with new blooms and tender asparagus. Roll cakes traditionally require a complex series of steps when it comes to shaping, but this version utilizes an oil-based chiffon sponge, making it particularly easy to roll with no cracks and no heartbreak.

After last month’s cheesy biscuits, we’re going back to our dessert-loving roots and baking chocolate cake. But not just any old chocolate cake—this is a malty, brawny loaf imbued with Guinness stout. The crumb is tender beyond belief because of how you mix the batter. You’ll combine the dry ingredients, then rub in the butter by hand, until it practically disappears. This mimics a technique called reverse creaming and prevents excess gluten from forming. And there’s no special equipment, like a stand mixer, required.

A biscuit warm from the oven, split open so the steam rises to meet you, rivals the pleasure of an exalted loaf of homemade bread, all for a mere fraction of the effort (and wait time). This month’s recipe is packed with cheese and zhuzhed up with Old Bay seasoning. These biscuits are tall and layered like a lasagna, thanks to a quick and dirty lamination technique not unlike croissants. You don’t need any special equipment for these, but I highly recommend availing yourself of a nice bench scraper. It makes shaping the dough so much easier. Chris recently handed me a set from Gestura and I’ve been loving it because it’s small but sturdy, with thoughtfully curved edges and a minimal handle.

With a few pantry staples and a little time, this recipe yields a dozen delightfully chewy bagels that rival the most beloved of NYC shops. The trick? A two-step process: The bagels are first boiled, then baked. This dual approach gives them their signature chew, tanned sheen, and pleasantly dense (not tough) interior. And for a little fun: You can top these bagels with just about anything you like. Some of our favorites are furikake, Parmesan, sesame seeds (classic), and flaky salt.

This bake is inspired by Black Forest cake, a Bavarian dessert defined by its layers: chocolate cake, cream, cherries, and kirsch, a cherry brandy. Over the years it spread far beyond its woodland origins, to countries like India, Fiji, the Philippines, and the Caribbean Islands. One bakery in Chennai, India, where I grew up, made tall triangular slices, a treat my parents brought home if we did well on our school tests. Pavlovas are prone to crack, weep, or turn soggy and chewy. The key is in the ratio of sugar to egg whites. Two parts sugar to one part egg whites (by weight, of course) gives you a sturdy, crisp, snow-white pavlova.

Designed to maximize the ratio of sticky, gooey insides, arguably the best part of the pastry, this giant cinnamon roll was received with joy almost every time I made it. A little instant vanilla pudding mixed with cinnamon sugar mimics the ooey-gooey texture of mall-famous cinnamon roll filling, thanks to the modified food starch it contains. It’s purposefully large enough to cut into slices like a cake, but if you’re like us, you won’t be able to resist tearing it apart with your bare hands. Nor should you.

For those unfamiliar with the old-school pageantry of this French pastry, let us enlighten you: A Paris-Brest is a giant wreath of pate à choux (a foundational pastry dough) that puffs and expands dramatically in the oven. This version swaps the traditional praline mousseline filling for a banana-peel-infused (yes!) diplomat cream (just a fancy term for pastry cream lightened with whipped cream) and layers it with candied nuts and slices of banana. Everything good about Southern banana pudding, just in a flashier, French package.

Turn on the AC, because this month we’re making a lovely, homey pie. It’s everything good about summer (fruit! leisure! long days!) tucked away in a crisp, flaky crust, lightly scented with cardamom, and topped with a brown sugar streusel. There are some powerful learning moments in this bake: How to make a crust that will never fail you. How to select the best fruit for a pie. Why it’s important to precook a high-moisture filling so your pie crust is crisp rather. And perhaps the hardest and most important lesson of all: How long to wait before you dig into your pie ( it’s longer than you think).

This is no squishy sandwich loaf, but rather a big, browned boule studded with fresh jalapeños and chunks of cheddar. It’s ultra-savory and just a touch spicy. For those who might be intimidated by homemade bread (we see you!), think of this recipe as an intro course. It’s made with instant yeast, so it comes together quickly, without having to fuss over finicky active dry yeast or sourdough starter. And you don’t have to knead it; a few quick folds is all it takes.

This month we’re making Hummingbird Cake, an imposing icon from the American South. It’s a storied dessert with an interesting history that involves a Caribbean island, possibly a bird, and a magazine that’s over five decades old. If you’re unfamiliar, think of it as a banana version of carrot cake, full of nuts, spices, fruit, and cream cheese frosting.

The tang of cultured dairy from sour cream makes these scones stand out, keeping them moist but not claggy. And with that addition, channeling coffee cake became the natural next step. With clusters of streusel on top and a cinnamon sugar swirl within, these are scones that anyone will love.

Millionaire’s shortbread is the ultimate show-off bake. Our version went through about 10 rounds of testing until every detail was just right. The base of these bars—a simple, ultra-tender shortbread—gets a special upgrade: toasting a bit of the flour beforehand. This lends a deep nuttiness, almost like coffee, without any extra ingredients. The caramel takes a hybrid approach, bolstering caramelized sugar with sweetened condensed milk, so you get a bittersweet flavor with a sliceable texture. The final layer combines chocolate with butter for a mirror-like shine and fudgy bite.

The key to this pistachio cake’s tender crumb and mowed-grass green hue? A blender. It does all the hard work for you, decimating the nuts into a coarse flour and evenly distributing the dry ingredients (no sifting needed). This cake is satisfyingly hefty and moist thanks to the pistachios’ natural fat content, a combination of melted butter and oil, plus a pearlescent lemon glaze.

It’s easy to see the appeal of Basque cheesecake—dramatic visuals aside, it’s astonishingly easy to make. You don’t need a crust, or a water bath, or the long, slow cook of a New York–style cheesecake. The trick lies in cooking it hot and fast, much like pizza or steak, resulting in a cheesecake of epic contrasts, deeply caramelized on the outside while remaining quiveringly soft inside. I’ve added buttery mascarpone and a not insignificant amount of instant espresso to the batter to mimic another custardy classic, the iconic tiramisu. Topped off with a rosette of cocoa-dusted cream, it is two desserts for the effort of one.

Our pizza recipe meets you where you are: It can come together in fewer than 4 hours and is adaptable to an overnight rest. You don’t need a stand mixer, a clunky baking stone, or a specialty oven. And you’ll still get a world-class pie. The decidedly untraditional two-step cooking method (stovetop plus broiler) is a game changer, guaranteeing a puffy crust with enviable char (or leoparding, as the pros call it). To make dough-handling easier, we highly recommend a flexible bowl scraper.

This one-bowl cake has olive oil in both the chocolate cake and the ganache-like frosting. It’s a low-effort, high-reward recipe. And if there are any leftovers, thanks to that olive oil, the crumb will stay moist for days. Using Dutch-process cocoa powder gives this cake an intense chocolaty flavor. Our go-to brand for pretty much anything baking-related is Guittard Cocoa Rouge. It has a bold, concentrated complexity without any of the dull chalkiness common in other brands.

This project bake screams autumn. The perfect follow-up to apple picking, it’s a fruit-studded beauty, drenched in a tangy cider caramel and using almost half a gallon of apple cider. Make sure to use a 12-cup or larger Bundt pan for this recipe. Using a smaller variety can result in the dough proofing out of the pan. Nordic Ware actually invented the Bundt pan, and we love their version for its sturdy construction and even heat distribution.

In this excerpt from "Killing the Dead," author John Blair looks at how the printed press ramped up tales of vampirism, leading to stories of people eating a supposed vampire's organs and drinking their blood in a bid to avoid the same fate.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 17th and 18th centuries, the fear of vampires reached extraordinarily heights. People believed corpses could reanimate and wander around, terrorizing villages and spreading disease. They went to extreme lengths to prevent a vampire from rising. Some chopped the deceased person's head off, others placed sickles across their necks. Many were placed face down in their graves. In one grave in Poland, the remains of a boy were found with an iron padlock around his foot.

In this excerpt from "Killing the Dead: Vampire Epidemics from Mesopotamia to the New World" (Princeton University Press, 2025), author and historian John Blair reveals the impact the printed press had on the spread of vampiric lore — and the grizzly purported practice of ingesting the blood and organs of a vampire to prevent other people becoming one.

With the invention of printing, the circulation of European stories about restless corpses moved up several gears. Occasional early references were followed by a clutch of theological and philosophical discussions during c. 1580-1610, and then — from the 1670s — a steadily growing volume of printed academic and historical debate and commentary, reaching a climax in 1732.

Another landmark came in 1746 when the Benedictine scholar Dom Augustin Calmet published his survey of supernatural beings, which was quickly reissued in several editions, including an English one of 1759. This book's section on vampires was the most influential academic work on the subject ever published. Its straightforwardly evidence-based approach was a breath of fresh air after a long series of increasingly derivative works.

It achieved its remarkable popularity because it entered the market at the right point: saturated with so much fragmented and repetitive discussion of "vampires" (still a relatively new word), the reading public wanted a textbook. Calmet inspired a huge progeny of followers and popularisers, bringing the stories to a much wider readership; a good example of the genre is the Histoire des vampires et des spectres malfaisants [History of Vampires and Malevolent Specters] of 1820, a pocketbook that re-packages Calmet for the mass market.

Calmet's book remains the ultimate source of much modern vampire literature in Europe and America, both fi­ctional and supposedly historical, and was transformative in bringing the topic to a wider reading public. There and elsewhere, stories were now frozen on the printed page, where later generations could read them. But they were stories still: not necessarily more reliable, and by no means stable in transmission.

The tangled story of consuming blood from vampire corpses starts in a different and very unexpected place.

The complexity of interactions between learned discourse and popular practice is illustrated by one particularly bizarre and repellant (not to say dangerous) strand in the belief-system. This is the practice of ingesting blood or organs from a supposed vampire corpse, or ashes derived from burning them, as a remedy for vampire-induced illness.

Although not wholly dissimilar from the idea that victims will recover as they watch the smoke rise from burning vampire organs — already known in 11th-century England — its shocking physicality sets it apart. Did people in pre-modern Europe really do this?

A complicating factor is the medicinal use of human blood and bodyparts, in accordance with the theories of the physician, philosopher, and alchemist "Paracelsus" (Theophrastus von Hohenheim, c. 1493–1541). A brilliant experimenter, Paracelsus believed that substances healed through occult 'influences' or 'spirits,' the most powerful being those derived from what they were meant to cure: the human body.

The fact that medicine now rejects these hypotheses should not make us view them patronizingly: in the early modern period, ingesting or anointing with substances from Egyptian mummies or the blood of executed criminals seemed as rational as doing the same with any other substance. These Paracelsian ideas entered popular practice: at a beheading in Vienna in 1668/9, a man ran forward and caught the spouting blood to cure his epilepsy.

An illustration of an execution of a vampire.

The tangled story of consuming blood from vampire corpses starts in a different and very unexpected place. In 1687, a major ethnographical account of parts of West Africa by the Capuchin missionary Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi was published in Bologna. In it, Cavazzi describes magical and medical practices among the Mbundu of Angola, including a method of obtaining vital curative fluid from undecayed corpses:

When they are in a fresh and intact state when unearthed, their heads are cut from their bodies, from which it is said that blood flows out (which may happen through some illusion or deceit). It is collected and made into poultices for the sick, or mixed into their food, which infallibly guarantees health. Thereafter the dead person, having lost his strength, will no longer be able to harass them.

From Angola to Paris: in May 1693, a story appeared in the society magazine Mercure Galant. The author was the courtier and polymath Pierre des Noyers (1607–93), who spent several years in Poland in the entourage of Queen Louise-Marie. Much earlier, in 1639, he had written to a friend about the being known as upior (Ruthenian) or striga (Polish): born with teeth; eating its shroud and then its hands and arms in the coffi­n; causing successive deaths of family members; and extinguished by decapitation and release of pent-up blood.

This story is rather highly coloured (eating the hands and arms is unusual), but it does probably originate in genuine oral accounts of the shroud-chewer belief.

Very different is des Noyers’s account from 1693. Now the striges and upierz have become corpse-hijacking demons: 'It is said that the demon takes this blood from the body of a living person, or from certain animals, and carries it into a dead body; for it is alleged that the demon goes out from this corpse during a certain period, between noon and midnight, after which it returns and stores there the blood that it has gathered.'

They denied cutting out the heart, mixing the blood into flour, and baking cakes with it, but the judges were sceptical and made them swear an oath.

The blood comes out of the mouth, nose, and ears of the corpse, the corpse swims in blood, and it starts to eat its shroud. The demon especially troubles former associates and relatives of the dead 'host,' appearing to them in the guise of parents or friends, and does not leave until all the family members have died in succession. The remedy is to exhume the corpse, which is found soft, flexible, bloated, and red:

When they are found in that state, having the likeness of those who had appeared in dreams, their heads are cut off and their hearts are opened, and a quantity of blood flows out. It is collected and kneaded into flour, which is made into bread, which is a certain remedy to guarantee against such a terrible affliction. After the heads [of the dead people] have been cut off, those whom the Spirit torments at night are no longer troubled by it, and are well thereafter.

This narrative has problems. The idea of the demon using the corpse as a safe-deposit for its hoard of blood seems to be unique; so, probably, is the time-slot between noon and midnight. These read like clerical rationalizations, perhaps fed to des Noyers by some Polish priest and overlaid on his earlier, more authentic observations. But more fundamentally, it seems obvious that des Noyers’s account of Poland shamelessly re-works Cavazzi's account of Angola, published eight years previously.

It might not be quite so simple. An earlier common source, still unidenti­fied, remains possible. The descriptions of mixing blood into food and poultices look remarkably close to Paracelsian ideas, extended from ordinary corpses to undead ones: was even Cavazzi's account distorted by his own medical learning? But in any case des Noyers’s account is a piece of unprincipled plagiarism, worthless as evidence for Polish folk-belief.

Even so, it has bounced down through the echo-chambers of vampire literature ever since. The following year, a lawyer called Marigner built on the narrative — which he took at face value — with long philosophical musings on the nature of vampires. Inevitably, in 1746, it was republished in Calmet's book, which made it permanently available to vampire-aware readers.

While otherwise faithful to des Noyers, Calmet's version irons out the motif of demonic corpse-possession by calling this predator a vampire 'or a demon in its form.' This process of moulding to a more familiar template culminates in a recent version that presents the story as straightforward ethnographic reporting, omitting the demonic motif completely.

So far, this has just been a morality tale of plagiarism and uncritical copying. But in 1713, at Dąbrówka (now western Ukraine), some villagers were tried in the Uniate episcopal court for exhuming a woman's corpse and mutilating it in inventive ways. They admitted to the exhumation (because the dead woman had been walking around and attacking people), and to drinking the corpse's blood mixed with vodka. They denied cutting out the heart, mixing the blood into flour, and baking cakes with it, but the judges were sceptical and made them swear an oath.

This will sound very familiar to readers of early modern witch trials, where suspects were regularly bullied into admitting bizarre fantasies formulated by the persecutors. In this case, it seems clear that at least the idea of the blood-cakes was suggested by the judges; the same could be true of the blood-drinking, even though the accused were induced to confess that. It is distinctly possible, not to say likely, that an ordinary corpse-killing was embellished with luridly fi­ctitious detail by judges who knew des Noyers's report from twenty years earlier.

Killing The Dead: Vampire Epidemics from Mesopotamia to the New World. Copyright © 2025 by John Blair, published by Princeton University Press and reprinted here by permission.

Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.

Killing the Dead provides the first in-depth, global account of one of the world’s most widespread yet misunderstood forms of mass hysteria—the vampire epidemic. In a spellbinding narrative, John Blair takes readers from ancient Mesopotamia to present-day Haiti to explore a macabre frontier of life and death where corpses are believed to wander or do harm from the grave, and where the vampire is a physical expression of society’s inexplicable terrors and anxieties.

John Blair is an emeritus fellow of The Queen’s College, Oxford, and emeritus professor of medieval history and archaeology at the University of Oxford. His many books include "Building Anglo-Saxon England" (Princeton University Press), "The Church in Anglo-Saxon Society, and The Anglo-Saxon Age: A Very Short Introduction" (Oxford University Press).

#6621. The Halloween Candy That Matches Your Zodiac Sign, According To An Astrologer

Whether you fully commit to spooky season or prefer to keep things low-key, you can’t truly celebrate Halloween without enjoying some candy. Different sweets have cultivated fierce brand loyalties. But the key to finding your favorite Halloween candy may be hiding among the stars.

We consulted astrologer and author Lisa Stardust to find which candy best reflects each zodiac sign's personality. From old-school chocolates to wild, wacky treats, her choices span the full sweet spectrum.

Aries is defined by its bold and ambitious approach to life. Stardust describes the cardinal fire sign as “passionate, electrifying, and intense.” But Aries can also be a bit impulsive. “You never know what you’re going to get next based on their emotions,” she adds.

In honor of Aries’ fiery spirit, Stardust chooses Hot Tamales as the candy that best reflects the sign. With its vibrant red hue, intense spice, and unapologetic cinnamon-forward flavor, there’s no better sweet to symbolize the sign.

Compared to Aries' bold energy, Taurus is decidedly more practical. The earth sign is known for being stable, dependable, and guided by logic over emotion. While Taurus may resist change, the sign also has good taste and knows its way around the finer things in life.

And what candy represents that tried-and-true energy better than a classic bar of Hershey’s milk chocolate? “They’re both iconic and never go out of style,” Stardust explains. “Their tastes might be simple, but they’re always decadent and indulgent.”

Gemini is the astrological embodiment of street smarts. The air sign is very astute, with the uncanny ability to read a room and adapt accordingly. This perceptiveness translates to strong social skills and the ability to elevate the mood of any room.

The candy that best reflects this energy is, unsurprisingly, Smarties. “Geminis are intellectual, and they have a little bit of zest to them,” explains Stardust. “They’re sugary and sweet but also a little messy.”

The cardinal water sign is not shy about expressing emotions. Cancers are best described as the teddy bears of the zodiac: sensitive, empathetic, and the embodiment of comfort. Those with Cancer in their chart are prone to shielding others from their complex emotions, but make no mistake—there are a lot of feelings.

A candy that matches Cancer’s mushy inner self is Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups. “They are very protective on the outside, but they're tender on the inside,” Stardust says.

Leo can’t help but be the life of the party. The fire sign is very extroverted, with a personality so big it verges on theatrical. Stardust describes Leos as “fun and flamboyant,” even if they sometimes get on other people’s nerves.

In her opinion, the sweets that represent Leo best are Twizzlers. Stardust notes that you “can have a lot of fun eating them,” whether it’s peeling them apart or biting off the ends to use as a straw. If it involves playing with your food, it’s perfect for Leo.

Virgos are Type A to their cores. The earth sign has a precise attention to detail and is always looking to solve problems. But the constant focus on logic and perfection often obscures a deep well of emotions.

“There’s more to them than you may think, and there’s definitely another flavor to them on the inside, because they’re ruled by Mercury,” Stardust explains. The candy that best mirrors this energy is a York Peppermint Patty. The seemingly simple chocolate exterior hides a sweet, sharp minty center (if that’s not Virgo, I don’t know what is).

Libra is represented by scales, which reflects the air sign’s desire for fairness and justice. The empathetic and compassionate Libra tends to consider all points of view to make the most measured decisions that’ll make everyone happy. (But sometimes, that may mean not making a decision at all.)

Libra’s balanced approach to life is why Stardust chooses Twix as their ideal candy. Left Twix or right Twix? Thankfully, Libra doesn’t have to choose. “They’re a package deal,” Stardust says. So whether they want to enjoy both or share with someone else, Libras are Twix’s target audience.

Scorpios embody the phrase, “looks like they could kill you, is a cinnamon roll.” The water sign is often misunderstood. While undoubtedly intense, Scorpio’s dark, almost brooding exterior hides a lot of emotional complexity.

The sign shares a lot of characteristics with one candy in particular: Sour Patch Kids. “They have a really deep personality to them; they’re sweet with a sharp, tangy bite.” And, like the multicolored gummy treats, Scorpio is the true manifestation of “sour, sweet, gone.”

Sagittarius is seemingly always on a journey—whether it be physical, emotional, or spiritual. The fire sign is known as an explorer, with lofty aspirations and an aversion to playing it safe.

This energy is exactly why Stardust chooses 3 Musketeers as the quintessential Sagittarius sweet. “The namesake is adventurous, and it speaks for itself,” she explains.

When you need someone reliable, responsible, and grounded, you can’t go wrong with a Capricorn. This pragmatic, logical earth sign is incredibly goal-oriented and has the Type A personality to make it happen.

How many licks does it take to get to the center of a Tootsie Pop? Capricorn may be the only sign in the zodiac that’s disciplined enough to find out, which is why Stardust chooses the lollipop as their ideal candy. “It’s a classic, just like Capricorn,” she says. “They’re traditional, steady, strong, and you have to have patience to eat them.”

Aquarius marches to the beat of its own drummer. The air sign loves to be a contrarian and will unapologetically take the road less traveled. Nothing is too unique or too strange for Aquarius.

And what candy matches that energy better than a bag of Pop Rocks? “They’re unexpected and veer from the norm of traditional candy,” Stardust explains. They’re shocking, surprising, and delightful in their own special way—just like Aquarius loves to be.

Pisces always seems to have its head in the clouds. The water sign has a dreamy, romantic approach to life and has an extremely vivid imagination. “They feel all the feels,” Stardust explains.

Pisces needs a candy that can keep up mentally and emotionally, which is why she chooses Skittles as their ideal sweet. “It’s all about the rainbow and the imagination,” Stardust says. “They get to taste the rainbow and all of the sensations in every bite.”

Stare into the transfixing eye of the "Seagull Nebula" in this newly-released test image from the visionary Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What it is: The head of the sassy Seagull Nebula (IC 2177)Where it is: Between the constellations Monoceros and Canis Major, about 3,700 light-years awayWhen it was shared: Oct. 22, 2026

When a seagull stares you down, scientists recommend that you stare right back at it to keep your dignity (and your french fries) intact.

Two years ago, astronomers at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory put this idea — and their brand-new telescope — to a test of cosmic proportions, aiming an experimental 144-megapixel camera at the menacing blue eye of the Seagull Nebula (IC 2177).

Located about 3,700 light-years from Earth, the Seagull Nebula is a conglomeration of three giant, billowing clouds of irradiated gas. The "head" of the bird, featured in Rubin's image above, is a cloud called Sharpless 2-292. Its pink plumage is made of hydrogen gas, which glows brightly as ionizing radiation flies forth from the young stars at the cloud's center. The bird's blue "feathers" are clouds of dust reflecting the light from young, blue stars nesting elsewhere in the region.

It's unclear who won this stellar stare-down. If the bird appeared to blink, that's only because its eye is really the triple-star system HD 53367, a flickering trio of very young and energetic stars actively shaping the cloud around them.

The Rubin Observatory, meanwhile, had to avert its gaze quickly; this image is just one of about 16,000 exposures taken of the night sky between Oct. 24 and Dec. 11, 2024, according to the National Science Foundation, which co-manages Rubin along with the U.S. Department of Energy. Taken with the aforementioned Commissioning Camera (ComCam), the deep-space photos served as an early test of the observatory's hardware, software and image-processing capabilities.

A comparison of ComCam's field of view (right box) with the LSST Cam's field of view (left box). The relative size of the full moon is shown for scale. LSST Cam, currently in use at the observatory, can see roughly 20 times more than ComCam saw in its test observations.

ComCam's test image is remarkably crisp — but what's even more impressive is that Rubin has since upgraded to a camera with more than 20 times the field of view. The Legacy Survey of Space and Time Camera currently mounted on the observatory's Simonyi Survey Telescope takes 3,200-megapixel images of the night sky every 30 seconds, completing a full scan of the entire southern sky every few nights, Tony Tyson, Rubin's chief scientist, previously told Live Science.

Now that the Legacy Survey of Space and Time has officially begun, Rubin will spend the next 10 years photographing the sky night after night, creating a time-lapse movie of the universe that is expected to reveal millions of cosmic wonders, from exploding supernovas to newfound comets and exoplanets. Perhaps it will even spot another bird.

#6618. The Best Teriyaki in Seattle

Who serves the best gorditas in Mexico City? Or Baltimore's can't-miss crab cakes? Welcome to Taste of the Town, where we call on a local expert to share the best versions of one of their city’s most iconic foods. Here, we explore Seattle’s take on teriyaki.

Seattle’s entire teriyaki universe exists because of one man, a pioneer of chargrilled chicken thighs. In 1976, Toshi Kasahara opened a restaurant serving lightly marinated and grilled chicken, glazed in a blend of soy sauce, ginger, garlic, and sugar. This wasn’t any teriyaki you’d find in Japan, but a cheap, filling, flavor-packed translation aimed at a working-class city still unaware of the tech boom on the horizon.

Kasahara established and sold about 30 shops over the years, and copycats began copycatting. Teriyaki became ubiquitous, the Japanese name concealing its hometown heritage. Some locals don’t even realize teriyaki joints are a Seattle thing—that is, until they move elsewhere and try to find one.

Kitchens with Vietnamese roots began dishing up teriyaki alongside steaming bowlfuls of pho. Many spots still specialize in a classic interpretation, typically served with scoops of rice, some fried gyoza, and iceberg lettuce bathed in a thin mayo dressing. Enterprising Korean immigrants embraced teriyaki and opened their own outfits, adding bulgogi to the menu and gochujang to the chicken’s marinade.

The forward march of time, trends, and real estate prices means there’s sadly no longer a teriyaki business every few blocks. Those that remain include a few clunkers: Many have succumbed to shortcuts, serving sad chicken in gloopy, way-too-sweet gravy, which obscure the dish’s appeal to outsiders. But find a place still making its own sauce and blasting thighs on high heat, delivering bits of caramelized char that balance its teriyaki sweetness. Then you’ll understand.

Local wisdom dictates the best shop is the one closest to you, but here are eight greats, new and old.

Toshi Kasahara’s original restaurant, now long shuttered, was the archetype of a Seattle-style teriyaki spot—a spare cafeteria-like space with a streamlined menu built around Kasahara’s iconic chicken. Just a sprinkling of these shops still exist, but today only one is the real deal: a take-out operation deep in a Mill Creek strip mall. It’s open just a few hours in the evenings, with the 77-year-old Kasahara at the grill. He’s tweaked his methods slightly over the years, but his chicken is just as juicy and smoky as ever. No one in Seattle does it exactly like Toshi, but his sons do farther afield. One runs a Toshi’s food truck in San Francisco; the other is opening a Toshi’s outpost this winter in his father’s hometown of Ashikaga, Japan.

Hawaii has its own relationship to teriyaki. When restaurateur Matthew Parker opened his ode to the teriyaki counters that fueled his first 20 years in Seattle, he looked to his family’s roots in Oahu—specifically to huli huli chicken. That dish inspires Grillbird’s glossy house sauce, sweetened just enough with pineapple juice and ketchup. There’s no iceberg salad here; sides include mac salad and marinated cucumbers, dishes standard to plate lunch, Hawaii’s answer to the meat-and-three. Purists can grouse about how teriyaki shops should be old-school in every sense, but I welcome Grillbird’s modern touches, like online ordering and a mostly gluten-free menu. Grillbird’s original West Seattle outfit occupies a former Pizza Hut, which feels just right for this utilitarian dish. A second location in Phinney Ridge operates alongside sister concept Salad Party, for those looking to get their greens in.

When the Lee family lost the lease on their longtime teriyaki restaurant, the new location they’d scouted came with a catch: The strip mall that housed it already had a teriyaki shop. So matriarch Yoo-Mi Lee camouflaged her teriyaki menu with dishes from her Korean heritage and influences from the years the family lived in Brazil. Be thankful for that other teriyaki business, because Tá Jóia’s highly specific Brazilian-Korean-teriyaki remix is so vibrant and delicious, it could (should!) be a national fast-casual restaurant chain. Feijoada, a hearty slow-cooked black bean stew made with pork, bacon, and sausage, fits right in next to bulgogi, while the kitchen’s spectacular teriyaki hides in plain sight under the moniker “spicy chicken bowl.” It’s the chicken teriyaki of your hottest, most chili-spiked dreams, brightened with a scoop of pico and a drizzle of creamy house cilantro sauce.

No matter which member of the Kim family is behind the counter here, chances are they will offer you tea while you wait for your order. If the hospitality is great, the food is even better. Chicken teriyaki looks like it came off a photo shoot, deeply juicy with properly charred edges. It’s chicken that needs no supporting cast, but with so many combos on the menu, it’s fun to compare how the gingery sauce hits different proteins including beef, pork, prawn, or tofu. (If you’re exceedingly hungry, go for the formidable triple combo, which delivers chicken and beef teriyaki, golden-fried gyoza with a flaky, blistered exterior, and fragrant mounds of fried rice.) Teriyaki lovers are especially protective of Rainier Teriyaki since its late owner, Hansoo Kim, was tragically killed during a 2023 attempted armed robbery; the family banded together and reopened the restaurant in his honor.

Most people show up at Fremont’s busy donburi shop craving its chirashi bowl, but the chicken teriyaki imagines what Seattle’s signature dish might have looked like if it actually hailed from Japan. Butterflied thighs with the lightest of marinades come straight off the grill to be dressed with a sauce that’s thin by Seattle standards, but nonetheless lands a careful balance of savory and sweet. I appreciate this subtler rendition of chicken teriyaki, which complements an otherwise traditionally Japanese menu of rice bowls. Granted, people don’t usually crave Seattle teriyaki for its subtlety; add a dose of the house chili oil for texture and kick. Fremont Bowl is a kiosk-driven take-out machine, but the dine-in vibes are friendly, provided you can find a free table.

Ask a local about their favorite teriyaki shop, and chances are high it’s this been-there-forever counter next to a laundromat not far from Lake Union’s north end—not to be confused with other very similarly named Seattle teriyaki practitioners, including one on this list. A high ratio of dark soy makes for a standout sauce, while the thin mayo-based salad dressing plays well against the crispness of the fresh iceberg lettuce. The kitchen even uses an old-school mold to press rice into a pleasing half-football shape. Many teriyaki shops also have chicken katsu and egg rolls on the menu, but the versions here are standouts for their nongreasy crispy exteriors. The tables are mostly waiting zones for people ordering takeout, destined for a lunch in Gas Works Park, the nearby brewery taprooms, or just back to the surrounding tech offices. Come hungry: Portions are huge, even by generous teriyaki shop standards.

Nikko is busy most of the day, feeding a bustling lunch rush, teenagers after school, and evening take-out crowds. That turnover means teriyaki that’s always fresh, swiped with sauce that’s more soy than sugar and thick without verging on gummy. Jong Kwon and his family have run this West Seattle staple with warmth for more than two decades. Step inside the narrow shop and you’re transported back to Seattle’s era of peak teriyaki, a simpler time when one ordered off pictures on the wall rather than QR codes and the cashier remembered your name.

Clamshell take-out containers are so inherent to the teriyaki experience that nobody asks if you want your food to go, they generally just assume you do. But visit this Georgetown favorite (no relation to I Love Teriyaki) and you’ll witness a rare sight: Diners eating off actual plates. After a three-year closure following a fire, owners Don and Eva Lo rebuilt the original building (once a KFC) into a shiny new space. Aromas of grilled meat hit you from the parking lot, and the cheerful dining room is usually full. Skip the newish teriyaki burritos, and run, don’t walk, to the short ribs teriyaki, so smoky and tender that you might almost be tempted to bypass the chicken altogether. Almost.

#6615. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

In a set of problem-solving experiments, researchers found that people who used AI to get answers were more likely to give up and fail when that help was removed, compared with people who did not use AI.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

People who rely on artificial intelligence (AI) to solve simple problems do worse at, and are more likely to give up on, similar tasks when that assistance is removed, compared with people who do not use AI for quick answers, new research finds.

The study, which was presented at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco earlier this month, investigated the impacts of shifting mental work onto an AI chatbot across arithmetic and reading comprehension tasks. A growing body of research suggests this process of "cognitive offloading" harms long-term learning and critical thinking abilities.

"The concern is about what cognitive scientists call 'desirable difficulties' — the productive struggle that builds skill over time," study first author Grace Liu, a doctoral student in machine learning at Carnegie Mellon University, told Live Science in an email. "If AI routinely removes that struggle, people may get the right answer in the moment but develop less robust independent capability."

Liu and her colleagues recruited 1,222 participants for the study, which was released as a preprint earlier this year and has now undergone peer review. The researchers designed three randomized controlled experiments, including two sets of mathematical fraction problems and a series of reading comprehension questions. The participants were split into three groups, so there was no overlap between the experiments. Each experiment took 13 to 15 minutes to complete.

In the first experiment, the team randomly assigned 354 participants to two groups: one that had access to an AI chatbot and one that didn't. The researchers gave both groups the same 12 fraction problems, which the AI group could get the answer to immediately or obtain clues about by prompting the chatbot. Then, the researchers removed the AI assistant without warning for a final set of three fractions, which all of the participants were given, regardless of their group.

Both groups had the option to skip problems. The researchers explicitly told the participants that there was no penalty for wrong answers, so skipping a problem was a deliberate decision to not engage with it, they wrote in the study. The participants in both groups were also given the correct answer to each problem if they got it wrong, so they could learn from their mistakes.

This first experiment showed that the participants in the AI group were more likely to solve fractions and less likely to give up when they had access to the chatbot compared with the other group. But when the AI was removed, their performance dropped and they skipped or failed more problems, suggesting that using AI impaired unassisted task performance, persistence and motivation.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The second experiment was a copy of the first experiment, but it had 667 participants and small tweaks in the trial design, including the addition of a pretest phase that helped the researchers eliminate participants who were unable to solve the most basic problems. The findings were similar to those of the first experiment, hinting that the use of AI for simple tasks harms perseverance and drive to complete those same tasks without AI, especially when AI is used to get direct solutions.

Liu acknowledged that calculators also allow people to offload computations, which could cause similar declines in independent performance. But "the reason we study AI specifically is that it allows people to offload reasoning across tasks across many domains," she said.

Calculators allow people to offload math problems, but their effects on reasoning aren't as far-reaching as the effects of AI.

In a third experiment, the team explored the impacts of AI assistance on reading comprehension, which draws on meaning-making skills and mental-model construction — the cognitive process of building internal representations of external reality. The trial included 201 participants, who were divided into a group with access to AI and a control group. The researchers gave both groups five comprehension questions before disabling the AI chatbot and handing each participant another three questions.

The results mirrored those of the first two experiments, suggesting that reduced persistence, in particular, was not an artifact of the math problems but a general outcome of cognitive offloading onto AI.

"The most significant finding is that people who offload more have higher declines in persistence (increased skip rate), which is an important skill that cuts across domains," Liu said.

One possible reason people stop trying once they have experienced help from AI is that they get used to the immediacy of answers and perceive any method that takes longer as inefficient, the researchers wrote in the study. But studies show that persistence through difficulty is essential for skill acquisition and learning, raising concerns about the long-term impacts of using AI for simple tasks.

Scientists don't yet have a full picture of how small instances of cognitive offloading affect lasting competence and independent ability. To find out, researchers would need to track the same people for a long time and regularly measure their learning outcomes across a wide range of tasks, Liu said. But research so far suggests that an overreliance on AI erodes our cognitive fitness and mastery of subjects, according to the study.

To encourage long-term learning, capability and autonomy in people, AI models and chatbots should be designed to give directions and instructions toward a solution, rather than the solution itself — more like a tutor, the researchers argued.

"We need to work toward a future in which human abilities are, as much as possible, augmented rather than supplanted," study co-author Brian Christian, a computer scientist and researcher in the Center for Human-Compatible AI at the University of California, Berkeley, said in a statement.

Liu, G., Christian, B., Dumbalska, T., Bakker, M. A. and Dubey, R. (2026). AI assistance reduces persistence and hurts independent performance. Proceedings of the Conference on Language Modeling (COLM); arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.04721 [cs.AI].

Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

#6606. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

The stunningly detailed gold cape is unique in Europe and may have belonged to a high-ranking woman.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The gold accessory was found in a Bronze Age grave near the town of Mold in Wales.

Where it is from: Bryn yr Ellyllon (Goblins' Hill), Wales

When it was made: Circa 1900 to 1600 B.C.

In 1833, stone quarry workers discovered an ancient burial mound at Goblins' Hill near the town of Mold in Wales. At the center was a stone-lined grave that contained a fragmented skeleton and a gold, cape-like accessory that had been crushed over time. The Mold gold cape has a unique shape and style, and it is one of the finest examples of prehistoric goldwork ever found, according to the British Museum, where the artifact is on display.

The cape dates to Britain's Early Bronze Age (2500 to 1200 B.C.), a time that saw a metalworking revolution as artisans shifted from crafting flint tools to making weapons and jewelry out of gold, copper and bronze.

When the cape was originally unearthed, experts assumed that it had belonged to an ancient warrior, chief or religious leader, due to the spectacular design of the object, Benjamin Roberts, then curator for the European Bronze Age collections at the British Museum, told the BBC in 2010. But after the broken pieces of the cape were put back together, the small size of the artifact suggested it may have been worn by a woman or a child.

The Mold gold cape measures roughly 9.3 inches (23.5 centimeters) tall and 18.3 inches (46.5 cm) wide. It weighs about 1.2 pounds (560 grams) and was probably crafted from a single lump of gold about the size of a ping-pong ball.

The gold ingot was beaten incredibly thin, fashioned into a cape, and then embellished with decorations that mimicked beads or necklaces, according to the British Museum. Additionally, several hundred amber beads were found on the cape in the grave, which likely added to the gilded appearance of the accessory. Perforations around the neck opening suggest the cape originally had a lining made of leather or another perishable material that did not survive.

Because the gold cape, when worn, would restrict a person's upper arm movements, it may have been a ceremonial accessory that conferred religious authority and was worn only on special occasions. But experts are still unsure why the cape was buried in a grave. Nor can they confirm whether the person it was interred with was male or female, as the skeleton was not recovered by the quarry workers in the 19th century.

"The cape is unique — there is really nothing to compare it to in the whole of Europe," Roberts told the BBC. "This makes it more difficult to understand why it was made and what significance it had."

#6603. 12 Of Your Favorite Foods That Were Invented By Accident

Sometimes the best things happen when everything goes wrong.

Here at Delish, we’re no strangers to a tasty creation. From our viral Marry Me Chicken to our delectable Dubai Chocolate Brownies, our talented food editors are always experimenting in the kitchen to come up with your next great dish. But not every beloved food comes from hard work and endless testing. Some of our favorites actually owe their existence to happy accidents. Here are 12 foods that we have pure dumb luck to thank for.

Named after the English county where it originated, Worcestershire sauce is the accidental brainchild of John Wheeley Lea and William Henry Perrins. In 1835, a nobleman tasked the two chemists with creating a sauce from a recipe he had brought back from Asia. The duo worked on the sauce, but their client was unenthused, so they stored it in a cellar to languish. Over a year later, they found and tried it again, noting that the aging process made it taste delicious. Two years later, they were selling it.

While ice cream cones are a staple in any ice cream shop today, they weren't always. At the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, a concessionaire named Ernest A. Hamwi sold a Middle Eastern pastry called zalabis, or zalabiyeh. Next to him, an ice cream vendor ran out of serving dishes and, thinking on his feet, Hamwi rolled up his waffle-like pastry into a cone so his neighbor could keep serving ice cream. The result? Clearly a success.

That said, Hamwi isn’t the only man credited with the ice cream cone. Just one year prior, Italo Marchiony received a patent in New York City for a mold used to make edible ice cream cups. Hamwi, however, brought them mass recognition.

While the inventor and origins of the potato chip are contested, one of the most popular stories credits a happy accident at Moon’s Lake House in Saratoga Springs, New York. A very particular customer sent back their order of fried potatoes, asking for thinner slices. Annoyed, the chef (often credited as George Crum) sliced them as thin as he could and fried them extra long—as it turned out, the customer loved them. And now we have our beloved potato chips.

Yogurt has been around for millennia, dating back to around 5,000 B.C. Many accounts credit its discovery to an accident: Milk stored in bags in warm weather was exposed to bacteria, causing it to ferment into yogurt. As it turned out, yogurt became a great way to preserve milk.

If you’ve ever been the victim of killer brain freeze due to chugging a Slurpee, this one’s for you. A man named Omar Knedlik is credited with inventing the drink after a soda fountain broke in his store. He put soda in the freezer to keep it cold, accidentally creating slushy drinks that customers loved. He later used parts from a car air conditioner to build a machine that could recreate the frozen beverages. He named the product ICEE, which 7-Eleven eventually licensed and began selling under a different name exclusively at its stores. And that’s how we got our Slurpee.

Nashville hot chicken has one of the best origin stories of any food. In the 1930s, a man named Thornton Prince was known as quite the ladies’ man. One of the women he was seeing decided to seek revenge after Prince had been out all night. For payback, she loaded his favorite fried chicken recipe with every spicy ingredient she could find in her kitchen. Lo and behold, her plan backfired, as Prince loved the result. He went on to open a fried chicken shop with his brothers, and the rest is history.

You have a forgetful 11-year-old to thank for Popsicles. Back in 1905, Frank Epperson accidentally left a glass of water with powdered soda mix and a stirring stick outside overnight. Come morning, the mixture was frozen, but he popped it out of the glass and enjoyed his creation. He began making these ice pops for his friends, and in 1924, he filed a patent. Up until then, he was calling them Eppsicles, but his children changed the name to Pop’s ‘sicles, and the name stuck.

We have a sanitarium to thank for our favorite breakfast cereal, if you can believe it. Dr. John Harvey Kellogg worked alongside his brother Will at Battle Creek Sanitarium, where he accidentally created what is now known as corn flakes. Kellogg was trying to make a wheat-based dough for his patients. After leaving the dough out overnight by accident, he put it through rollers and found that it produced thin flakes, which the patients ended up loving. He later substituted corn and added sugar to commercialize the product.

Raisins date all the way back to around 2000 B.C. Historians believe ancient Persians and Egyptians discovered grapes that had dried on the vine and realized they could eat them. Wall paintings from that time period show dried fruit being both eaten and used as decor.

While the exact origins of pink lemonade are contested, two popular theories trace its creation back to the circus. In the first story, a teenage circus worker invented the drink after accidentally dropping red cinnamon candies into a vat of lemonade. Rather than toss the batch, he went with the flow and sold the now-pink lemonade.

The other story is a bit more off-putting. One circus worker reportedly ran out of water for the lemonade and used a bucket of dirty water that a performer had just used to wash her pink tights instead. He then sold the resulting beverage as pink lemonade. I really hope the first story is the accurate one.

It’s hard to believe that cheese puffs were initially created for animals, not humans. Animal food manufacturer Flakall Corporation created the cheesy snack we love today in 1935. To make animal feed, the company used a machine that ground corn. During the cleaning process, introducing moist corn into the machine produced airy corn puffs. An employee brought some home and experimented with seasoning them to create a product for humans.

The result was called Korn Kurls, and the company began producing them. The snack became so successful that the company changed its name to help distance itself from its humble beginnings in animal feed.

Now a beloved staple on many a Tex-Mex menu, the chimichanga is younger than you might think. The most common legend credits El Charro Café founder Monica Flin with inventing the fried dish. Apparently, she accidentally dropped a burrito into a deep fryer and started swearing at the mistake. Because children were present, she quickly switched gears and shouted “chimichanga”—which translates to “thingamajig”—instead. The rest, as they say, is history.

#6600. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6598. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

Archaeologists have uncovered the 1,500-year-old burial of an elite toddler from the Moche culture in Peru.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The child was buried alongside two ceramic objects depicting defeated warriors about to be sacrificed.

Archaeologists in Peru have found an elaborate 1,500-year-old tomb that may hold the remains of a high-status toddler from a pre-Inca civilization.

The burial, which is from the Moche culture, also contained vessels depicting prisoners with rope around each of their necks and a sculpture of a human-bird deity.

Moche (also known as Mochica) culture developed along the northern coast of what is now Peru from the third to the ninth century. They created agricultural lands in the region's desert landscape, and their archaeological record includes monumental temples, water canals, pottery, metallurgy, textiles and a distinctive form of art. The Moche didn't have a written language, but they left behind thousands of realistic portrait vessels, which are somewhat similar to the prisoner sculptors found in the toddler's burial.

In the newfound tomb, the team unearthed a small skeleton, which is likely the remains of a toddler who was, at most, 2 years old, Carlos Rengifo-Chunga, director of the University of Trujillo's Huacas de Moche Archaeological Project, told Live Science. The child's sex is unknown.

The child was buried alongside 32 ceramic objects associated with Moche culture.

Rengifo-Chunga and his colleagues also found two copper objects in the burial: a mask-like disk covering the child's face, and a half-moon object on their feet. In addition, the burial contained 32 ceramic objects associated with Moche culture, including those depicting the prisoners and the deity.

The tomb was large compared to the child's small size, and could have easily held an adult, Rengifo-Chunga said. It dates to the sixth or seventh century, he added.

The team unearthed the tomb inside the Uhle Platform at the Huacas de Moche archaeological site in northern Peru. The Uhle Platform is a mausoleum, attached to the Huaca de la Luna temple, with a patio archaeologists call the Patio of the Serpents. Of the more than 80 burials previously uncovered there, the tomb represents the only known child to receive this sort of lavish burial.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The elaborate funerary treatment, including the use of copper, and the location of the tomb all suggest that the child belonged to an elite class of Moche society, Rengifo-Chunga said.

The two prisoner sculptures are associated with the "ritual of combat," a common theme in Moche art. In this sort of imagery, two warriors fight each other, and the loser is stripped of his clothes and weapons, tied around the neck with a rope and offered as a human sacrifice, Rengifo-Chunga said. The prisoners depicted on these two vessels were the losing warriors, and their presence in the burial of a child is rare.

"One would normally presume that these kinds of vessels represent something related to the deceased's life," Rengifo-Chunga said. For example, a vessel like this might signify that the individual took part in combat.

One of the ceramic objects depicts a presumed deity with human and bird features.

An archaeological team discovered a likely elite child burial at the Huacas de Moche archaeological site in Peru.

One of the two ceramics depicting prisoners that archaeologists found in the toddler's burial.

But a toddler couldn't have taken part in such an activity. In general, archaeologists wouldn't expect to see elements of an adult ritual in the burial of a child. "This expands our knowledge on Moche funerary practices," he added.

The sculpture of the presumed deity depicts a human body with bird wings and a bird tail, although for some scholars it might be interpreted as a god in transformation, Rengifo-Chunga said. The deity holds a square shield in one hand and a goblet in the other, and is flanked by two bird "assistants" wearing ceremonial garments.

Researchers will have to investigate whether the deity is a known Moche god, or a newfound addition to the pantheon. Either way, the object joins a contentious debate over whether the Moche pantheon consists of many gods, or just a few that can transform into many different versions, Rengifo-Chunga said.

The artifacts are now in the laboratories of the Santiago Uceda Castillo Museum in Peru, where they will undergo conservation treatment.

How much do you know about the first people to reach the Americas? Find out with our First Americans quiz.

Margherita is a trilingual freelance writer specializing in science and history writing with a particular interest in archaeology, palaeontology, astronomy and human behavior. She earned her BA from Boston College in English literature, ancient history and French, and her journalism MA from L'École Du Journalisme de Nice in International New Media Journalism. #6594. Carne Guisada

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

With its warm spices and a rich gravy, this slow-braised carne guisada is perfect in tacos or on a bed of rice.

Carne guisada, a classic Mexican beef stew whose name translates to “stewed meat,” has a rich culinary backstory. Its roots stretch across northern Mexico and into Texas, where slow-braised beef dishes are a staple of home kitchens, taquerias and Tex-Mex restaurants alike. Tender beef simmers in a chili-based sauce, then is often served as a taco filling with soft flour tortillas. Some versions (especially in Texas) include potatoes to make it a one-pot meal. Others focus solely on the fall-apart meat and the smooth, peppery sauce built from dried chiles. You win either way.

For our carne guisada recipe, we keep the signature slow-cooked, deeply seasoned beef and rich gravy, but say yes to the potatoes for extra body and comfort. The use of beer, Worcestershire sauce and tomato paste brings layered depth that complements the traditional spices like cumin and chili powder. We aren’t claiming this is the only version because, honestly, that doesn’t exist. But this dish absolutely captures the spirit of classic carne guisada: tender meat, bold flavor and something meant to be shared.

In a large bowl, toss the beef with 1/4 teaspoon of salt. In a separate large bowl, combine the flour and paprika. Add the beef to the flour a few pieces at a time, tossing to coat them.

In a Dutch oven, heat the oil over medium heat. Brown the beef in batches, adding additional oil as necessary. Remove the pieces with a slotted spoon.

Editor’s Tip: Those browned bits stuck to the bottom of the pot are called fond, and they’re flavor gold. Don’t even think about washing them away.

To the same pan, add the onion. Cook and stir until it’s tender, three to five minutes. Stir in the tomato, jalapeno and garlic, and cook until they’re fragrant and the color starts to darken slightly.

Add the browned beef back to the pan. Add the beer, and bring it to a boil, scraping the bottom to release the browned bits. Simmer until the liquid is reduced by half, about five minutes.

Stir in the broth, Worcestershire sauce, crushed red pepper flakes, chili powder, cumin, bay leaf and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt, and bring the mixture to a boil. Reduce the heat, then cover the pot and simmer the stew until the meat is almost tender, about 1 hour and 30 minutes.

Add the potatoes and red wine vinegar. Cover the pot and simmer the stew until the meat and vegetables are tender, about 30 minutes longer.

Discard the bay leaf. Using the back of a spoon or ladle, slightly mash the potatoes. If desired, shred the beef slightly with two forks. Serve with tortillas, rice, lime and cilantro.

Let the carne guisada cool completely before transferring it to an airtight container. Store it in the refrigerator, where the flavors will actually deepen and improve overnight. It’s one of those dishes that might taste even better the next day. Carne guisada lasts up to four days in the refrigerator.

Carne guisada freezes very well. Store it in freezer-safe containers for up to three months, and thaw it overnight in the refrigerator before reheating.

Reheat carne guisada gently on the stovetop over medium-low heat until it’s warmed through. Add a splash of broth if the sauce has thickened too much.

You can use beef shoulder, bottom round or beef stew meat for carne guisada. The key is choosing a tougher cut with connective tissue that breaks down during the long, slow cooking time. This gives you that tender, fall-apart texture.

Whether you serve carne guisada on tortillas or rice, it also pairs beautifully with black beans, fresh salsa or even a side of warm cornbread.
