#6593. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6592. I Tried the New Bentgo Lift Water Bottle—And the Ring Handle Makes It So Easy to Stay Hydrated

The new Bentgo water bottle is easy to use, carry and clean, plus it comes in gorgeous, candy-colored hues.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

For someone who works and works out at home, I’ve amassed quite the collection of reusable water bottles. Maintaining the healthy habit of drinking more water is always my excuse for adding yet another to the mix. After all, the cuter the water bottle, the more likely I am to reach for it and take a swig.

So when I saw the new Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle, I knew I had to try it. As much as I love my Stanley Flowstate, I like to ditch the straw every so often, even if it does save me from dousing myself every time I go in for a sip. But with the Bentgo’s unique lid and leakproof design, I had high expectations that this strawless bottle would become a regular in my hydration rotation. And it has! Here’s why I’m toting around the new Bentgo Lift water bottle like it’s my favorite purse.

The major draw of the Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle is the soft-grip ring handle that’s attached to the lid. It does double the work by keeping the flip top securely closed and offering a comfortable way to tote it around. My major gripe with other water bottles has always been that their handles and/or straws make them unwieldy for carrying and commuting. But not the Bentgo. Just lift the handle and carry it like a bag. I’ve even hung it from the handle of my Peloton Bike during a ride!

It did take me a moment to get used to drinking from the bottle, only because it’s different from others I’ve had. But all you have to do is lift the ring handle and push the little lever with your thumb to pop open the cap (you could also wedge your thumb in under the handle to hit the button so it lifts the cap and the handle at the same time, but I found it easier to open the handle first). I like that the handle folds flat against the bottle so everything stays compact. The mouth is wide enough to comfortably drink from, although I do turn the bottle so that my nose doesn’t bump the edge of the ring handle.

At first I thought the smooth cylindrical shape of the bottle might be a problem because, other than the handle, there is nothing to grip the bottle when you’re actually drinking. But the powder-coated exterior offers plenty of grip so it won’t slip in your hand.

The lid twists off easily from the wide-mouth bottle, which makes it easy to fill with liquid and ice. It also makes it very easy to clean. The Bentgo is top-rack dishwasher friendly, although the manufacturer does recommend handwashing to protect the exterior. I’ve definitely popped the lid in the dishwasher several times already but I’ve been handwashing the bottle itself, at least for now.

The Bentgo Lift Chug Lid Bottle is available in 24-, 32- and 40-ounce sizes in a host of colors. I chose both the 24-ounce in Bubblegum and the 32-ounce in Denim, but soon found myself gravitating toward the more petite 24-ounce bottle. It wasn’t only because of the candy hue—I just prefer a smaller bottle!

With all this talk about design and color, you’re probably wondering: Does it even keep your water cold? Yes, it sure does. The Bentgo Lift water bottle features a stainless steel interior with triple-layer insulation (BPA-free with no PFAs) that keeps liquids cold for up to 24 hours. And yes, I can confirm this to be true: I left ice water in a bottle on my desk after the work day and came back the next morning to surprisingly cold water!

You can purchase the Bentgo Lift Chug Lid Water Bottle right on the brand’s website, as well as on Walmart and Amazon. It comes in 24-, 32- and 40-ounce sizes, which cost $29.99, $34.99 and $39.99, respectively. The two smaller sizes come in six colors: Bubblegum, Denim, Latte, Blanc, Back to Black and Amalfi Coast. The 40-ounce is currently available only in Blanc and Back to Black. These will make great gifts for the holidays, so shop soon for the best size and color availability!

While rare, colorectal cancer is becoming more common in kids, teens and young adults, and the disease appears particularly aggressive in this age group.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More children, teens and very young adults are being diagnosed with colorectal cancer in the United States, and new research suggests they often experience aggressive forms of the disease.

While diagnosis rates are rising, the disease is still rare among young people. Colorectal cancer, which affects the lower intestines and rectum, is largely a disease of age: 55% of all colorectal cancers are diagnosed in people over 65, and only 16% occur in people ages 49 or younger, according to a 2026 study published in the flagship journal of the American Cancer Society. Only a few hundred cases per year are diagnosed in people under age 21 in the U.S.

Nevertheless, the numbers of cases in the very young are rising, even as colorectal cancer rates decline or hold steady in older individuals. This increase coincides with an overall rise in colon and rectal cancer rates in people under 50.

The reasons for this schism aren't entirely understood. People over 50 receive routine colonoscopies in which precancerous polyps are removed, and that likely accounts for much of the decline in colorectal cancer diagnoses in older adults. But researchers suspect that environmental factors, such as ultraprocessed foods and sedentary lifestyles, might be behind the growing rates in young people.

Scientists are looking to the gut microbiome for clues about why colorectal cancer is on the rise in young people.

"Most of the research has really focused on the gut microbiome," the community of bacteria and other microbes that live in the gut, said Dr. Christopher Lieu, a professor of medical oncology at the University of Colorado Anschutz and a medical adviser to the nonprofit Colorectal Cancer Alliance.

Microbiome disruptions may spur inflammation, which, in turn, may trigger DNA mutations that cause cancer. But these mechanisms are complicated, Lieu told Live Science, and there likely isn't one simple reason young people's microbiomes may be getting disturbed.

"It's going to be extraordinarily more complex than that," he said.

What researchers are starting to learn is that colorectal cancer in people in their early 20s or younger tends to be a more aggressive disease than that often seen in older people.

"We do feel like it is a bit of a distinct disease than what we're seeing in older adults," said Dr. Erica Arnold, a pediatric surgery research fellow at Nationwide Children's Hospital in Columbus, Ohio. In October, Arnold presented new research on colorectal cancer in people ages 21 or younger at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Arnold and her colleagues analyzed the cases of 84 patients diagnosed between 2012 and 2023. They found that the median age of diagnosis was 16 years old and the median duration of symptoms before diagnosis was only 12 weeks long.

Only about 20% of the patients had a close relative with colorectal cancer, suggesting that for many of these young people, the disease did not necessarily emerge due to hereditary factors.

If you want my honest opinion, it does suggest that these cancers are developing differently.

Eighty percent of the study participants were diagnosed with Stage III or Stage IV disease, meaning the cancer had already spread locally and to lymph nodes or to other, distant organs when the patients were diagnosed. For comparison, in colorectal cancer patients of all ages, 60% are diagnosed in Stage III or IV, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In addition, Arnold said, one-third of the patients in their study had cellular markers of particularly aggressive cancer.

"Some of that might be related to delays in diagnosis," Lieu said, "but if you want my honest opinion, it does suggest that these cancers are developing differently."

The study's data was not nationally representative, but a recent analysis of CDC data has also found that colorectal cancer rates in youth are on the rise. In 1999, the diagnosis rate in kids ages 10 to 14 was 1 in a million. By 2020, it had risen to 6 in a million. For teens between 15 and 19, the rate of diagnosis went from 3 in a million to 13 in a million in that same time frame.

There is no definitive reason for this rise, Lieu said. Research on the microbiome has suggested that processed food, antibiotic exposure in childhood, stress, reduced exercise and other lifestyle factors may contribute to this increased risk of colorectal cancer.

Some microbes may play a particularly strong role, at least in some cases of colorectal cancer. For instance, a specific variant of the common gut bacterium Escherichia coli is strongly associated with colorectal cancer; the variant carries a genetic segment and produces compounds that are toxic to genes. But this variant alone cannot explain all colorectal cancer cases in young people. Nor is it clear why the gut microbiome might be undergoing a shift in the first place.

"It may be a combination of food, antibiotic use and environmental exposures," Lieu suggested.

Regardless of the exact causes behind the cases, Arnold's new research pointed to the symptoms that deserve closer scrutiny in young people. Among the 84 patients in the study, 75% reported experiencing back and abdominal pain before their diagnosis, 45% had changes in their bowel movements, 43% experienced unexplained weight loss and 38% had rectal bleeding.

These are classic colorectal cancer symptoms, Arnold said, but they might be overlooked in this young age group because these same symptoms can have more common causes.

Parents should know that in most cases, stomach pain and gastrointestinal disruptions in kids are not caused by colorectal cancer, Lieu said, calling the cancer an "extraordinarily rare event." Nevertheless, pain or gastrointestinal upset that doesn't ease or that worsens over time needs a checkup, and symptoms like weight loss and blood in the stool are very unusual in kids and deserve extra attention.

"It's just important to investigate it to make sure we're catching colorectal cancer earlier rather than later in these patients," Arnold said.

#6590. Paul Hollywood Once Had A Very Different Look & Bake Off Fans Know Exactly Who He Resembles

Turns out the man behind the Hollywood handshake has quite the origin story.

If you know Paul Hollywood from The Great British Bake Off, you know the routine: a steely blue-eyed stare, a brutally honest critique, and, if you're lucky, one of those coveted Hollywood handshakes. But the man who's been judging everybody else's baking since 2010 nearly ended up in an entirely different creative field—and he had a whole lot more hair while figuring it out.

In an Instagram video posted on October 25, Hollywood revealed how he went from aspiring artist to professional baker, a career change that apparently came down to a £500 haircut.

After leaving school at 16, Hollywood enrolled in art school, where he tried everything from pottery and photography to textiles, fine art, and sculpture. He eventually settled on the latter, and by all accounts, was having a pretty great time. Then his father, who owned several bakeries, came along with a different career proposal.

Hollywood wasn't exactly eager to leave art school behind as he was enjoying life there all while sporting a glorious head of long hair. So his dad sweetened the deal by offering him a hefty chunk of change to chop it all off and join the family business.

Apparently, that was enough to get the scissors moving. Hollywood shaved his head, traded sculpture for sourdough, and started learning the ropes.

He said he took to baking surprisingly quickly, even embracing the rather brutal hours. Hollywood recalled getting up at 1 or 2 a.m. six days a week, with Friday shifts sometimes starting at 11 p.m.

From there, he went on to work at major hotels across the U.K., eventually took his talents abroad, and found himself on television. As Hollywood put it, "The rest is history."

But the most entertaining part of this story arrived the following day, when Hollywood posted photographic evidence of the hair that’d been worth £500.

"Pictures mid long hair obviously with cat too !!" he captioned the throwback, which shows a much younger Hollywood holding a fluffy cat while sporting shoulder-length dark hair. It's quite a departure from the neatly cropped silver look we've come to know, and somehow, the cat isn't even the most talked-about part of the picture.

That's because fans immediately noticed a striking resemblance to someone else in the Bake Off tent: co-host Noel Fielding.

"Looking like Noel here Mr H!" one person commented. "Thought this was Noel for a second 😆," another admitted, while a third agreed, "this could easily be Noel."

Hollywood wasn't about to let the comparisons go unanswered, either. "Agree, I’m older so he was channeling me!" he joked in response.

Now I'd like Noel to dig up a photo of himself with short hair. It seems only fair.

#6589. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6588. ‘The Gilded Age’ Is Back! Here’s What to Eat While You Watch the Show

The good china is coming out, but the sweatpants are staying on. The Gilded Age season four is back on Nov. 1, and this is everything I'm eating for the series return.

I can be persuaded to watch almost anything that promises extravagant set designs and beautiful costumes. If there’s history and a little mischievous social maneuvering involved, even better. My coworkers recently recommended The Gilded Age, and within two weeks, I’d watched all three seasons just in time for season four to drop.

There’s plenty to admire: Bertha Russell’s determination, Peggy Scott’s writing career and rooms furnished with a reassuring disregard for minimalism. I love the history, too, from the railroad fortunes and New York bankers to Lewis Latimer’s work in electric lighting and the woman who helped bring the Brooklyn Bridge to completion. Every episode gave me another reason to keep watching.

My husband is often still at the restaurant in the evenings, so once the kids are asleep, I have a few hours to settle in with a show. While I watched The Gilded Age, I usually poured a glass of wine (some of my favorites are under $25 at Walmart) and enjoyed the fire as Christine Baranski made an art of Agnes’s disapproval. But with the new season arriving on Nov. 1, I’m borrowing a few ideas from the show to make a watch party spread.

I have a decidedly romantic streak when it comes to my surroundings, so the show’s interiors have my full attention. I’m particularly taken with the glassware and china that can make even a small supper feel indulgent. With a few soft lamps and the fire going, I’m looking forward to borrowing a little of that grandeur for my own evening.

Dan Roberts for Taste of Home, Courtesy Barbra Nitke/ Courtesy Hbo

I’m more than happy to borrow the show’s habit of pouring wine into crystal glasses. Mine usually contains Champagne, but Ada’s season-three temperance campaign gives us a reason to put some thought into an alcohol-free option too.

Agnes’s feelings about wine appear to be settled, but there’s room for both sisters.

Jonathan Melendez for taste of Home, Courtesy Barbra Nitke/ Courtesy Hbo

The Russells may require a meticulously planned succession of courses, but I’d be content with a small selection of savory bites. Oysters, warm crab dip or little sandwiches would make a perfectly elegant dinner by the fire.

Mark Derse for Taste of Home, Courtesy Alison Cohen Rosa/ Courtesy Hbo

For something more substantial, you can look to the show’s luncheons as much as its elaborate dinner parties. A bowl of soup or a sandwich can feel quite grand when the ingredients are good and someone else is responsible for the evening’s drama.

Dan Roberts for taste of Home, Courtesy Karolina Wojtasik/ Courtesy Hbo

A pot of tea and something sweet would be enough for me on an evening when dinner is already behind us. I like having dessert ready before I sit down, whether that means a trifle waiting in the fridge or a few pastries brought home in a paper bag.

#6587. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6586. French Onion Stuffing

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin

This recipe for French onion stuffing takes caramelized onions, beef broth and Gruyere, and transforms them into a holiday-ready side dish.

Every year at Thanksgiving, I consider filling my plate with all the sides and foregoing the turkey altogether. (That’s what I did during my decade as a vegetarian—and I did not miss the meat.) Give me all the cranberry sauce, green bean casserole and mashed potatoes. But my absolute favorite Thanksgiving side dish is the stuffing. Since my vegetarian days, I’ve preferred the stuffing cooked outside the bird. Not only does this prevent common food-safety issues, it also ensures the stuffing cooks evenly and crisps up on top. Although I’m partial to my mom’s (a classic stuffing with celery, onions and day-old bread), I also like to experiment with new recipes and flavor combinations.

This recipe for French onion stuffing is a real crowd-pleaser. It takes the ingredients of classic French onion soup—caramelized onions, beef broth and Gruyere cheese—and transforms them into a savory stuffing recipe. The most important ingredient you need for this recipe is patience. Caramelization is a process that cannot be rushed, but the results are oh-so worth it. The sweet-savory onions truly take this stuffing recipe to the next level. Just like in a bowl of French onion soup, a generous amount of grated Gruyere cheese melted over top ensures each bite is mix of sweet and savory flavors.

Preheat the oven to 350°F. Spread the bread cubes in an even layer on two baking sheets. Bake them for 10 minutes, then flip the cubes and rotate the baking sheets. Bake them until they’re very dry and golden brown, about five to eight minutes. Remove from the oven and set aside to cool.

Meanwhile, in a Dutch oven, heat the butter and olive oil over medium heat. Add the onions, and cook them until they’re softened, 10 to 15 minutes, stirring frequently. Stir in the salt and pepper. Reduce the heat to medium-low, and cook the onions until they’re deep golden brown, 40 to 50 minutes, stirring occasionally. Add the garlic, and cook until it’s fragrant, 30 to 60 seconds. Add the dry sherry, and use a wooden spoon to scrape up any browned bits. Stir in the thyme. Remove the pan from the heat.

In a large bowl, whisk the eggs until they’re smooth. Stir in the cooked onions and bread cubes. Stir in the beef broth until the bread is evenly moistened.

Editor’s Tip: The stuffing should be moist but not soggy. If the mixture seems too dry, add more broth in 1/4-cup increments until evenly moistened.

Spoon the stuffing into a greased 13×9-inch or 3-quart baking dish. Cover it with foil, and bake the stuffing for 30 minutes. Uncover the dish, and bake the stuffing until it’s crispy and browned, 15 to 20 minutes.

Remove the stuffing from the oven, and increase the oven temperature to 425°. Sprinkle the cheese on top. Bake the stuffing until the cheese is melted and bubbly, three to five minutes. Garnish the stuffing with thyme before serving it.

After allowing the French onion stuffing to cool completely, store any leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to four days.

Absolutely! Caramelizing the onions requires low and slow cooking, and the process can’t be rushed. If you don’t have the time or the space to dedicate to making this dish all at once, you can make the caramelized onions up to four days in advance.

After caramelizing the onions, allow them to come to room temperature, then store them in an airtight container the fridge until you’re ready to use them. You can also prep the entire stuffing in advance up to a day in advance. Follow the recipe until it’s ready to bake, then cover and refrigerate it. Allow it to sit at room temperature for about 30 minutes, then bake it as directed, adding an extra 5 to 10 minutes to the baking time.

Or, you could try something new and use the microwave to caramelize onions. Yes, we tested it and it works!

Stuffing actually freezes really well. Cut the stuffing into large squares and wrap in a layer of storage wrap followed by a layer of foil. Freeze the stuffing squares for up to one month.

While there is a way to safely bake stuffing inside a turkey, this stuffing recipe is not an ideal candidate. By cooking it in the bird, it won’t be able to crisp up like it does when cooked it separately in a casserole dish.

You can start out with fresh bread for this recipe, but you will need to dry out the bread cubes in the oven before using them. Doing so helps to ensure the bread will soak up all the flavors of the stuffing without getting too soggy.

This stuffing recipe is baked both covered and uncovered. Covering the dish tightly with foil traps in steam, locking in moisture and allowing the stuffing to cook through without over-crisping the top. Cooking it uncovered allows the top to crisp up to golden brown.

#6585. Chipotle's Smoked Brisket Is Making A Comeback—Here's When You Can Get It

It might be time to give your usual protein the day off.

Chipotle has been pretty generous with second chances this year, at least when it comes to its proteins. Chicken al Pastor made its comeback in January, followed by Chipotle Honey Chicken in April. And apparently, the chain isn't finished digging through its greatest hits just yet.

Starting November 5, Chipotle's Smoked Brisket is returning to restaurants across the U.S. and Canada for a limited time. And with football season in full swing, the timing couldn't be better for anyone whose game-day cooking plans begin and end with opening the Chipotle app.

"Bringing it back in the heart of football season gives fans one more reason to make Chipotle part of their game-day lineup," Stephanie Perdue, Chipotle's senior vice president of brand marketing, said in a statement.

But there's quite a bit more going on with this brisket than simply tossing another protein onto the menu.

Chipotle is pretty particular about the beef it buys. In fact, the chain estimates that only about 5 percent of the country's beef supply qualifies under its sourcing requirements. To make the cut, cattle must be raised on a vegetarian diet without added growth hormones or routine antibiotics, and Chipotle must be able to trace the beef back to the ranch it came from.

And the smoky part of Smoked Brisket isn't just a name. According to Chipotle, the meat spends hours over mesquite wood after being seasoned with a pepper-heavy spice blend featuring serrano and chipotle. The work continues in restaurants, where employees sear it on the plancha, add another round of seasoning and a chili-pepper sauce, and chop it into smaller portions throughout the day.

Chipotle's senior vice president of culinary, Nevielle Panthaky, says the preparation is designed to give the brisket its rich, smoky flavor while letting the sauce bring some tang and heat into the mix.

And if you're already mentally assembling your next burrito bowl, Panthaky has a recommendation. His ideal order starts with white rice, pinto beans, and Smoked Brisket, then adds fresh tomato salsa, a little tomatillo-red chili salsa, cheese, and Queso Blanco. According to Chipotle, the combination packs 45 grams of protein and 11 grams of fiber.

There's also a little incentive to stay firmly planted on the couch. From November 5 through November 18, Chipotle is offering $0 delivery fees on Smoked Brisket orders placed through its app or website in the U.S. and Canada.

As for how long the brisket will stick around, Chipotle hasn't announced an end date. So if you missed your chance during its last appearance, you might not want to put off this reunion for too long.

For the first time, researchers have identified a new type of landslide of permafrost in Canada's Northwest Territories.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's a new type of landslide affecting northern latitudes, and it could affect more areas as the planet continues to warm.

These landslides, called permafrost detachment slides, occur in areas with relatively thin permafrost and seem to be a long-term impact of wildfire in these environments, according to a paper published Sept. 23 in the journal Geophysical Research Letters. Such slides have not been observed in the region before and may be unprecedented over the past 10,000 years or more, said study leader Joseph Young, who completed the work as part of his doctoral degree at the University of Alberta.

"It has been stable, and then it just flipped a switch, essentially," Young told Live Science.

Young and his colleagues were doing field observations in Canada's Northwest Territories when they noticed large landslide scars in valleys that have long hosted stable permafrost, which is sediment that remains frozen year-round. They began using satellite imagery to map the changes and also conducted fieldwork, which revealed that the slides weren't standard melting permafrost.

"Typically with permafrost, everything just thaws and melts in a slurry and moves like a mud downslope," Young said. "But with these large landslides, we found blocks of frozen material in the debris."

Some of these blocks were 33 feet (10 meters) tall, the height of a two-story house. The researchers ran an electrical current through the ground to determine the depth of the permafrost on the slopes.

They focused on two slides. One, in the Johnson River Valley, took place in 2017 and moved more than 636 million cubic feet (18 million cubic meters) of soil and rock. The other, in the Redstone River Valley, moved almost 159 million cubic feet (4.5 million cubic meters) of debris in 2018. The smaller slide left a scar three-quarters of a mile (1.2 kilometers) long, while the larger one gouged nearly 2 miles (3.2 km) out of the hillside.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers then used the data they'd collected to build a model of how these icy slides occurred. The permafrost in this area has been warming by about 0.54 degrees Fahrenheit (0.3 degrees Celsius) per decade since 1980, when monitoring began, and there were also severe wildfires nearby in 1995.

The researchers found that instead of a top-down melting process by which the permafrost thawed to a muddy slurry from above, the slides were instead caused by a combination of fire-related thaw and warming temperatures, leading to cracks near the top of the slopes. These cracks allowed the thaw to penetrate deeper, eventually melting the bottom of the permafrost layer. This propagation can take 20 years to penetrate 66 feet (20 m), which is exactly what happened in the Johnson River and Redstone River valleys.

"We had a fire in '95 and then 20 years later, we start to get a lot of these widespread disturbances," Young said.

The two large slides the researchers studied are among more than 150 in the area, Young said. The others are smaller, but they still typically move over 35 million cubic feet (1 million cubic meters) of land apiece. Canada's Northwest Territories are remote, so the permafrost detachment slides have yet to damage any infrastructure. But the two in the study did dam rivers, creating brand-new lakes and rapidly dumping sediment into the waterways downstream, Young said.

There are many other places in Canada and Alaska where the permafrost is 66 to 130 feet (20 to 40 m) deep and thus vulnerable to the same type of slide. This is especially true given the increasing intensity of wildfire at northern latitudes, Young said.

"This is almost a potential glimpse into the future of what we might be able to expect in these areas with changing forest fire dynamics," he said.

Young, J. M., Van Der Sluijs, J., Kokelj, S. V., Gruber, S., Herring, T., Rudy, A. C. A., Alvarez, A., & Froese, D. (2026). Permafrost detachment slides: a distinct High‐Magnitude Permafrost mass wasting process. Geophysical Research Letters, 53(18). https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl124103

#6583. Cherry Peach Pie with Salted Pecan Streusel

Recipe by Molly Stephens, Oconomowoc, Wisconsin

This pie celebrates a road trip we took to explore our family's history. I paired southern peaches and pecans with tart Door County cherries to reflect who we are: Wisconsin Yankees with strong roots in Kentucky and Tennessee. I can't think of a better way to put my heritage on a plate. #6582. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6581. Serious Choking Reports Spark Nationwide Recall Of Once Upon A Farm Toddler Bars

The FDA is urging parents to stop serving the affected snacks immediately.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

If Once Upon a Farm's Tractor Wheels are part of your toddler's regular snack rotation, it's time to take them off the menu. The company announced a voluntary recall of its Organic Toddler Soft-Baked Bars on October 30 after receiving three customer complaints involving choking.

The FDA is also urging parents not to buy or serve the snacks, citing several reports involving children between 18 months and 2½ years old, some of whom couldn't breathe after eating them.

The agency explained why these incidents have been especially dangerous, saying that “when chewed, the product reportedly forms a dry, sticky mass that standard choking interventions—including back blows and the Heimlich maneuver—may fail to dislodge." Some of the reported cases were serious enough that emergency personnel had to step in, with children also requiring monitoring at hospitals.

The recall includes three flavors: Apple, Sweet Potato & Spinach, Strawberry, Pumpkin & Beet, and Banana, Pumpkin & Cauliflower. No package sizes, production batches, or expiration dates are excluded, and the bars have been sold nationwide, including online and at retailers like Costco, Target, and Walmart.

In a statement, Once Upon a Farm explained its decision to remove the snacks from sale.

"We acted out of an abundance of caution, in the best interest of our customers and our commitment to quality. We are working with the U.S. Food & Drug Administration (FDA) to make sure affected products are removed and families have the information they need."

The company also acknowledged the seriousness of what happened.

"We know that parents place their trust in us every time they buy one of our products. We fell short of that, and that is why we are taking these aggressive actions."

No other Once Upon a Farm products are included in the recall. The FDA is telling families to discard any Tractor Wheels they have at home, while the company says customers can return unopened packages to the store where they purchased them for a full refund.

#6579. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

A hypothetical particle could have briefly held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which could help explain how matter won out over antimatter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A neglected "ghost particle" may have dominated the universe right after the Big Bang ‪—‬ changing how the cosmos expanded in its first moments and reshaping the conditions under which matter won out over antimatter, a new study suggests. In other words, it may explain why anything exists at all.

The particle, a hypothetical "right-handed" neutrino, briefly could have held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which would have sped up cosmic expansion and delayed key particle interactions, the study proposes. The research was published Sept. 8 in the journal Physical Review Letters.

Neutrinos are ghostly particles that rarely interact with anything. A typical neutrino from the sun could pass through a slab of lead a light-year thick — about 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion kilometers) — before striking a single atom. Neutrinos come in three types, or "flavors," and switch between them as they travel, making use of a subtle quantum effect that works only if they have mass. Yet the Standard Model of particle physics predicts they should be massless.

One popular fix involves "right-handed" neutrinos. Particles spin a bit like tiny tops, and physicists call them left- or right-handed depending on how they spin relative to their direction of travel. A right-handed particle rotates like an ordinary screw being driven in, turning clockwise as it moves away from you. Every neutrino detected so far is left-handed and turns counterclockwise as it flies away, like a screw with a reverse thread.

"Right-handed neutrinos are hypothetical particles that do not feel the weak nuclear force, "unlike their left-handed counterparts, which are part of the Standard Model," study co-author Rishav Roshan, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southampton in the U.K., told Live Science via email. "They are characterized by having no electric charge and being much heavier."

"Right-handed neutrinos may mix with left-handed neutrinos, helping to explain the mass of the latter" and why they switch flavors, Roshan said.

The IceCube facility, photographed here beneath the Southern Lights, is Earth's premier neutrino detection facility. The proposed 'right-handed' neutrino has not yet been detected.

In quantum physics, particles that mix can exist as a blend of two identities at once. In a theoretical framework called the seesaw mechanism, each ordinary neutrino carries a faint trace of a heavy right-handed partner, and that trace gives it a tiny mass. The heavier the partner, the fainter the trace and the lighter the ordinary neutrino — hence the name, after the playground ride whose ends move in opposite directions.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The particles could solve other puzzles, too. They "aim to address several issues, including the origin of neutrino masses, the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe, and the nature of dark matter," Roshan said.

The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated each other, forbidding the universe as we know it from ever taking shape. Right-handed neutrinos play a crucial role in models' proposals that the "observed matter-antimatter imbalance arose from processes involving these neutrinos in the early universe," Roshan said.

In this picture, decaying heavy neutrinos left behind a slight excess of leptons — the particle family that includes electrons — that later became today's surplus of matter, he explained.

The seesaw framework usually includes three right-handed neutrinos, but because two are enough to explain the data, physicists often ignore the third, assuming it is too heavy or interacts too feebly with matter.

In the new study, Roshan and Sudipta Show, a physicist at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur, examined what this neglected particle — which, in the team's main example, was about 100 trillion times as heavy as a proton — would have done after the Big Bang.

At first, the particle would have zipped around at nearly light speed, so its energy would have faded like that of light, which would have both spread out and stretched to weaker wavelengths as space expanded. But as the cosmos cooled, the particle would have slowed down and most of its energy would have become locked in its mass, which would have been only spread out. Its share of the cosmic energy therefore would have grown until it dominated, and the long-lived particle would have stayed in charge until it decayed into other particles, according to the team's computations.

The study reveals that the neglected right-handed neutrino "significantly impacts the early universe's expansion dynamics, driving a period of early matter domination," Roshan said. This change "affects various Standard Model interactions"‬ that could help to explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry, Roshan added.

Each interaction would have switched on only once it outpaced the expansion of space. Because a universe dominated by the heavy neutrino would have expanded faster, the interactions would have had to wait until it cooled further.

These interactions would have let the early universe distinguish lepton flavors, which would have affected how the matter surplus formed. Thanks to the delay, the team found, a lighter right-handed neutrino about 100 billion times as heavy as a proton could have produced the observed amount of matter before the flavors could be told apart — even after the heavy neutrino's decay diluted part of it.

The heavy neutrino is far too massive to create in any particle accelerator, so tests must be indirect.

Gravitational waves — ripples in space-time — offer one such route. An era dominated by the heavy neutrino would have left a telltale kink in the background of early-universe gravitational waves, such as those from "cosmic strings" ‪—‬ hypothetical thread-like defects in space. The results can be tested through forthcoming facilities such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) and the Square Kilometer Array Observatory (SKAO), Roshan noted.

LISA, a space-based European Space Agency mission, is scheduled to launch around 2035, while SKAO, a giant radio telescope project being built in Australia and South Africa, could catch such waves by timing distant pulsars. Tests could come "as these facilities come online and begin data collection," Roshan said. A faint hum from the hot primordial plasma would carry the era's imprint too, but at frequencies beyond what existing detectors could pick up.

Roshan, R., & Show, S. (2026). Delayed charged Lepton Yukawa equilibration in minimal seesaw. Physical Review Letters, 137(11), 111802. https://doi.org/10.1103/nfkx-q6z7

Andrey got his B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in elementary particle physics from Novosibirsk State University in Russia, and a Ph.D. in string theory from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. He works as a science writer, specializing in physics, space, and technology. His articles have been published in AdvancedScienceNews, PhysicsWorld, Science, and other outlets.

#6574. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has officially ended its mission after more than 20 years, as it approaches a fiery reentry through Earth's atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A pioneering NASA space telescope is no more. In sad news for Swifties everywhere, the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has officially ended its mission after more than 20 years of tracking the most powerful explosions in the universe since the Big Bang.

According to a NASA announcement, the Swift team shut down the telescope's science operations Tuesday (Oct. 20) after the observatory fell too low in its orbit to continue taking reliable measurements of the cosmos. In the coming weeks, Swift will drop even further, eventually passing a point of no return and taking a fiery plunge through Earth's atmosphere.

The observatory is the latest victim of intense solar activity, which increases the drag on satellites in Earth orbit and makes it harder for spacecraft to stay aloft. Swift has been losing altitude for a while, but the final straw came in August, when a costly mission to boost Swift's orbit with a private spacecraft failed, ending with the would-be rescue craft burning up in the atmosphere after a series of hardware malfunctions.

Swift is now beyond saving and, orbiting at just 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth, can no longer take reliable observations of space. NASA expects the spacecraft to break up upon reentry "in the next few weeks."

NASA knew Swift was in trouble when it went in; soon, it'll be lying on the cold hard ground. However, the Swift mission surpassed its goals by decades. According to NASA, the satellite launched in November 2004 on a primary mission intended to last just two years. In the end, Swift survived for 22 years, surpassing its intended lifespan by more than 10 times.

In that time, Swift made thousands of observations of exploding supernovas, intense gamma-ray bursts, and black-hole-related episodes of stellar destruction, contributing data to about 7,000 scientific papers, according to NASA.

An illustration of a stellar 'mega-flare' detected by Swift. The observatory excelled at catching powerful, fast-acting cosmic events.

Designed as a multiwavelength observatory, Swift watched the sky in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light that made it well suited to track the aftermath of powerful energy bursts. Its greatest asset, perhaps, was its rapid response time; if an explosion flashed somewhere in the sky, engineers could swivel Swift to study it within minutes, NASA said.

"Swift was designed as a satellite dedicated to studying gamma-ray bursts, outbursts that came and went so quickly that no one could target them with large telescopes to learn more," S. Bradley Cenko, the mission's principal investigator at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, said in the statement.

Swift's fast-acting observations "played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics," added Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA headquarters.

His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

#6571. Azalea Cocktail

Recipe by Kate McKiernan, Chicago, Illinois

The Azalea cocktail is the signature bright pink, lemonade-and-vodka drink of the Masters Tournament, delivering spring and summer party refreshment.

The Azalea is the signature cocktail of the Masters Tournament, and as a hostess with the mostest, I love leaning into a theme. This drink is a hole-in-one crowd pleaser, whether you’re a golf fan or not. No one can deny the lure of a pretty-in-pink, citrusy vodka cocktail like this one, a perfect sipper on a warm, breezy day on or off the green.

Named for the stunning azalea blooms that famously line the grounds of the 13th hole at the Augusta National Golf Club, the Azalea cocktail is refreshing and perfectly sweet. It’s simple on the page with only a few ingredients, but the bright acid of the lemonade and the sweet kick of the grenadine go perfectly together and work well with a neutral spirit like vodka. It’s an easy cocktail to scale up for a crowd, making it perfect for Masters watch parties, spring brunches or any gatherings that could use a little extra pink charm.

Fill a chilled rocks glass with fresh ice.

Add ice, vodka and grenadine to an empty cocktail shaker. Fill the shaker with ice, and shake the cocktail until it’s well chilled, 15 to 20 seconds.

Editor’s Tip: For a more layered look, add the grenadine directly to the glass and only shake the vodka and lemonade, allowing the pink color to settle to the bottom.

Strain the cocktail into the prepared glass.

Garnish the cocktail with an orange slice and a cocktail cherry.

Editor’s Tip: You can also use the syrup from the cherries to stand in for grenadine in a pinch.

To make Azalea cocktails for a crowd, multiply the portions by the number of people you’re serving. Combine the vodka, lemonade and grenadine in a large pitcher or beverage dispenser ahead of time, then refrigerate the mixture until you’re ready to serve. If you don’t plan to shake each drink individually, you’ll want to add water to the mixture to compensate for the dilution you get from shaking a cocktail over ice. To achieve the proper dilution, add water equal to 20% to 25% the total volume of the base mixture.

Another way to gauge: Make a single serving of your cocktail. Measure the total volume of liquid, stir the mixture with ice until it’s chilled, and measure it again. The difference is the exact amount of water you need to add per serving in your batch.

Stir the mixture well before pouring it over ice, and wait to add garnishes until serving so everything feels fresh.

A rocks glass, aka a double old-fashioned, is the traditional glassware choice for an Azalea cocktail, giving it a classic, country-club feel while keeping things simple and elegant. If you want to dress things up for brunch or spring entertaining, a highball glass also works beautifully, offering extra room for ice and garnishes.

#6569. Brownie Batter Bark

Recipe by Molly Allen, Hood River, Oregon

This egg-free brownie batter bark is quick and easy, and tastes just like brownie batter straight from the bowl.

When I’m making brownies, I always want to swipe my finger against the edge of the bowl and taste the brownie batter. The problem? While it’s delicious, brownie batter contains raw eggs and raw flour, which can make you sick. When you want to lick the spatula but don’t want to risk food poisoning, this brownie batter bark recipe is the perfect solution.

Line a 15x10x1-inch baking sheet with parchment paper.

In a large bowl, combine almond flour, brown sugar, cocoa powder and salt. Stir in the melted coconut oil and vanilla extract until the mixture is smooth.

Spread the mixture on the prepared baking sheet into an even layer. Freeze it for 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, in a small microwave-safe bowl, microwave 1 cup of chocolate chips in 30-second increments until they’re melted, stirring between the intervals. Spread them over the frozen base. Sprinkle the bark with the remaining 1/2 cup of chocolate chips.

Freeze the bark for one hour or until it’s firm. Break it into pieces.

Brownie batter bark is best stored in a zip-top bag or airtight container in the freezer. The cold freezer temperature will keep the bark hard, and provides the best texture when you pull out a few pieces to enjoy. Keep the bark stored in the freezer for up to two months.

This is a great make-ahead potluck dessert. Make it any time, and then store it in the freezer. Grab a few pieces at a time, or serve a whole platter to a crowd.

No almond flour on hand? You can swap in all-purpose flour, but keep in mind the texture may not be the same. If you use all-purpose flour, it should be heat treated before consuming raw.

Spread the flour on a baking sheet and heat it in a 400ºF oven for about five minutes or until it reaches an internal temperature of 160º. Then add it to the dry ingredient mixture.

This recipe calls for unsweetened cocoa powder to deliver deep chocolate flavor. Semisweet chocolate chips are used for the melted chocolate topping for a balance of sweetness. It’s best to stick with semisweet chocolate for a more robust flavor (as opposed to milk chocolate).

You can melt chocolate either in the microwave or over a double-boiler on the stove top. Heat the chocolate slowly on low heat for the smoothest consistency.

#6568. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6567. I Flew United Polaris To Try Its Chef's Table Menu—And Didn't Expect To Enjoy Dinner This Much

From chilled crab soup to coffee-glazed short ribs, this was hardly your typical airplane meal.

With airlines constantly trying to one-up each other in premium cabins, United is hoping its food can give it an edge. As part of a broader overhaul of its food and beverage program, the airline introduced chef-created meals for United Polaris, its international business class, through a collaboration with Chef's Table.

I wrote about the menus when they were first announced, so naturally I was curious when I had the chance to actually eat one myself on an overnight flight from Newark to Edinburgh.

I’ve flown up front on a handful of other airlines, but this was my first time in Polaris—and I planned to approach it like any other overnight flight: Eat dinner, get comfortable, and pass out until Europe.

Before the flight, I preordered the Chef’s Table menu created by Fariyal Abdullahi, chef partner at New York City’s Hav & Mar. And while I don’t find myself eating at ultra-luxury restaurants all that often—I did eventually make it to a Michelin-starred one once I landed in Edinburgh—having a meal like this at 35,000 feet felt like a treat.

Abdullahi says her menu was guided by “two pillars that inform all my cooking: geography and seasonality.” Tomatoes and endive nodded to what was in season around New York and New Jersey, while other parts of the meal pulled directly from her Ethiopian roots. The pepitas were seasoned with berbere, and the short ribs were braised with coffee, nodding to Ethiopia’s connection to the ingredient.

Of course, creating a restaurant dish and serving one several miles above the ground are two very different assignments. Aaron McMillan, United’s Managing Director of Hospitality Programs, told me the airline considers everything from ingredients and preparation to presentation when adapting a chef’s recipe for the air. The goal, he says, is to preserve what makes the original dish work while ensuring it can be prepared and served consistently onboard.

Because this was an overnight flight, my appetizer, salad, and entree arrived together, which was honestly ideal. I wanted to eat, settle in, and begin the nightly debate over whether I was actually going to sleep.

Cold soup on a plane? Crab on a plane? Those are two concepts I would ordinarily approach with at least a little caution, but this ended up being one of the highlights of the meal.

The tomato soup had plenty of actual tomato flavor without being watery or oily, and there was enough crab that it didn’t feel like somebody had sprinkled three sad pieces on top and called it a day. It tasted like real crab, too, rather than the imitation stuff that would have immediately made the whole thing feel considerably less special.

More importantly, the two actually worked together. I went into this course most prepared to question my life choices and instead finished basically all of it.

I love a big meal as much as the next person, but eating something rich immediately before trying to sleep on a plane can be a dangerous game. So I was grateful to see some greenery sharing the tray.

The salad combined baby gem and endive with berbere-spiced pepitas, dried cranberries, pecorino Romano, and a creamy anchovy vinaigrette.

The cranberries brought some sweetness against the salty pecorino and vinaigrette, while the pepitas gave everything the crunch a pile of airplane greens desperately needs. And if “anchovy vinaigrette” has you picturing a salad that tastes aggressively fishy, this wasn’t that. The dressing had enough punch to make it interesting without overpowering everything underneath it.

If it isn’t already obvious, this was not the most photogenic meal I’ve ever been served. Purple mashed potatoes topped with glazed short ribs under airplane lighting don't necessarily set anyone up for Instagram greatness—but don’t judge a Chef’s Table entree by its cover.

The short ribs were extremely tender and came apart easily, which is especially appreciated when your dining room is an airplane seat and you don’t particularly want to start sawing away at a piece of meat with tiny cutlery. They also weren’t overly fatty, something that can quickly ruin short ribs for me.

Alongside the purple mashed potatoes were sautéed Thumbelina carrots and charred scallions, and everything worked together without any one element taking over the plate.

Saucy short ribs and mashed potatoes right before several more hours trapped on an airplane can also make you start mentally mapping the location of every bathroom pretty quickly, but thankfully, I wasn’t punished for my confidence.

United set out to make its airplane food something passengers might actually remember after landing, and at least on this flight, the Chef’s Table program feels like a pretty convincing step in that direction.

The cabin around me may have been showing its age a little, but dinner certainly wasn’t.
