#6521. A Brief-ish History of METI. Part II: From Interplanetary to Interstellar

Welcome back to our ongoing series on the Brief-ish History of METI, where we examine the rise, development, and possible implications of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence. In our first installment, we explored some of the foundational principles and how METI emerged as a possible answer to the "SETI Paradox." In a Universe where everyone is listening, and no one is broadcasting, should we as a species take the first step?

Naturally, this subject has sparked controversy and heated debate. In a Universe so vast and filled with so many unknowns and possibilities, is it wise to announce ourselves to potential alien civilizations? If we assume only 1 in 100 are hostile, what would be the consequences of sending a message saying, "Here we are!"? On the other hand, if we choose to remain silent and only listen to the cosmos, could we be missing out? By imposing isolation on ourselves, might we be damning ourselves to extinction?

Alas, the debate over the ethics of METI is far from over and will likely continue until (dare we say it?) we make contact someday. But that's a discussion for another installment. In the meantime, we'll continue our examination of the important milestones that led to METI as a distinct field of study. And in the midst of all that, we will be looking at the luminaries who were chiefly responsible for advancing it.

By the latter half of the 20th century, SETI shifted from a relatively obscure pursuit carried out largely by independently wealthy individuals to a serious scientific endeavor. With advances in rocketry and spaceflight, and the launch of national space programs, interest in the possibility of extraterrestrial life surged again. Rather than being fueled by science fiction and scientific inaccuracies (the misinterpretation of Schiaparelli's "canali"), the fascination was fueled by questions of what humanity might find on other worlds.

Cornell Professor and SETI pioneer Frank Drake standing in front of the 25-meter Howard E. Tatel Radio Telescope at the Green Bank Observatory. Credit: NRAO/AUI/NSF

This, in turn, led to experiments designed to test the capabilities of modern technology and perhaps make contact with other intelligent beings. A prime example is The Morse Message, which scientists at the Evpatoria Planetary Radar (EPR) center in Crimea carried out between November 19th and 24th, 1962. Using the facility's RT-70 radio telescope, the science team transmitted a Morse Code signal toward Venus. The message included the letters M-I-R (Mir, the Russian word for "peace") followed by "Lenin" and "USSR."

The message's main purpose was not to contact an intelligent civilization, but to test the radar station. The signals reflected off Venus's surface and were received back on Earth about four and a half minutes after transmission. Nevertheless, this experiment occured at a time when Venus was still thought to be potentially habitable, with many scientists believing that Venus' dense cloud cover (which obscured its surface) was due to heavy precipitation.

A few months later (December 14th, 1962), the Mariner 4 probe made the first detailed measurements of the planet's surface temperature. In the years that followed, multiple Soviet probes and landers revealed the true extent of Venus' hellish conditions: a carbon dioxide atmosphere, sulfuric-acid rain, and the hottest surface temperatures in the Solar System. This forever dispelled the idea that Venus could be a watery planet covered in bogs and oceans.

More importantly, it was also during this time that a transition occured in METI, reflecting a similar transition with SETI. Rather than listening or messaging neighboring planets for signs of life (on behalf of one nation), efforts in the latter half of the 20th century would reach interstellar space. Between 1999 and 2015, the EPR center played a vital role in METI by providing the necessary communications infrastructure for multiple publicly funded experiments.

While the Cold War Era added impetus to SETI and METI efforts, with both superpowers seeing a strategic advantage in making contact first, the scientific motivation reflected a broader, more universal awareness, with messages sent on behalf of all humanity.

When it comes to the pioneering work that made the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) a legitimate scientific field, few people were more integral than Frank Drake. Born in Chicago in 1930, Drake showed an early interest in science and later pursued a degree in astronomy at Cornell University. His interest in extraterrestrial life was reinforced by a 1951 lecture by Russian-American astronomer Otto Struve. One of the most distinguished and prolific astronomers of the mid-20th century, Struve was an early SETI advocate and greatly raised its international prestige.

After receiving a B.A. in Engineering Physics, Drake served briefly in the Naval Reserve before attending graduate school at Harvard University. By 1955, he received an M.S. and Ph.D. in astronomy. From 1958 to 1963, Drake began his career as a radio astronomer with the National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO) in Green Bank, West Virginia. There, he studied radio emissions from the Solar System's planets using the GBT, as well as those coming from the center of the Milky Way.

Drake was also deeply involved in the development of the Arecibo Observatory, which began construction in 1960, and helped extend its capabilities to include radio astronomy. Originally, the observatory was designed for ionosphere studies and to help track incoming missiles in the event of nuclear war. A year before Arecibo began construction, Drake obtained the approval of Otto Struve (then director of the NRAO) to begin humanity's first true SETI experiment.

The project began observations in 1960, using the NRAO 26-meter radio telescope at the Greenbank Observatory in West Virginia to listen for possible signals from Tau Ceti and Epsilon Eridani - two Sun-like stars located 12 and 10.5 light-years from Earth (respectively). While the project did not detect any extraterrestrial signals, it garnered international attention and drew the attention of many prominent scientists. This included Carl Sagan, who met Drake a year later at the first SETI symposium, and the two began a lifelong collaboration.

It was at this symposium, held at the Greenbank Observatory, that Drake unveiled his famous equation for estimating the number of extraterrestrial civilizations (ETCs) that humanity could communicate with in our galaxy at any given time: The Drake Equation. Rather than a scientific equation or method for calculating the existence of ETI, Drake created it as a thought experiment to summarize the challenges SETI researchers face.

In essence, knowing the number of civilizations (N) meant knowing all the parameters, the most important of which was how long civilizations could broadcast before going extinct (L). At the time, scientists knew that all of these parameters, except for the first (the average rate of star formation in the Milky Way), were subject to immense uncertainties. Nevertheless, the equation remains foundational to SETI and is considered the second-best known equation in human history (the first being Einstein's equation for Special Relativity (E=mc2)

Illustration of the Drake Equation (Credit: NOIRLab/AURA/NSF/P. Marenfeld)

After completing what was arguably humanity's first true SETI experiment, Drake began work on what would become humanity's first true METI effort: The Arecibo Message. Work began in the early 1970s, as Frank Drake organized a campaign to compose a message to be broadcast via Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305-meter (1000-foot) antenna.

The message was transmitted on November 16th, 1974, at 2380 MHz with an effective bandwidth of 10 Hz and a raw carrier power of 450 kilowatts (kW). However, Arecibo's huge dish focused that energy into an incredibly narrow, directional beam that magnified its intensity exponentially, making it equivalent to a 20-gigawatt omnidirectional broadcast. This meant any radio antenna in the galaxy could detect the message, provided it was about the same size as Arecibo.

The total broadcast lasted less than three minutes and was directed at Messier 13 (M13), a globular star cluster located about 25,000 light-years from Earth. This cluster contains 300,000 to 500,000 stars and spans 145 to 165 light-years in diameter. Because of the number of stars and the cluster's age (an estimated 11.65 billion years), it was considered a likely place for an extraterrestrial civilization.

Drake composed the message with help from Carl Sagan and other prominent astronomers, who arranged it using prime numbers because they believed this would make it easier for an ETC to decode. It consisted of a 1679-binary-digit picture (210 bytes), the product of two prime numbers, arranged rectangularly into 73 lines of 23 characters per line (also prime numbers). The binary digits (ones and zeroes) were transmitted via frequency shifting at 10 bits per second.

The decoded message was a simple pictograph depicting a series of scientific, geographical, biological, and astronomical information in different colors. These included:

The legacy of the Arecibo Message is comparable only to that of Project Ozma, as both experiments are recognized as humanity's first true attempts to find ETI. The message also became the subject of a hoax in 2001, known as the "Arecibo Answer." Near the Chilbolton telescope in Hampshire, UK, an imprint was found in a crop field that was a near-replica of the original message, using the same 73 x 23 grid pattern and most of the same chemical data.

However, the section on the elements of DNA substituted silicon for carbon, implying silicon-based life, and the DNA diagram was rewritten. The image of a human body was also replaced with a figure with a bulbous head and enlarged eyes. A system of nine planets was also depicted, but with emphasis placed on the 3rd, 4th, and 5th planets. The Arecibo telescope was replaced with a replica of a crop circle found in the same field a year earlier, and the transmitter's diameter was altered.

These align with common science fiction tropes about silicon-based extraterrestrials and urban myths about "greys" or "little green men." The medium, a burnt crop circle, is also a common hoax technique, meant to resemble burn marks from a landing craft. The SETI Institute issued a statement saying that the crop formation was a hoax, undoubtedly perpetrated by the same people who had made crop circles in the same area during the previous two years.

"The crop circles are decorative, impressive, and provocative, but not informative," they wrote. "We can expect better from true extraterrestrial intelligence."

By the 1970s, SETI and METI efforts had matured considerably, with developments in one field mirroring those in the other. Beyond the Arecibo Message, this decade saw the first (and, to date, greatest) attempts to send physical messages into space, a collaborative effort led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan: the Pioneer Plaques and Voyager Golden Records. Stay tuned!

The PBS Nature film "Tiger Island" captures rare glimpses of tiger behavior, including a mother, father and cubs spending time together ‪—‬ a first for these usually solitary cats.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A male tiger approaches his cubs and greets them with a head-bobbing motion while their mother rests nearby. The surprising interaction, captured in the PBS Nature documentary "Tiger Island," a two-part series that follows two big-cat families across Nepal.

The footage marks the first time a tiger "family" has been documented spending time together, and it could challenge conventional assumptions about how the seemingly solitary cats behave around their young, said Dan O'Neill, a wildlife biologist and filmmaker who contributed to "Tiger Island." Previously, it was thought that tiger moms raise their cubs for up to two years without any help from the male tiger.

"It just shows that we really know nothing about them," O'Neill told Live Science. "And they're so much more complex than people realize."

That's just one of the scenes in Tiger Island that challenges our understanding of the tigers' solitary nature. In another scene, a female tiger cares for another tigress's cubs.

"We have these very rigid ideas of how these animals live," O'Neill told Live Science. But the natural world is "diverse and ever-changing," and tigers are no exception, he said.

The footage of the female caring for another tiger's cubs could offer clues about how mother tigers protect their young. Male tigers, like male lions, sometimes kill cubs ‪—‬ a behavior known as infanticide ‪—‬ particularly when a new male takes over a territory. Allowing another female tiger to care for cubs might help more cubs survive to adulthood, O'Neill suggested. Previous observations of female tigers have shown females helping to co-parent each other's cubs, but it's a rare event.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To capture these scenes, the crew used drones with powerful optical-zoom lenses and quiet propellers to observe the tigers in places that were difficult to access without disturbing the big cats. Traditional camera traps often capture animals along trails, leaving much of their private lives unseen. O'Neill noted that the drone propellers were quieter than the local bees where the filming took place, thus giving the crew candid views of the tigers as they went about their lives.

Though tigers (Panthera tigris) are solitary animals, they often live close to or share habitat with human communities. That means tigers sometimes attack people and kill livestock, O'Neill said. "It would be absolutely naive and wrong to suggest that they [attacks on people] don't happen," O'Neill said. As a result, conservation efforts must account for the circumstances in which people and big cats encounter one another, rather than treating human communities as separate from wildlife, he said.

The same issue affects other big cats. O'Neill, a researcher with the wild-cat conservation organization Panthera, has spent years studying jaguars, pumas and snow leopards. He said the popular image of these animals living in remote wilderness can obscure how closely they overlap with human lives.

For O'Neill, conservation requires more than studying the animals' behaviors or protecting their habitats. It also means helping people who bear the cost of living alongside these apex predators.

"Helping those people is how you help tiger conservation," he said.

In the U.S. "Tiger Island" Part Two airs on Wednesday, Oct. 28 at 12:30 am on the PBS channel.

#6519. Examining the Cat's Head Nebula with the Hubble and JWST

The Cat's Head nebula gets its name from its appearance: it looks like a cat sitting so that it's facing away from the viewer, with its head turned around on the top of its neck, highlighted by a star that looks like a glowing eye. The unusual shape is made of gas and dust carved and formed by the radiation of young stars.

It's a small part of the larger Carina Nebula, a complex star-forming region about 7,500 light years away. Recently, both the Hubble and the JWST cast their gaze on the Cat's Head in an effort to learn more about star formation, a constant research subject in astronomy.

The Carina Nebula hosts some of the most massive stars in the entire Milky Way in its Carina OB1 assocation. Of particular interest is Eta Carinae, a stellar system that hosts many stars, two of which have a combined luminosity more than 5 million times greater than the Sun. Eta Carinae is also known for being at the heart of the eerily creepy Homunculous Nebula, not visible in these images. Massive stars like the ones in Eta Carinae and their powerful radiation have a pronounced effect on the region, and on star formation itself.

Hubble's image of the Cat's Head is in visible light, while the JWST imaged it in both near and mid-infrared. Each of the images shows a different aspect of the Cat's Head.

The pillar that makes the Cat's Head is composed of thick, dark dust, so far resisting the onslaught of stellar wind and radiation from massive stars. The yellow outline on its right side is likely where photoevaporation is taking place, driven by the same powerful stars. The UV radiation is ionizing the gas on the rim, and will eventually evaporate it completely.

In astronomy images like these, different filters isolate different chemicals like sulphur, oxygen, and hydrogen. The ionization level of the chemicals, along with how highly they're energized and how much dust is present, all affect the colours. Whether we know which colours represent which chemicals or not, these images are awe-inspiring.

The massive stars in the region are also responsible for the arcs and shoals in the images, again caused by their powerful radiation and stellar winds.

This zoomed-in portion of the Hubble's image highlights the "eyeball", likely a star in just the right position. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, STScI. Image Processing: J. Depasquale (STScI).

The JWST, as an infrared telescope, presents different, yet no less gorgeous, images of the Cat's Head. It's infrared instruments see things differently than the Hubble does. This gives the Cat's Headâalready ethereal in the Hubble imageâan even more ghostly, almost unreal appearance. Some parts of the Cat's Head in the JWST images appear to be only half-there, with background stars shining brightly through them.

The JWST's near-infrared image doesn't show different chemical elements the same way the Hubble image does. Instead, it shows more of the stars themselves. Even background galaxies are visible beyond the Cat's Head, along with the black background of space. The JWST also shows how massive stars are shaping the region, with the wispy filaments on the images left side. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI. Image Processing: J. Depasquale (STScI)

Some of the turbulence in the gas, driven by the massive stars, appears more substantial in the JWST image. The star that makes the Cat's Eye is also brighter, with less of its light blocked by dust in infrared.

A zoomed-in JWST NIR image of the head in the Cat's Head Nebula. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI. Image Processing: J. Depasquale (STScI)

In the JWST's mid-infrared image, the Cat's Head Nebula is transformed yet again. It's muted and ghost-sheet white, surrounded by pastel gas clouds punctuated with stars. The clouds look almost Earth-like in their white colour. This time, it's carbon molecules and warm dust emissions that take the stage. What is most likely an infant star pops into view in this image, embedded in thick dust that it's yet to dissipate, to the right of the head itself.

The white colour of the gas in this mid-infrared JWST image makes it look like Earthly clouds. Fewer stars are visible in the background, their light blocked out by the gas, which appears thicker. In the gas to the left, finer detail is visible in the gas clouds. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI. Image Processing: J. Depasquale (STScI).

The head itself is muted in the MIR image, along with the rest of the nebula. It's eye, almost malevolent in the other images, blends in with the gas and is less striking.

In this zoom-in of the MIR image, the edges are softened, and so are the colours. The star that makes they eye blends in with the gas in gradients of white. Globules below the head look like they're reaching for the head, rather than being blown back by stellar wind and radiation. The blackness of space is visible in the upper right, and a little in the upper left. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI. Image Processing: J. Depasquale (STScI).

Though these images are easy to appreciate by almost anyone, their primary purpose is scientific. By emphasizing and de-emphasizing different aspects of the Cat's Head nebula, astronomers can see stars more clearly, along with the dust, the gas, and the chemistry. Together, they help researchers see the effects of stellar radiation and wind, called stellar feedback, on the ongoing process of star formation.

Stellar feedback can both encourage and stifle star formation, depending on circumstances. It's complicated, and it's an ongoing topic of astronomical study. One of the JWST's main, defining science themes is star formation, and images like these are one of the reasons it was built. The Hubble helps too, and illustrates how the gas, the dust, the metallicity, and the stars of different sizes and ages, all play a role. Those factors all interact in different ways, making it difficult to come up with concrete theories of how it all works.

These gorgeous images are more than eye candy to astronomers. They're working hard on understanding a process fundamental to the cosmos. Wrapped up in all this visual chaos and beauty, Nature's laws are defining how stars form. Astronomers' mission is to decipher it all.

Enjoying these images on their visual merit alone is our mission, if we accept it.

#6518. A Nutrient Found in Red Meat Could Make Dangerous Inflammation Even Worse

A nutrient known for helping the body burn fat may also cause inflammation when the immune system is in overdrive.

Yale researchers found that L-carnitine, a nutrient abundant in red meat and widely used in exercise and weight-loss supplements, could worsen severe inflammation in mice. After a bacterial component triggered inflammation and sharply lowered blood levels of L-carnitine, restoring the nutrient made the animals sicker, suggesting the decline was protective.

The findings were published October 19 in Cell.

L-carnitine is best known for helping cells turn fat into energy. The body produces it naturally, and skeletal muscle contains particularly high concentrations.

“L-carnitine helps transport fats into mitochondria so they can be broken down for energy,” says Eric Elliott, MD, PhD, assistant professor of medicine (infectious diseases) at Yale School of Medicine (YSM) and the study’s first author. “In simpler terms, it has become synonymous with fat burning, which is why it has also gained prominence as an exercise and weight-loss supplement.”

The team was investigating metabolic changes during sepsis, a life-threatening condition in which the body’s response to infection damages its own tissues and organs. Much of that damage can come from uncontrolled inflammation rather than a failure to contain the infection.

“Sepsis is incredibly challenging,” Elliott says. “Patients with sepsis can become critically ill, and among patients with sepsis treated in intensive care units, some studies report mortality rates approaching 40%.”

To model the inflammation associated with sepsis, the researchers exposed mice to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a bacterial component. When L-carnitine levels in the animals’ blood dropped sharply, the team tested whether restoring the nutrient would improve their outcomes.

“We predicted giving carnitine back to these animals might improve their outcomes, but they actually did much worse,” Elliott says. “That told us the reduction in carnitine was an adaptive response.”

To understand why, the researchers conducted experiments in mouse and human immune cells. They found that L-carnitine activated part of the cell’s internal alarm system called the pyrin inflammasome. This triggered an inflammatory response involving the immune signaling molecule IL-17 and increased deaths among the mice.

“What was particularly striking was how detrimental IL-17 was in this model,” Elliott says. The team now wants to investigate whether blocking IL-17 might eventually help a subset of patients with sepsis, although that possibility remains untested.

The findings offer a potential research direction in a field where treatment advances have been limited. “We have made frustratingly little progress in improving sepsis treatment beyond learning how to better deliver fluids, antibiotics, and medications that support blood pressure,” Elliott says.

Because skeletal muscle contains high levels of L-carnitine, the researchers suspected that its release from damaged muscle could help drive inflammation. Senior author Andrew Wang, MD, PhD, associate professor of medicine (rheumatology, allergy & immunology) and of immunobiology at YSM, says the pathway may have implications beyond sepsis.

“There is tantalizing genetic evidence that the pathway we uncovered could be contributing to inflammation in a variety of diseases, particularly diseases in which muscle involvement has perhaps been thought to be a casualty of the disease rather than a potential driver,” Wang says.

The team found support for this idea in rhabdomyolysis, a condition in which skeletal muscle rapidly breaks down and releases its contents into the bloodstream, potentially causing acute kidney injury. In a mouse model, L-carnitine transport and pyrin inflammasome activation contributed to inflammation, suggesting that immune cells may interpret L-carnitine released from damaged muscle as a warning signal.

The pathway could also be relevant to cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and cancer. Further research is needed to determine whether it contributes to these chronic inflammatory conditions.

People who eat meat get most of their L-carnitine from food. Vegetarians and vegans tend to make more of it within their bodies, but their overall levels remain lower. The study examined L-carnitine on its own, so the findings do not directly show how eating red meat or taking supplements affects inflammation.

“We did not study red meat as a whole, and carnitine by itself did not induce inflammation,” Elliott says. “A substantial background of inflammation was required, and we do not yet know what inflammatory context might produce this effect in people. We cannot say that carnitine supplementation or heavy red meat consumption is always harmful. It is probably safe most of the time, but there may be specific circumstances in which it becomes a problem.”

Understanding those circumstances is a priority for the team. The researchers want to learn how individual food components interact with a person’s underlying health and inflammatory state and why the same nutrient might have different effects under different conditions.

“Food science currently exists in the realm of phenomenology,” Wang says. “I think that a deep understanding of all the elements that make up food, akin to a periodic table, will be required to understand what makes a ‘good’ or ‘bad’ diet for a particular individual in a particular health state.”

Reference: “The pyrin inflammasome senses OCTN2-mediated uptake of extracellular ʟ-carnitine from muscle injury or ingestion” by Eric I. Elliott, Tomomi M. Yoshida, Susana C.B.R. Nakandakari, Scott Pope, Cuiling Zhang, Timothy Nottoli, Jae Jin Chae, Daniel L. Kastner, Richard A. Flavell, Vishwa Deep Dixit, Vijay A. Rathinam, Fayyaz S. Sutterwala and Andrew Wang, 19 October 2026, Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.015

#6517. It's a Ghost! No, It's a Stellar Crèche!

Astronomers using the Chandra X-ray Observatory (CXO) and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) zeroed in on a wispy-looking region of the Carina Nebula and found a ghostly looking cloud seemingly floating in isolation among the other clouds of gas and dust. Just in time for Halloween, although, it turns out that little cloud isn't the soul of a departed star. Instead, it's a region of the nebula that has been actively engaged in creating batches of hot, young new stars.

By studying this region in X-rays and infrared light, astronomers are getting a good look at the structure of the cloud as well as the stars it has formed. Not only that, but it helps them piece together more information about the larger Carina Nebula, which lies more than 7,500 light-years away from us.

Most of us are familiar with one of the brilliant and weird objects that lights up the nebula: Eta Carinae. It looks like one star, but is actually a binary that has a combined brightness of around 5 million times that of our Sun. Periodically, this object brightens and dims, probably due to clouds of condensed dust that coalesced around the binary stars. It experienced a huge outburst in the 1840s called the "Great Eruption", which boosted tremendous amounts of gas and dust into space. It has since experienced other, smaller outbursts.

An ultraviolet image of the Homunculus Nebula (Eta Carinae) taken by the Hubble Telescope. Credit: NASA/ESA/StSci

The Carina complex is a huge diffuse nebula containing a collection of newborn stars nestled in a sea of starmaking gas and dust. It continues to produce new stars, many of them extremely bright and massive. Many telescopes have studied it, most notably the Hubble Space Telescope and JWST. Each view brings new insights into the makeup of the cloud as well as the objects it contains. In addition, astronomers are also keeping an eye on Eta Carinae because its primary star — a luminous blue variable star &emdash; is likely to explode as a supernova. When that happens, the shock waves will transform much of the nebula, probably spurring new rounds of star birth.

A broad panorama of the Carina Nebula, a region of massive star formation in the southern skies. This new method of determining the age of stars will help astronomers better understand the process of star formation. Credit: ESO/T. Preibisch

Obviously, the Eta Carina binary is a tantalizing subject, but there are also places such as the Keyhole Nebula. It's a dark and cold molecular cloud that covers about 7 light-years of space. Ionizing radiation from the nearby Eta Carina binary is shaping and eating away at the Keyhole.

There's also the open cluster Trumpler 14, which is a six light-year-wide grouping of more than 2,000 OB-type stars. These are massive and short-lived stars and are very bright in ultraviolet light. These are very young stars, ranging in age from about 300,000 to 500,000 years old.

The ghostly nebula that CXO and JWST imaged is still making stars at its heart. At the same time, ionizing radiation from the nearby Eta Carina binary, as well as hot young stars, is eating away the materials in the cloud. Thanks to that "cannibalizing" ultraviolet radiation from those stars, the cloud has developed several comet-like "knots". Astronomers often refer to them as cometary globules because of their familiar shapes. The Carina Nebula is not the only place where such cometary knots are seen. Astronomers have spotted them in other star-forming regions as well as in planetary nebulae, where stellar winds collide with material previously ejected from a dying star like the Sun. As those collisions happen, they shape similar types of knots in the clouds of gas and dust.

Since the stars will have much shorter lifetimes than that of the Sun, someday this region will look more like a stellar graveyard. The remains of those stars we see as newborn today will, in tens of millions of years, be ghosts of their former selves, spreading their materials to interstellar space.

Helpful Cosmic Ghost Brings Stellar Birth, Not Death https://chandra.si.edu/photo/2026/reaper/

#6515. Can Cats Really Go Vegan? New Research Reveals a Surprising Health Connection

More cat owners are turning to vegan diets for their pets. But is a plant-based diet actually safe for cats?

An online survey of 1,305 cats found that those eating vegan diets had 34% lower odds of being assessed as overweight than those eating conventional meat-based food.

The findings came from caregiver reports of veterinary assessments. All cats had followed their diets for at least one year, with conventional meat-based diets accounting for most (90%) and vegan diets for the remainder (10%).

Researchers calculated the difference after accounting for age, sex, neuter status, activity, and feeding practices.

The lower rates of excess weight came despite feeding habits that might have tipped the scales the other way, as Knight explained, “Interestingly, most vegan-fed cats were eating predominantly dry food and were more likely to have food available throughout the day. These are feeding patterns normally associated with increased overweight risk. Yet we still observed lower rates of overweight in this group.”

That observation came from study author Andrew Knight, an adjunct professor at Australia’s Griffith University School of Environment and Science. He emphasized that the relatively small vegan-fed group limited what researchers could conclude.

Veterinary studies estimate that around 30–60% of domestic cats are overweight or obese. Excess weight is associated with arthritis, diabetes, urinary tract disease, and reduced quality of life, giving researchers a reason to investigate dietary patterns that might help.

Caregivers of vegan-fed cats reported fewer weight-related disorders, with no cases reported for several conditions examined. However, the small number of cats in this group made those results uncertain.

“Carers feeding cats vegan diets also reported lower rates of body weight-related disorders such as osteoarthritis and other musculoskeletal and mobility problems,” Knight said. “However, the relatively small number of vegan-fed cats means these results cannot be considered conclusive.”

The survey could not establish why vegan-fed cats appeared less likely to be overweight. Researchers did not analyze the foods themselves, so explanations involving their ingredients or nutritional composition remain possibilities.

Some commercial vegan cat foods may provide more fiber and fewer calories or less fat than comparable meat-based products, potentially supporting weight control. Differences in L-carnitine, a nutrient involved in energy metabolism and maintaining lean body tissue, could also contribute.

The results do not establish that avoiding meat prevents excess weight. Determining whether the diets themselves explain the pattern would require direct measurements of food consumption, calorie intake, and body condition over time.

Knight said the findings provide a reason for further investigation, rather than a definitive answer about vegan diets and feline weight.

“We can’t conclude from this study that vegan diets definitely protect cats against becoming overweight, but we have found a consistent pattern that is worth further investigation. An ideal next step would be a larger, prospective study that directly measured what cats are eating, their energy intake, and their body condition.”

“Additionally, cat carers should always ensure their cats receive nutritionally complete diets, choosing commercial vegan foods that are appropriately supplemented to provide all essential nutrients.”

Reference: “Impacts of a vegan diet on body weight and related health disorders in 1,305 cats: an exploratory cross-sectional survey” by Andrew Knight, Alexander Bauer and Jenny L. Mace, 11 September 2026, Frontiers in Animal Science. DOI: 10.3389/fanim.2026.1939965

#6514. How You Squeeze Planetary Minerals Changes Everything

Studying the interiors of planets is essential for understanding planetary formation, evolution, and their ability to potentially host life as we know it. To accomplish this, researchers use a combination of Earth as an analog, computer models, meteorites, and data collected from other planetary bodies for studying their interior compositions. As a result, scientists have determined that the elements of magnesium and silicon are the most abundant planetary building blocks. And, under extreme pressures like the interior mantle of our planet, it forms magnesium oxide (MgO) crystals. But how does this same process occur under different pressures and temperatures on other planets like gas giants and larger rocky exoplanets called super-Earths?

Now, a collaborative team of researchers from the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) and Johns Hopkins University might be one step closer to solving this conundrum. As discussed in a recent study published in Physical Review X, the researchers unveiled intriguing findings that could solve a 12-year investigation regarding the geochemical processes that occur deep inside planets, specifically related to the formation of magnesium oxide. This study is a third study in a series that builds off two previous studies, a 2015 study published in Physical Review Letters and a 2024 study published in Science Advances.

Artist's impression of the interior layers of Earth, Mars and the Moon. (Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech)

For the study, the researchers conducted a series of laboratory experiments using lasers on a cubic crystal structure of magnesium oxide to compress and simulate the extreme temperatures and pressures it experiences in planetary interiors. For example, the researchers tested as high as 572 Gigapascals (GPa) and 13,000 Kelvin (K) (12,927 degrees Celsius/23,300 degrees Fahrenheit), which are much higher than the pressures and temperatures near the center of the Earth at about 360 GPa and 6,000 K (5,727 degrees Celsius/10,340 degrees Fahrenheit), respectively.

The laser compressed the MgO cube from various directions, which challenged longstanding scientific theories that the extreme temperatures and pressures made the direction of compression irrelevant. The three directions included diagonally along the face, perpendicular to a cube face, and along the diagonal through the face.

Credit: NASA/Lunar and Planetary Institute

In the end, the researchers found that the direction of the incoming laser onto the MgO cube resulted in different responses regarding its compression. For example, while the cubeâs transformation along the diagonal through the cube, whereas the other two directions resulted in different responses, specifically disordered and irregular crystal growth behind a shock wave from the compression. While this finding refuted longstanding theories regarding the behavior of crystals based on direction, the researchers also found that the MgO cube melted at 572 GPa and 13,000 K, which set a new experimental known material record for pressure and temperature.

âMagnesium oxide is an important ingredient in our understanding of planetary interiors,â said Dr. June Wicks, who is a professor in Johns Hopkinsâ Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences and a co-author on the study. âThese experiments help us determine where it can remain solid and where it becomes liquid, which matters for how planets transport heat and evolve.â

As noted, magnesium and silicon comprise the most abundant elements in planetary interiors, with its combined form of MgO revealing the temperatures and pressures of those same planetary interiors. The three main geologic layers of a rock planetary object are the crust, mantle, and core, with the Earth having a liquid outer core and a rocky inner core, with MgO forming near the bottom of the mantle near the core-mantle boundary. However, this process is different depending on the type of planet.

For example, on super-Earth exoplanets, MgO can transform into a conductive liquid within the mantle (whereas this conductivity exists within the Earthâs outer core), resulting in magnetic fields much stronger than Earthâs. Additionally, MgO on gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn can exist either as a solid or liquid deep within their cores and depending on the temperatures.

What new insights into planetary interior processes will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6513. A Hidden DNA Mechanism Could Explain How 20% of Human Cancers Develop

Mutations found in roughly 20% of human cancers may promote tumor growth by changing how DNA is organized inside cells. Researchers have identified a mechanism that allows a regulatory protein to reshape the genome’s three-dimensional structure, altering the activity of genes involved in cell division.

The study, published October 28 in Nature, links these changes to mutations affecting a protein complex called BAF. Scientists at Weill Cornell Medicine found that blocking a key protein involved in the process reversed the cancer-promoting effects in an animal model, suggesting potential new approaches to treatment.

The BAF complex helps control gene activity by regulating how accessible DNA is to other proteins. Its numerous subunits are encoded by more than two dozen genes, and mutations affecting these components occur in cancers of the breast, ovaries, liver, and lymphatic system. Until now, researchers had struggled to explain how such mutations could contribute to malignancy across so many different tissues.

The new findings challenge expectations about how BAF normally functions. “We normally think of the BAF complex as making DNA more accessible, and so we expected its loss to have the opposite effect,” Dr. Meydan said. “Instead, its loss made DNA more accessible to CTCF, with surprisingly far-reaching effects.”

CTCF helps organize DNA into distinct regions by establishing boundaries that influence which genes interact with regulatory elements. These interactions depend partly on how DNA folds and loops within the nucleus. When BAF activity is lost, CTCF gains access to sites that would normally be less accessible, potentially disrupting this intricate organization.

“The challenge for us was to find a potential cancer-promoting effect occurring across many different cell types and tissue models,” said Dr. Barisic, who is also the John P. Leonard, M.D./Gwirtzman Family Research Scholar in Lymphoma.

Using several animal and cell models with impaired BAF function, the researchers discovered that CTCF binding increased at thousands of locations throughout the genome. This widespread change reorganized DNA loops and folds, disrupting normal connections between genes and the regulatory regions that control their activity. The resulting shifts in gene expression encouraged faster cell division.

Evidence from mouse experiments and human cancer patient data further supported CTCF’s involvement. In particular, disruptions affecting CTCF were associated with better patient outcomes. The researchers also demonstrated that deleting CTCF in an animal model could reverse the effects of BAF mutations, providing experimental evidence that the protein contributes to the cancer-promoting process.

The team identified two additional protein complexes, PBAF and ISWI, that cooperate with CTCF in driving these changes. Removing either complex also blocked the effects of BAF mutations in experimental models, making all three potential targets for future therapies.

“These findings help us establish a unifying mechanism for one of the most common classes of cancer mutations, and identify CTCF and its partner proteins as candidate therapeutic targets in these cancers,” said study co-corresponding author Dr. Darko Barisic, an assistant professor of cancer biology in medicine and a member of the Sandra and Edward Meyer Cancer Center at Weill Cornell Medicine.

Although the experiments identify promising molecular targets, researchers have not yet established whether blocking these proteins can safely treat cancer in humans. The next challenge is understanding precisely how increased CTCF binding changes the genome and finding ways to interfere with that process.

“We’re currently investigating in more detail what this extensive gain of CTCF does to the genome, and we hope before long to find a drug that blocks this process,” Dr. Barisic said.

Reference: “SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin” by Sonia Debek, Cem Meydan, Christopher R. #6511. The Eggs Scene in ‘You Can See Everything’ Scrambles Reality

One of the most revealing scenes in the Nathan Fielder doc shows Elizabeth Holmes beating eggs — and what happens next

This review contains spoilers for the film You Can See Everything.

I saw You Can See Everything — the new documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim — on Thursday, and I still feel like my brain is trying to punch its way out of a bag, or like I’ve just awakened from an Inception-esque dream within a dream. It’s difficult to describe the winding, twisting, nearly three-hour film to someone unfamiliar with its many layers of context, from Fielder’s Dadaist, boundaryless approach to his subjects to Holmes’s hypnotic affect, which is either highly effective gaslighting or blinding, self-deluded earnestness. (Which is it? I still don’t know.)

What happens when you take two unreliable narrators — make that three, if you include Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, whose on-camera persona morphs from protective, naive tech bro to unscrupulous grifter — put them in a jar, and shake them? The result is that the more questions are asked, the further the truth drifts out of reach. It’s like staring at a Magic Eye image, slightly crossing your eyes, desperate to make out the hidden 3D subject but never quite managing to see it. Eventually, you start worrying your eyes might get stuck that way.

The discourse surrounding the film is already abundant, but we’re here to talk about the eggs.

If you’re familiar with the hallmarks of Fielderian programming, you know that Fielder is prone to hyperfixating on seemingly mundane details that later return to completely upend viewers’ expectations. In You Can See Everything, one such detail is observed in an exchange between Holmes and Evans as they make eggs. How much can be gleaned from watching someone make breakfast? A lot, apparently.

In the first half of the film, Fielder is fully embedded in the rental home of Holmes and Evans, who have invited the filmmakers to document the final weeks before Holmes reports to federal prison. (How and why they agreed to this arrangement is incomprehensible if they knew anything about Fielder’s work.) During this time, the narrative takes a surprisingly sympathetic turn for Holmes, who seems intent on convincing the filmmakers — and Fielder specifically — that she is actually a sweet, misunderstood victim of circumstance, not a Machiavellian con woman who defrauded investors. Frankly, aspects of this claim feel convincing at times. Viewers are invited to witness her ostensibly less guarded moments, including a scene in which she makes breakfast with Evans. As Fielder interviews her, Holmes somewhat unenthusiastically and limply beats a bowl of eggs with a fork. The camera lingers on her feeble whisking technique. Then, after a few seconds, another set of hands enters the frame: those of Evans. Without a word, he takes the bowl and fork from Holmes and begins whipping the eggs with considerably greater fervor.

Now, backseat driving in the kitchen is hardly uncommon among couples, though it feels like a fast track to bickering. (Evans tells Fielder that he and Holmes “never fight”; Holmes is also emphatic that she’s never lied in her life. Again, unreliable narrators.) What’s less common — or at least generally considered pretty rude and aggressive — is grabbing something out of your partner’s hands mid-task to take over. Fielder points this out, asking Evans why he felt the need to grab the eggs; Holmes explains that Evans doesn’t like the way she mixes them and thinks he can do it better.

It’s a tiny interaction, but a remarkably revealing one. Evans feels comfortable taking control of something Holmes is doing, without so much as asking, and seems largely unaware of how his behavior might come across on camera. Holmes, meanwhile, appears accustomed to the intrusion, offering an explanation rather than an objection. (Granted, unlike sustained and unblinking eye contact, beating eggs does not appear to be one of Ms. Holmes’s strong suits. Typically, one does so vigorously to aerate them and make them fluffier for an omelet or scramble.)

But with this being Elizabeth Holmes, we must also ask: Could it be a case of weaponized incompetence? Is it possible that, not wanting the task of beating the eggs, she intentionally does so insufficiently to make Evans take over? Is she being controlled, or is she getting someone else to do her work for her? Or is this evidence of her “different” way of thinking, that she truly doesn’t know the “right” way to beat them?

In interviews in the film, Holmes portrays the Theranos years as a period during which she was manipulated by her former boyfriend and business partner, Sunny Balwani, and maintains that her intentions were ultimately good for humanity, regardless of the consequences for investors and patients who received unreliable test results. Whether she actually believes this account of events, or simply knows how to sell it, remains one of the film’s central mysteries — as does the extent to which her romantic relationships lead her to take the fall for the actions of bad worse men.

These questions reverberate in the second half of the film, when — with Holmes now in prison — we learn some unsettling things about Evans. He has power of attorney over Holmes, and has been using her X account to post odd, profanity-laced remarks that seem entirely incongruent with her own manner of speaking. Suddenly, the eggs scene looks like an early indication that Evans is far more domineering than the protective-partner persona he’s been presenting. His ostensible vigilance toward Holmes may be genuine on some level, but it’s difficult to reconcile with his willingness to license her image for billboards promoting another (bizarre-seeming) entrepreneur’s Theranos obsession, or his apparent acceptance of the possibility that her AI-generated likeness could be used to create pornography or other content antithetical to her interests.

And yet, even as Evans emerges as an increasingly unsavory character, Holmes remains inscrutable. Does she know what he’s doing? Does she approve? Is he exploiting her circumstances, or are they working toward a shared objective — reputational, monetary, or otherwise? The film offers kaleidoscopic evidence for competing interpretations, including that even if Holmes is being dominated, she may be content with that dynamic.

What’s extraordinary about Fielder and Oppenheim’s documentary is its optical-illusion-like layers of “truth.” Despite the film’s many harrowing close-ups of microexpressions, there is what Holmes and Evans say, then there is what they do, or have done, or plan to do (launch a Theranos 2.0 called Haemanthus, apparently). There is also Fielder’s own history as a provocateur, a faux-earnest magician who will go to virtually any lengths to actualize a concept, and who seems remarkably capable of keeping a stone-cold straight face through any scenario.

We know enough about Fielder to question his sincerity, too. There are several moments in the film where I — and the several friends I went to see the film with — wondered if there was palpable sexual chemistry between him and Holmes, and whether Fielder would act on it. If he did, we couldn’t agree on whether it would be genuine or an act of performance art, or whether he has any barriers between those things.

The film’s most revealing moments are the ones that feel off-script for everyone involved: a fleeting facial expression, an odd word choice in an otherwise emphatic statement, a series of gestures exchanged over a bowl of scrambled eggs. The subjects, who have invited themselves to be watched, have few moments when they seem to forget that; those instances are when we ostensibly have the clearest insight into their reality. Frankly, it’s still murky, and that seems to be both the point and the irony in the film’s title.

You Can See Everything elevates Nathan Fielder’s reputation far beyond simply a master of cringe humor; there is, here, a glimmer of genius. This story feels almost fateful in its ability to showcase his gifts, illuminating the bottomless strangeness, the infinite complexities, of how humans interact with one another. Even when an idea is big, it’s the little things that matter the most. And in a documentary that promises you can see everything, we learn that it’s up to us to look closely — and even then, what we see might look different in another light.

#6510. Earth’s “Impenetrable” Space Radiation Shield Was Just Breached From Within

Remember the big solar storm back in May 2024? The one that caused auroras as far south as Florida and Mexico? Scientists are still parsing out the impacts that storm had on the local environment, and a new paper published in Geophysical Research Letters by Yoshizumi Miyoshi of Nagoya University and his co-authors shows it might have allowed some nearby electrons to accelerate to relativistic speeds using something called a chorus wave.

To understand why thatâs important, letâs first take a look at Earthâs local radiation environment. Itâs dominated by what scientists call the Van Allen belts. These were discovered early on in the Space Age by Explorer 1, and they are Earthâs primary defense against high energy electrons and other ions spewed out by the Sun. Scientists have long split them into two categories - the âinnerâ belt is made mainly of protons, and the âouterâ belt is covered in high-energy electrons.

But in 2014, NASAâs Van Allen Probe mission discovered a noticeable boundary - the ultra-relativistic âkiller electronsâ that move near the speed of light seem to hit some sort of glass wall at around 11,500 kilometers above the Earthâs surface. To scientists, it seemed that this âshieldâ protected the inner area directly around the planet from the most dangerous form of radiation.

Fraser talks about what the Van Allen radiation belts are.

Which sounded great - until Nature decided not to do it anymore. Luckily we know when exactly that happened, because Japanâs Arase satellite (also known as the Exploration of energization and Radiation in Geospace - ERG mission), which has been flying through Earthâs magnetosphere since 2017, was watching. For its entire lifetime up to that point, it noted that high energy electrons were being held at bay. Until May 2024.

During that storm, solar wind gusts topping out at 1,200 kilometers per second compressed Earthâs magnetic field, and triggered the most intense geomagnetic disturbance since the arguably even more famous Halloween storm of 2003. As the storm peaked, Arase counted ultra-relativistic electrons at levels 5,000 times higher than the typical background. This wasn't the first time we had seen spikes in radiation during solar storms, but older spacecraft werenât able to tell what was actually happening.

Arase provided the key data to help guide the researchers, who used a mathematical method called electron phase space density. This tracks the particle distribution of those electrons by energy and motion. If, say, the electrons were coming in from outside where the protective barrier originally was, this metric should very clearly show a downward trend from outer space towards Earth. However, Arase saw a very distinct peak right where the barrier used to be. To space physics, that represents a smoking gun for âlocalâ acceleration - i.e. electrons being sped up exactly where they were detected.

NASA Goddard video about the radiation environment surrounding Earth. Credit - NASA Goddard YouTube Channel

Which then begs the question, what was accelerating them? According to the paper, it was something called a âchorus waveâ. Typically, the inner radiation belt is covered in a shroud of charged gas known as the plasmasphere. Charged gases do a great job of dampening high frequency electromagnetic waves, as they simply absorb their energy. But when the May 2024 storm hit, the plasmasphere was crushed back toward Earth, creating a void where it would normally be.

Combine that with a ânegative ionospheric stormâ, which massively depletes local plasma densities, and you create a very empty electromagnetic environment. Which is the perfect situation for chorus waves. These are low frequency electromagnetic waves, which sound like whistling when translated into audio, that are generated by lower-energy particles during magnetic storms. In a depleted plasma environment, these waves are able to transfer their energy very efficiently to the surrounding low energy electrons, boosting them from sub-million electron volt energies to multi-MeV ranges - essentially creating high energy electron radiation within what is normally an exclusion zone.

Over time this new high energy radiation spread out both towards and away from Earth - and the effect lasted for months. Its effects were visible to Arase until another solar storm hit five months later in October 2024, and changed the magnetic field situation up again.

But ultimately, this paper acts as a warning of a new type of space weather hazard - localized radiation caused not by a massive solar explosion but by a retreat of our own protective plasma sheath. As we start to expand out into the area most affected by this, itâs certainly better to be aware of that phenomenon now, but unfortunately it might require even more shielding to protect our sensitive electronic and biological cargo in the future.

Nagoya University - 2024 solar storm triggered ultra-relativistic electrons inside Earthâs âimpenetrable barrierâ

Y. Miyoshi et al - Local Acceleration of Multi-MeV Electrons Inside Earth's Impenetrable Barrier During the May 2024 Superstorm

The promise of AI automation to fix the administrative problems facing universities is a fallacy. These systems will only increase the burdens of already-struggling institutions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Universities are at a critical point as students and faculty embrace the use of AI. Already, universities like Harvard are introducing courses that feature an AI avatar as an "instructor."

The promises AI offers higher education are familiar: an increase in efficiency as a consequence of less administration, more teaching coverage, better feedback and smarter assessment. But introducing artificial intelligence (AI) systems in an attempt to fix these problems is not the answer. If anything, AI systems will magnify and speed up the bureaucracy that is driving universities' decline.

In practice, the more likely outcome is darker: AI will not simply sweep away the bureaucratic machinery of universities; it will give that machinery a new regime of AI compliance — more policies, more forms, more trackers, more oversight roles and more work downloaded onto faculty who are already stretched thin.

The danger is not that AI will destroy universities but that universities will use AI to preserve the very processes that make them dysfunctional. If this happens, we might see faculty spending less time on research, less time on teaching, and more time on activities that do not directly contribute to the production of knowledge and education of students.

This is already evident in the existing assessment system in the U.K., but shades are creeping into systems elsewhere, providing a window into the future for U.S institutions. A single piece of student work may pass through a plagiarism-detection platform, a grading interface, a moderation spreadsheet for faculty to share feedback, a grade-transfer system, and an exam-board record. Each stage generates its own logins, deadlines, exception rules and audit trails. None of this is inherently malicious. Anonymous marking, moderation, appeals, accessibility and academic integrity are legitimate concerns. But when each concern is implemented as a separate system, the combined effect is administrative incoherence.

In essence, faculty become the human interface between incompatible platforms, spending their time reconciling grades and chasing missing evidence rather than teaching. While this example pertains to U.K. universities, the trend to expand the administrative staff extends to North America. AI simply introduces a new opportunity to increase administration.

AI could, in principle, solve this. It could integrate systems, automate routine reporting, draft feedback, identify inconsistencies and remove duplicate data entry. Yet the institutional incentive is rarely to remove work; it is to make work visible. A university that automates a broken workflow does not necessarily simplify it. It may simply produce faster reports about the broken workflow, more sophisticated dashboards and more elaborate evidence of compliance. The bureaucratic impulse survives by changing its vocabulary: risk management, assurance, transparency, governance, responsible innovation.

At least one possible outcome is that universities will create AI-use policies, require module-level AI statements, mandate disclosure forms, introduce approved-tool lists and establish review committees. Faculty will be asked to redesign assessments, monitor suspected misuse, document their decisions, complete training, and explain their approach to students. Much of this labor will be invisible. It will appear not as a new job title but as an additional expectation attached to teaching.

When something goes wrong, the academic is exposed; when the system works, the institution claims the credit. That asymmetry is corrosive.

That asymmetry is corrosive. It teaches committed staff that careful judgment is not valued as expertise but rather as a compliance risk to be managed, and the consequences will fall unevenly. Experienced faculty, after voicing their concern to no avail, may leave, retire early or disengage. Early-career academics, already precarious because they don't have tenure, will have the least power to resist. Students will receive less of the resource that matters most: sustained intellectual attention.

One possible outcome is that universities will encourage the development of faculty AI avatars and cut hours and employment. The institution will then justify hiring more ‪—‬ not fewer ‪—‬ compliance and "educational enhancement" staff to manage and maintain these AI avatars, negating the idea of efficiency and cost savings. In this scenario, bureaucracy will expand to manage the problems created by its own expansion while undercutting quality for the students who are paying high tuition fees. One might need to hire staff for oversight of these avatars, administrators and lawyers to manage licensing agreements, quality control staff in case things go wrong, and IT teams for integrating them into learning platforms and websites.

There is an alternative to the administrative tasks. AI should be governed by a simple institutional rule: no new compliance requirement without the removal of an equivalent existing burden. If a university requires assessment redesign to accommodate AI, or the introduction of new technology, it should provide protected time, technical support and a single integrated platform. If it expects faculty to manage AI use, it must give them clear institutional backing rather than leaving them to improvise. And critically, it should show how the technology makes work more efficient before rolling it out across the board.

But the deeper issue is not technology but institutional purpose. A university exists — or should exist — to cultivate understanding, judgment and intellectual independence. If its systems consume faculty time, fragment the student experience, and reward documentation over learning, then AI becomes another instrument of managerial self-preservation. The question is not whether universities can adopt AI. It is whether they can resist using AI to automate their own absurdities.

If they cannot, the outcome will be an educational system that looks progressively sophisticated while becoming increasingly hollow ‪—‬ full of monitoring, low on trust; rich in measuring, poor in teaching; obsessed with compliance, indifferent to the people who make education possible; overly procedural sans intellectual life. It will become an audited theater of learning not worth students' time.

#6508. “Nearly Everybody Had Given Up” – Scientists Finally Solve a 60-Year Chemistry Mystery

After more than six decades of failed attempts, chemists have achieved a breakthrough involving a class of molecules long considered too unstable to isolate.

Chemists have succeeded in isolating a group of molecules that researchers have struggled to capture for more than 60 years. Known as oxoboranes, these compounds contain an unusual triple bond between boron and oxygen, a combination long considered too unstable to isolate in a lasting form.

Researchers led by Professor Holger Braunschweig at the University of Würzburg have now developed a method that produces three surprisingly stable oxoboranes. Published in Nature Chemistry, the work was supported by computational research from Professor Ashwini K. Phukan’s team at Tezpur University in India.

The breakthrough began when Würzburg doctoral students Lukas Lubczyk and Christian Markl independently reacted a compound called a diboracumulene with different ketones, chemicals commonly used in organic synthesis. Instead of the anticipated products, they obtained unusual orange or yellow solids. The reactions had unexpectedly produced oxoboranes as their main products.

“The discovery was a pleasant surprise. I never thought the diboracumulene would react the way it did, let alone with multiple different, simple substrates. And when Christian came to me with his compound, I knew we were onto something,” says Lukas Lubczyk.

Boron has a strong tendency to avoid forming triple bonds, making these molecules particularly difficult to synthesize. Braunschweig has spent more than 15 years investigating this type of chemical bonding. His team created the first molecule containing a boron-boron triple bond in 2012, followed by the first neutral molecule with a boron-carbon triple bond in 2025. Organic oxoboranes represented the remaining challenge involving triple bonds between boron and other elements in the first row of the periodic table’s p-block.

Chemists have pursued oxoboranes since at least the early 1960s. Although previous experiments detected or trapped them under extreme conditions, inferred their presence from chemical reactions, or produced related derivatives, researchers had been unable to isolate stable examples.

“Nearly everybody in the field had given up on oxoboranes, as they were thought to be just too unstable to be isolated. So we were stunned to see them spontaneously form in these reactions and stick around long enough that we could study them,” says Holger Braunschweig.

The successful preparation of three oxoboranes suggests that the new approach could provide access to additional members of this difficult-to-synthesize molecular family. The researchers are now investigating whether the method can be extended to produce other elusive compounds involving elements across the periodic table.

Reference: “Synthesis and isolation of stable oxoboranes” by Lukas Lubczyk, Christian Markl, Mudit Jain, Sourav Kar, Thomas Kupfer, Rian D. Dewhurst, Ashwini K. Phukan and Holger Braunschweig, 27 October 2026, Nature Chemistry. DOI: 10.1038/s41557-026-02272-w

The work was funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG), the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) of India.

#6506. Has Substitution Culture Gone Too Far?

Guests are increasingly asking for their meals to be customized. These restaurants say it’s gone too far.

When Chanita Chayaluk decided to open her restaurant and wine bar Taan, she hoped “to showcase Thai food in Chicago in a different light,” she says. “The first [wave of] immigration of Thai people in Chicago was in the 1970s, and a lot of [Thai] food here still feels like it’s from that time.” In September, she opened with a menu including miang, a Northern Thai dish made with fermented tea leaves, and a whole, deep-fried fish in a fish-sauce caramel.

Another quirk of operating in Chicago? “We’re still pretty ‘Midwest nice,’” says Chayaluk. “We try to overaccommodate and appease the masses.” In the early days of service, guests made frequent requests for substitutions or accommodations due to preferences and dietary restrictions. “It would slow down service and speed, and that was not just affecting us, but the guest experience in many ways,” she says. With a small kitchen and staff, it was hard to keep up. “It just felt like we were Chipotle.” When a guest asked for green curry mussels “but without the mussels,” it was a turning point.

Chayaluk implemented a limited substitution policy at Taan, stating on Instagram that ingredients like fish sauce and shrimp paste are “the fabric that defines our cuisine,” and therefore, could not be removed from any dishes that include it.

A decade or so ago, substitution culture was generally frowned upon and derided. Recently, though, some restaurants report it bubbling back up—and in full force. There’s a swirl of factors that got us here: Lunch slop bowl spots primed customers to expect a detailed level of customization with their orders. Unreasonable Hospitality pushed an intensified “customer is always right” mentality. And influencers entering the food-review space have made criticism of anything—including a restaurant choosing not to honor certain dietary preferences—ripe for an immediate, viral takedown. Couple all of that with the fact that it is hard to keep a restaurant afloat these days, and you’ve got several operators giving in, whether to specific requests, or to altering their menus altogether (see also: the great de-spicification of menus.)

At the same time, restaurants like Taan and New York’s Ha’s Snack Bar—which proudly announces in its Instagram bio that everything contains fish sauce—are standing their ground.

For Lom Wong in Phoenix, Arizona, substitution and modification requests have ramped up after receiving national attention. Chef Yotaka “Sunny” Martin was recognized by the James Beard Awards last year, and the restaurant was named a Michelin Bib Gourmand in August. “[After the award,] we had more guests than we were used to picking things apart. They were asking us to modify dishes or not understanding our service style and why we weren’t coursing things in a European fashion,” says chef and co-owner Alex Martin. “[There is a] European distinction of what an award-winning restaurant looks like, so people equated that recognition with a white-tablecloth restaurant. We were just like, ‘Well, that’s not who we’ve ever been, and it’s never what our restaurant will ever be.’”

Like Taan, Lom Wong took to social media to set expectations, including that the restaurant would not “make substitutions simply to make a dish more familiar,” and that certain dishes might differ from Western expectations of them; beef might have gristle, fishes will be whole, and both choices are fully intentional. “Sunny is our guiding light of cultural context,” says Martin. “[She advises, considering if] changing something about a dish compromises the integrity of the dish.” For example, the mango salad can be ordered with the shrimp on the side, but the restaurant won’t remove beef or shrimp paste from dishes that necessitate them.

Chayaluk takes a similar approach at Taan; there is always a vegan, gluten-free option (currently a fried rice) that she describes as a “catchall” for those who can’t have other items on the menu. “We make sure that that dish is also really, really good and substantial; it’s not just an appetizer,” she says. “It’s not an afterthought.”

Staff at both restaurants are encouraged to uphold the boundaries, which both Chayaluk and Martin say are as much in place for protecting their staff’s peace as they are for ensuring quality control for guests. While there has been some backlash, the expectation-setting at the start of the meal (and before, thanks to the social media posts) has for the most part been taken well. “The way we explain [our policy] to guests is kindly saying we respect your preferences, but they’re your preferences,” says Martin, “and steering them toward dishes on the menu that might already align with those.”
