#6505. This Gamma-Ray Burst Wasn't Dim, It Was Just Misunderstood

Every photon that reaches us tells us something about the Universe. Most of them come from the Sun and are well-understood. But others aren't so easily understood.

The highest energy photons are gamma photons, and they reach us in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). They were first detected by accident in the 1960s by a satellite watching for covert nuclear weapons tests, an unnatural, Earthly source of gamma radiation. Now we've detected large numbers of GRBs with satellites dedicated to sensing them.

GRBs are extremely energetic events in the Universe, second only to the Big Bang. In only a few seconds, they can release as much energy as our Sun will across its nearly 10 billion years of fusion. They're the calling cards of supernovae, when the core of a massive star collapses in on itself at the end of its life, leaving behind a neutron star or a black hole.

GRBs are rare, but they're not difficult to detect, due to their extreme bursts of energy. So despite being rare, they're regularly detected in distant galaxies. A typical GRB from a supernova lasts about 20 or 30 seconds, followed by an afterglow with stages of declining energy. A GRB's energy is in its jets, which are ultrarelativistic beams of plasma and radiation that approach the speed of light.

This artist's illustration shows two jets from a GRB emitted in opposite directions. The jets lose energy and fade into longer wavelengths as they travel through the surrounding medium. Image Credit: By NASA/Swift/Mary Pat Hrybyk-Keith and John Jones - http://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/features/news/10sep08.html [1]Transferred from en.wikipedia to Commons by TheDJ using CommonsHelper., Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=8807284

The GRB is followed by an x-ray phase, then an optical phase, then a radio phase, as the jet decelerates into the surrounding medium, losing energy in stages. (Another class of GRBs, short GRBs, are separate and have a different source.)

On March 10, 2026, NASAâs Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope detected a GRB with an unusual light signature.

This one, named GRB 260310A, had an initial flash of gamma-rays that lasted almost one minute, releasing a relatively small amount of energy. Then, in another twist, its visible light afterglow gradually brightened over the course of a few hours. The optical light was brighter than the supernova's host galaxy. If that wasn't unusual enough, after its initial x-ray flash, the x-ray afterglow also brightened again, and remained visible for months.

In astronomy and astrophysics, outliers always attract attention because they have something new to tell us. GRB 260310A was no different. An international group of researchers studied the burst to try and understand its unusual signature.

Their results are in research titled "An Extremely Bright Slow-rising Afterglow from an Off-axis Jet in GRB 260310A," published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. The lead author is Yu-Han Yang, a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Physics at the University of Rome Tor Vergata. As the title says, the GRB strange signal is related to our viewing angle.

âWe see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,â said co-author Roberto Ricci, who led the radio observations. âWe could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder.â

To understand them, GRBs have to be observed across multiple wavelengths. Once the Fermi Gamma-Ray Telescope detected GRB 260310A, it sent out alerts for quick follow-up observations. NASAâs Chandra X-ray Observatory, ESAâs XMM-Newton, the China/ESA Einstein Probe mission, the Large Binocular Telescope, and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array all contributed. The Calar Alto Observatory in Spain also contributed observations confirming that a supernova was behind the GRB.

"We present a multiwavelength study of GRB 260310A, a nearby long-duration gamma-ray burst (GRB) at z â 0.153 associated with a broad-lined Type Ic supernova," the authors write. "Despite its modest prompt gamma-ray output, GRB 260310A exhibits one of the brightest afterglows ever observed in the X-ray, optical, and radio bands."

This figure compares GRB 260310A with a broader population of GRB afterglows. From top to bottom, the rows of panels compare x-ray flux and luminosity, then optical apparent magnitude and absolute magnitude, then radio flux density and radio luminosity. All panels show how GRB 260310A is different than the broader population and how it peaked later than others. Image Credit: Yu-Han Yang et al 2026 ApJL 1011 L22

Most GRBs are detected when one of its jets is pointed right at us. âMuch like a flashlight, the jet appears brightest when seen head-on," said lead author Yu-Han Yang. "Most of our models are calibrated using events seen from that same perspective. This burst gave us a chance to look beyond that glare."

GRB 260310A wasn't pointed at us, and that explains some of its unusual light pattern, especially its weaker initial gamma flash. But its later stages were among the brightest. Both its x-ray and optical afterglows ranked among the top 1% in brightness, and its radio brightness was among the top 5% of GRBs. âWe looked at it from a side angle," Yang said. "As the jet slowed down, its light became visible over a wider range of angles, allowing us to probe the jetâs shape, from its outer edges toward its inner core.â

Strangely, after about three weeks, the x-rays brightened again and stayed bright for about one week. Then, it gradually faded away. âThat was unexpected. At first, I thought another X-ray source was contaminating our observations. But the brightening really came from the afterglow,â said Yang, who coordinated the X-ray monitoring. âThis prompted us to explore a more complex jetâs shape.â

Only NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory has the angular resolution required to detect a contaminating source, and the researchers used some of its Director's Discretionary Time to examine GRB 260310A. Those observations ruled out a contaminating x-ray source.

This figure shows the Large Binocular Telescope's optical image of GRB 260310A's field in the left panel. The right panel shows the Chandra X-ray Observatory's image of the GRB. The cyan circle is the NuSTAR's Fast X-ray Transients observation, which helps show how Chandra has the power to see the source more clearly compared to other x-ray observatories. Its observations ruled out a contaminating x-ray source. Image Credit: Yu-Han Yang et al 2026 ApJL 1011 L22

So what's the overall explanation for GRB 260310A?

"We argue that the combination of weak prompt emission, hard peak energy, and late afterglow onset is naturally explained by a GRB jet viewed off-axis," the authors write in their research. The critical part is that it had two separate shocks.

"Our analysis of the broadband spectrum favors the presence of two emission components: a bright RS (reverse shock) dominating the radio and extending to the optical band, and an FS (forward shock) contributing to the optical and dominating in the X-rays," the researchers explain.

There are existing models of GRBs with two shock components, but they didn't match GRB 260310A. "However, as often occurs for bright GRB afterglows, none of our standard RS plus FS models..." could explain the GRB.

A different explanation matches the light from this GRB.

"Our long-term X-ray monitoring of the X-ray afterglow identifies a peculiar late-time rebrightening at â¼20â30 days, after a phase of rapid decay," the authors write. "This behavior is difficult to accommodate within a single FS model and may instead indicate a late episode of energy injection that refreshes the shock or additional structure in the outflow, such as a two-component jet."

While GRBs were initially seen as single-angle cones emanating outward from supernovae, that explanation hasn't held up. Two component jets with forward and reverse shocks more accurately explain complex light from some GRBs. In this model, the jet features a bright, inner core, and a dimmer outlying sheath.

This schematic shows a two-component jet model. It shows a central, compact jet surrounded by a wider, sheath-like jet. It also shows the Reverse Shock and Forward Shock. Image Credit: J.D. Myers (NASA).

A jet seen head-on like other GRBs is also ruled out, whereas a jet seen from the side, and having two components, can explain the observations. "A low-velocity jet seen (approximately) on-axis would not be able to combine the early peak and late rebrightening in a single jet model, whereas an off-axis two-component jet can accommodate both these peaks," the researchers explain.

The GRB's relative dimness compared to others is not because it's intrinsically less bright. It's because of our viewing angle. "We showed that viewing effects solve the apparent tension in the burstâs properties. The slow rise and delayed onset of its optical afterglow support the scenario of a jet seen off-axis," the authors write.

Understanding the viewing angle only explains some of this oddball GRB. It's unusual late re-brightening phase is also odd, even for a two-component jet.

"This late-time rebrightening represents a critical test for the two-component jet model," the researchers explain. "If interpreted as the emergence of a narrow jet core viewed further off-axis, it would imply extreme luminosities and energetics for an on-axis observer."

So what seemed like an unusually dim GRB, followed by an unexpected re-brightening, stems from our viewing angle.

âWhat appeared to us as an unremarkable GRB might have looked like a monster explosion to an observer looking straight down the jet's core,â notes Yang. âOur models suggest that the explosion packed roughly a billion years of the Sunâs energy output into a pencil-thin beam.â

#6504. A Mysterious Explosion in Space Just Did Something Scientists Didn’t Expect

An explosion that initially appeared unremarkable in gamma rays went on to produce one of the brightest afterglows astronomers have recorded in the past 20 years. Its visible light became brighter than its host galaxy, and its X-ray emission unexpectedly intensified again weeks later.

An international research team believes the extraordinary behavior can be explained by the direction of the explosion’s powerful jet. Rather than pointing directly toward Earth, the jet was viewed from an angle that initially concealed its most energetic region. The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, suggest that some exceptionally powerful stellar explosions may be difficult to recognize from their initial gamma-ray flashes alone.

NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope detected the event, designated GRB 260310A, on March 10, 2026. Its initial burst of gamma rays lasted approximately 53 seconds and appeared to release relatively little energy. Over the following hours, however, its visible afterglow steadily grew brighter before eventually fading.

The contrast became even more pronounced at other wavelengths. Compared with samples of previously observed gamma-ray bursts, the event’s X-ray and optical afterglows ranked among the brightest 1%, while its radio emission placed it among the brightest 5%. Approximately three weeks after the explosion, the X-ray afterglow brightened again, remaining unusually luminous for more than a week and detectable for months.

“We see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,” says co-author Roberto Ricci, who led the radio observations. “We could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder.”

Gamma-ray bursts are among the most energetic explosions in the universe. Many occur when massive stars collapse and launch narrow jets of matter traveling at nearly the speed of light. As these jets collide with surrounding gas, they generate afterglows that can be detected in X-rays, visible light, and radio waves.

Astronomers typically observe the brightest gamma-ray flashes when a jet points almost directly at Earth. GRB 260310A appears to have been different. Its relatively weak initial emission, followed by an exceptionally bright afterglow, is consistent with a jet viewed from outside its most intensely beamed region.

“Much like a flashlight, the jet appears brightest when seen head-on. Most of our models are calibrated using events seen from that same perspective. This burst gave us a chance to look beyond that glare,” explains Yu-Han Yang, a postdoctoral scholar and lead author of the study.

The researchers propose that the explosion produced a jet with a narrow, highly energetic core surrounded by a wider, slower outflow. From Earth’s viewing angle, the broader outer regions would dominate the early afterglow, while much of the core’s radiation would initially be directed elsewhere.

As the jet slowed, its emission became visible across a wider range of angles. Radiation from the energetic core could then reach Earth, potentially explaining the delayed increase in X-ray brightness. This structured jet model offers a possible explanation for the unusual observations, although the precise configuration remains uncertain.

“We looked at it from a side angle. As the jet slowed down, its light became visible over a wider range of angles, allowing us to probe the jet’s shape, from its outer edges toward its inner core.”

The delayed X-ray brightening was particularly difficult to explain. “That was unexpected. At first, I thought another X-ray source was contaminating our observations. But the brightening really came from the afterglow,” recalls Yang, who coordinated the X-ray monitoring. “This prompted us to explore a more complex jet’s shape.”

To investigate the event, the international team, led by the ERC-funded BHianca group at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, combined observations from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, ESA’s XMM-Newton, the Einstein Probe mission, the Large Binocular Telescope, and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array. Additional observations from Calar Alto Observatory detected the signature of a supernova, confirming that the gamma-ray burst accompanied the death of a massive star.

The team’s models indicate that the jet’s central region may have carried vastly more energy than the initial gamma-ray measurements suggested. “What appeared to us as an unremarkable GRB might have looked like a monster explosion to an observer looking straight down the jet’s core,” notes Yang. “Our models suggest that the explosion packed roughly a billion years of the Sun’s energy output into a pencil-thin beam.”

The findings also point toward a population of stellar explosions that conventional gamma-ray observations may overlook. As powerful new sky surveys, including those conducted by the Vera Rubin Observatory, expand their coverage, astronomers expect to identify more afterglows from jets that are not directed toward Earth. Such detections could help establish how frequently collapsing massive stars produce relativistic jets and how those jets escape through the stars’ outer layers.

“Gamma rays are not the most efficient route to spot these hidden jets: we find them once in a blue moon,” concludes Muskan Yadav, a graduate student who contributed to the study. “Upcoming surveys will pick up hundreds of them. Identifying them among millions of variable sources won’t be easy, but it’s a challenge I’m excited to take on.”

Reference: “An Extremely Bright Slow-rising Afterglow from an Off-axis Jet in GRB 260310A” by Yu-Han Yang, Roberto Ricci, Eleonora Troja, Muskan Yadav, Yi-Han Iris Yin, Rubén Sánchez-Ramírez, Brendan O’Connor, Niccolò Passaleva, Alberto J. Castro-Tirado, Hendrik van Eerten, Simone Dichiara, Vincenzo Galluzzi, Narjes Shahamat Dehsorkh, Iván Agudo, Jesús Aceituno, Malte Busmann, Maria D. Caballero-García, Emilio Fernández-García, Daniel Gruen, Maria Gritsevich, Sergiy Guziy, David Hiriart, You-Dong Hu, Martin Jelínek, Alexander Kutyrev, Alzbeta Malenakova, Filip Novotny, Ignacio Pérez-García, Shashi B. Pandey, Jorma Ryske, Alfredo Sota, Jan Strobl, Hira Waseem and Siyu Wu, 28 October 2026, The Astrophysical Journal Letters. DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/aea990

#6503. Inside the New D.C. Restaurant That Only Sells Five Curry Steak Frites Every Night

In a Georgetown alleyway, Alfie’s serves northern Thai dishes that are built around local ingredients

The hottest new spot in Washington, D.C. focuses on the traditional heat-packed cooking methods of northern Thailand, while still using local ingredients from around the DMV. Alfie’s, from chefs Justin Ahn and Alex McCoy, started as a pop-up in Petworth in 2017 before traveling around the world, serving diners in New York and London. This year, the restaurant put down permanent roots in a Georgetown alleyway. The co-owners led us through a day in the new kitchen, preparing everything from hand-cut green papaya in som tam salad to the limited-quantity Thai steak frites with a massaman curry peppercorn sauce.In the video, the kitchen team breaks down rib-eye steaks for their take on a steak au poivre, which they only make five of each night. The steaks are carefully seared for each order, with the au poivre massaman curry sauce is finished in the pan with the leftover beef fat. Classic “bar fries” are served up with the massive 26-ounce rib-eye.

Elsewhere in the kitchen, another chef carves green papayas. The irregular slices of papaya get tossed in a funky, spicy dressing for each order. Ko calls it the “most labor intensive dish on the line;” each order is carefully mixed with fresh tomatoes, peanuts, and a palm syrup and tamarind-heavy dressing. A rich pork belly curry is simmering in the background. Gaeng hung lay (a traditional northern Thai curry) cooks down large pieces of pork belly to get that fatty layer, with pickled garlic and pineapple balancing out the rich flavors of curry paste, tamarind, and fish sauce.

Right before service, the chefs begin prepping herbs and sticky rice that has been soaking overnight and is quickly steamed for that malleable, glutinous texture. McCoy talks about how being a chef is more of a lifestyle than a job, but there’s immense payoff when you get to see diners enjoy your hard work every night. He hopes that Alfie’s will become a place where “you can just forget where you are, have a good time, and just lose yourself in the experience and the food.”

Watch the kitchen team at Aflie’s cook classic Thai dishes and fusion plates like curry steak frites in this episode of Now Open.

#6501. A Breakthrough in Magnetism Could Make Computer Chips Use Dramatically Less Energy

Researchers have overcome a longstanding obstacle that has prevented promising materials from being used in ultra-low-power computer chips.

A promising class of materials could help dramatically reduce the electricity needed for computing, but a persistent problem has kept them out of computer chips. When these materials are made thin enough for modern electronics, the electrical and magnetic properties that make them valuable can disappear.

Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces ultrathin films of bismuth ferrite that retain their essential properties and develop an additional form of magnetism with potential advantages for future computing devices. The findings were published in Nature Materials.

Bismuth ferrite belongs to a class of materials called multiferroics, which have interconnected electrical and magnetic properties. Within their crystalline structures, positive and negative charges are displaced in opposite directions, creating electrical polarization. Applying a small voltage can reverse that polarization, allowing information to be stored as binary data (ones and zeros). Because the electrical and magnetic states are linked, the stored information could also be read magnetically, potentially enabling memory and logic devices that consume far less power.

The obstacle is a phenomenon known as the “dead layer” effect. When multiferroic films become extremely thin, their atomic structures and chemical environments can change enough to disrupt their functionality. At the same time, internal electric fields can destabilize their polarization. Together, these effects can eliminate the ferroelectric and magnetic behavior needed for electronic applications.

The Brown team addressed both problems by carefully engineering the layers surrounding the bismuth ferrite. First, they grew the material on dysprosium scandate, a rare earth-based crystalline substrate with a smaller lattice spacing than bismuth ferrite. The mismatch places the film under compressive strain, helping preserve the atomic arrangement required for its electrical and magnetic properties.

The researchers also incorporated a metallic layer that screens unwanted electric fields, preventing them from destabilizing the film’s polarization. With both effects controlled, bismuth ferrite remained functional even at thicknesses of only a few angstroms. An angstrom measures approximately four billionths of an inch.

“We’ve established that we can get rid of the dead layer,” said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. “We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want — down to a few angstroms — and it’s still ferroelectric, and it’s still magnetic.”

Beyond preserving the material’s original properties, the engineered structure enhanced its magnetic behavior. The researchers demonstrated that the thin film exhibits altermagnetism, a magnetic state with characteristics that could overcome some limitations of conventional magnetic materials.

“Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out,” Caretta said. “The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds — they can be fast, densely integrated, and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout.”

These characteristics could eventually support faster, more densely packed electronic components while reducing energy consumption. Although the researchers have demonstrated the material’s properties rather than a finished computing device, the technique addresses a major barrier to incorporating multiferroics into practical chips, particularly as artificial intelligence increases demand for computing power.

“We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials,” Caretta said. “The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that’s useful — and sometimes even better than what nature gives us.”

Reference: “Altermagnetic signatures and topological textures in ultrathin multiferroic BiFeO3” by Geo Fratian, Maya Ramesh, Xinyan Li, Evangelos Golias, Yousra Nahas, Sebastian Maria Ulrich Schultheis, Julian Skolaut, Marti Checa, Arundhati Ghosal, Evan Krysko, Paul Malinowski, Brendan D. Faeth, Jan Priessnitz, F. C. Fobasso Mbognou, Atsushi Hariki, Kosuke Sakurai, Mizuki Furo, Shashank Kumar Ojha, Morgan Congdon, Shiyu Zhou, Alexander Qualls, Kai Litzius, Christoph Klewe, Peter Meisenheimer, Jan Kuneš, Kyle Shen, Laurent Bellaiche, Libor Šmejkal, Darrell G. Schlom, Yimo Han, Sergei Prokhorenko, Ramamoorthy Ramesh, Paul Stevenson, Angela Wittmann and Lucas Caretta, 28 October 2026, Nature Materials. DOI: 10.1038/s41563-026-02786-1

The research was supported by the U.S. Army Research Office (W911NF-21-2-0162), the National Science Foundation (DMR-2039380, OIA-2327352) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-AC02-05CH11231).

Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter.Follow us on Google and Google News.

Based on Topological Vortex Theory (TVT), altermagnetism should be regarded as an experimental clue toward geometric magnetic ordering, rather than a mature chip-ready solution. The notion that “engineering structures enable materials to outperform their natural states” represents a direction that human science has always pursued; however, researchers should further interrogate the topology, symmetry, and transport mechanisms, instead of mechanically adopting the performance promises found in mainstream narratives:

(1) Interrogate the geometric origin: Does this altermagnetic response arise from lattice symmetry, strain fields, or interfacial topological defects? Do not remain at the superficial level of describing merely “strong” or “weak” signals. (2) Distinguish between bulk materials and thin films: The potential properties already exist in the bulk material, while thin-film engineering merely “manifests” them. It is necessary to analyze which boundary conditions and symmetries are altered by the engineered structure. (3) Focus on the readout mechanism: Does the so-called “strong electrical signal” originate from the anomalous Hall effect, spin Hall effect, magnetoresistance, or other geometric transport effects? This is key to judging its true applicability. (4) Evaluate the speed advantage: One must consider dynamic time scales, damping, energy consumption, and thermal stability, rather than drawing conclusions solely based on the analogy that “antiferromagnets are faster.” (5) Be wary of overhyped claims: The increasing demand for AI computing power does not automatically imply that such materials can be integrated into practical chips; process compatibility and the difficulty of device integration must still be carefully assessed.

Mainstream physics frequently makes the leap from material properties to device performance; in contrast, the TVT framework demands that we ground our understanding in geometric structures, topological constraints, and observable mechanisms.

A woman's unexplained abdominal pain led doctors to a diagnosis that has only been documented a few hundred times over the past 400 years.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 42-year-old woman in Somaliland, Africa

The symptoms: The woman went to the hospital after having three years of chronic, dull pain in her lower abdomen, as well as a growing sense of heaviness in her abdomen that had worsened in recent months.

When doctors reviewed her medical history, they learned that, three years earlier, she had experienced a number of symptoms that seemed to indicate a pregnancy. She recalled her abdomen growing over time and feeling "fetal movements," her doctors noted in a report of the case. Then, the movements stopped, the abdominal growth halted, and the enlargement gradually subsided. She had not sought medical care during or after this apparent pregnancy.

What happened next: When doctors physically examined the woman's abdomen, they found a hard, irregular mass that extended to her belly button and barely moved when they touched it. Blood tests showed mild anemia, meaning she had fewer healthy red blood cells than normal. Her white blood cell count and kidney and liver tests were normal, and a pregnancy test was negative.

An ultrasound revealed a calcified mass and an empty uterus. Calcification is a buildup of calcium that hardens tissue into a solid mass.

To get a better look at the mass, which occupied the woman's lower abdomen and pelvis, the doctors ordered an advanced CT scan to create a 3D model. The imaging revealed that the mass contained clearly identifiable fetal skeletal structures, including a skull, a spinal column, ribs, and arm and leg bones. The mass measured roughly 7 by 5 inches (18 by 13 centimeters).

The diagnosis: Doctors concluded that the woman had a lithopedion, or "stone baby." The term comes from the Greek words "lithos," meaning stone, and "paidion," meaning child.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a typical pregnancy, an egg is fertilized in a fallopian tube — the structure between the ovaries and the womb — and then travels into the uterus, where it implants in the uterine lining. By contrast, lithopedions most often start as abdominal pregnancies,‬ a type of ectopic pregnancy in which the embryo instead implants on the lining of the abdominal cavity.

There, the embryo shares the space with organs like the stomach, kidneys and appendix. These misplaced pregnancies are almost never viable and are highly life-threatening for the mother. Because the placenta attaches directly to delicate abdominal organs and blood vessels, these carry a severe risk of catastrophic internal bleeding.

If the fetus dies at a developmental stage when it is too large for the mother's body to naturally break down and absorb, her immune system can sometimes treat the retained tissue as a foreign object. To protect the mother from inflammatory complications and infection, the body progressively deposits calcium over the fetal remains, creating a protective casing. In this case, the calcified fetus likely accounted for the woman's chronic abdominal pain and increasing sense of heaviness, her doctors concluded.

The treatment: The doctors performed abdominal surgery to completely remove the calcified fetal mass from the woman's pelvis.

The day after surgery, she developed a mild fever and nausea, but both resolved with treatment. She remained stable and improved during her hospital stay before being discharged in good condition.

Follow-up visits over the next six months showed she had healed well, with a complete resolution of her abdominal pain.

What makes this case unique: Only about 340 cases of lithopedion have been documented in the medical literature over the past 400 years, with the earliest documented in 1582.

This woman's case stands out because she was 42 years old, while many recent cases have been diagnosed in postmenopausal women. (Women typically experience menopause around 51 to 52 years old.) In these cases, the initial ectopic pregnancy occurred during the woman's childbearing years, but she unknowingly carried the calcified remains for decades before developing symptoms. For example, a 74-year old woman from India carried her "stone baby" for more than three decades. By contrast, the woman's recent case was caught after only three years.

The case also highlights the challenges of maternal healthcare in resource-limited settings such as Somaliland, where a lack of access to routine prenatal care and early pregnancy scans can lead to delayed diagnoses. That said, the successful use of advanced 3D imaging and complete surgical recovery demonstrate that excellent outcomes are possible even in these constrained environments, the doctors noted.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6499. This Ancient Meteorite Hints at Mars' Warm, Wet Past

Mars is the subject of an ongoing, decades-long effort to understand its past. Its potential ancient habitability drives that effort. More than 20 missions have been sent to its surface (though many didn't survive the entry and landing). Two are operating there currently, Curiosity and Perserverance, and multiple orbiters scan the planet's surface from above.

Clues to Mars' past are in its rock, and the more ancient a piece of rock, the deeper the clues it can contain about the planet's ancient past. Visiting Mars with rovers is only one way to access the planet's rock. Fortunately, some chunks of Mars have been sent to Earth. Violent impacts have sent chunks of Mars rock into space, where they've eventually found their way to Earth as meteorites.

A Martian meteorite named Black Beauty set the standard for ancient meteorites from Mars when it was found in 2011. Most meteorites are found in deserts or in snowy/icy areas simply because they're more easily seen, and Black Beauty (Northwest Africa 7034, or NWA 7034) was found by nomads in the Western Sahara. Portions of it are about 4.43 billion years old, and Mars is about 4.5, maybe 4.6 billion years old. So Black Beauty is extremely ancient.

The Sahara Desert has yielded other ancient Martian meteorites, including Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), found in Mali in 2022. New research uncovered some unusual properties in Teg 001, and they're presented in new research.

The research is titled "A Martian meteorite that formed â³4.1 billion years ago samples Marsâ early crust and mantle," and it's published in the journal Science. The lead author is Yang Liu from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology. Scientist Carl Agee, director and curator at the University of New Mexicoâs Institute of Meteoritics (IOM), also played a leading role in the work.

"This sample probably came from an environment on Mars that was more Earth-like." - Carl Agee, University of New Mexico.

(A) shows the largest of the eight pieces of Teg001. (B) shows a cut section of a smaller chunk. Image Credit: Yang Liu et al., A Martian meteorite that formed â³4.1 billion years ago samples Marsâ early crust and mantle. Science0,eadz5646DOI:10.1126/science.adz5646

Ancient meteorites are rare finds and they're extremely valuable scientifically.

"Martian meteorites provide a record of the planetâs geological history," the authors explain in their research. "However, most are geologically young samples that are not representative of Marsâ surface, which is dominated by ancient rocks."

Most meteorites are young just because of selection effects. Meteorites are launched into space by impacts, and that favours young rocks, which are stronger. So meteorites tend to come from younger, basaltic volcanic rocks. More ancient parts of Mars crust are weaker because they're fractured and brecciated by impacts. Some ancient rocks are also sedimentary or clay-bearing rock. These rocks are weaker and much less likely to survive an impact that can launch them into space.

Teghaza is one of the rare ancient Martian meteorites.

"We describe the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), a slowly cooled igneous rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago," the authors write. "Its composition, mineralogy, and texture are distinct from other Martian meteorites." Distinct from other Martian meteorites, but also similar to likewise ancient Black Beauty.

âI realized that this one was a little bit like Black Beauty, not exactly, but it resembled it in the oxygen isotope values,â Agee said in a press release. "I looked at it microscopically and found domains within it that had high levels of manganese oxide, a compound being looked for on Mars by the rovers as an indicator of environments conducive to life.â

MSL Curiosity found rock fractures in Gale Crater that were filled with material rich in MnO. It suggests, but doesn't prove, that the planet's atmosphere once had free oxygen and oxygen-rich groundwater. That's still being debated.

Lead author Yang Liu and other Caltech scientists used a dating technique to find the age of tiny zircon crystals in Teg 001. Zircon crystals are important finding the age of ancient rocks because they can survive geological processes. They also contain trace amounts of elements with long half-lives. This is how Liu determined that Teg 001 is 4.1 billion years old. "We conducted ten measurements of U and Pb isotopes, in six shocked zircon grains with different morphologies, to determine their U-Pb and Pb-Pb ages," the authors explain.

Though Black Beauty is also ancient, the pair of meteorites are quite different from one another.

âThere are a few parts to Black Beauty that are around that age, but that whole meteorite itself is a conglomeration of many different rock types. Teghaza 001 is just one unadulterated rock type, and it's 4.1 billion years or older, so that was a big surprise,â said Agee. âIt's the oldest Martian igneous rock ever found by a huge margin, but in addition to that, it seemed to have these clues in its composition that suggested it had been in an environment that had fluids and water coursing through it.â

Teghaza 001 was found in several chunks adding up to almost 800 grams. Unlike Black Beauty, which is a congolomeration of different chunks, Teg 001 is a single rock type. Image Credit: UNM.

The isotope Oxygen-18 indicated that it had interacted with water in the past, most likely on the Martian surface. "The high Î´ 18O value of Teg 001 probably reflects assimilation of Î´18O-rich crustal material that had interacted with surficial fluids, or direct reaction of the magma with high-Î´18O fluids," the authors write. That finding supports the hypothesis that Mars was once warm and wet, a hypothesis supported by a growing body of evidence.

âWe also had these anomalous oxygen isotopes, and these domains that had high manganese levels, Agee said. "All of that was consistent with it being from a time on Mars, from the very, very beginning when the Martian environment was different from the time in which most of the Martian meteorites that we see were formed and erupted a few 100 million years ago when Mars was a dry desert, just like it is now. This sample probably came from an environment on Mars that was more Earth-like.â

This image shows a cut section of Teg001, with some of its features and contents labelled. Pigeonite (PgT) is particularly relevant, because it hosts fluid-altered Magnesium. "The Mg-rich interiors of pigeonite have been heavily altered by reactions with a fluid phase," the authors write. Image Credit: Yang Liu et al., A Martian meteorite that formed â³4.1 billion years ago samples Marsâ early crust and mantle. Science0,eadz5646DOI:10.1126/science.adz5646

Mars' early, potentially more Earth-like time period is called the Pre-Noachian period. Planetary scientists struggle to paint a clear picture of the Pre-Noachian because it was so long ago, and geologica processes and weathering have erased much of the ancient. Some research shows that Mars may have had global oceans during this period, a stunning difference from the frigid, dessicated planet it is today.

It's possible that billions of years ago, Mars had a global ocean, as shown in this illustration. That could explain the aqueous alteration in Teg001. Image Credit: By Ittiz - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=7861829

It's possible that Mars still has some simple, extant life. If it does, that life is hiding somewhere underground where the last of the planet's ancient water might be sequestered, away from the harsh radiation on the surface. But if the emerging picture of an ancient, warm and wet Mars is true, that would be the Pre-Noachian.

âIf there was ever abundant life on Mars, on the surface, not sequestered away in some subsurface, that would be the time that you would be looking at, the Pre-Noachian period,â said Agee. âIt's the very earliest time, and that was when maybe Mars still had a magnetic field, and it was shielded from radiation, and there were surface waters. There was a denser atmosphere. If primitive life was abundant in Mars. That is the time that is most likely for it to have happened.â

Most Martian meteorites are much younger than Teg001, only a few hundred million years old. It likely came from a place no rover has visited, possibly from Mars' southern highlands. Remote sensing shows that that ancient region has a similar composition to Teg001.

âThis is just one single meteorite. It's like going out, going back in time and chipping off a hunk of an outcrop, 4 billion years ago on Mars, and then we have this example of what was actually happening,â said Agee. âThat is why it's such a valuable sample. Weâve never found one like this before. The most exciting part about this find is its age, plus the alteration in the meteorite that indicates it has been in what I would call an Earth-like environment, with fluids coursing over the surface and volcanoes creating hydrothermal systems. There are surface waters and so on. And that's all reflected in the way that the meteorite has been sort of altered from its original state.â

"The presence of aqueously altered minerals, combined with bulk and mineral-specific oxygen isotope measurements, indicate that Teg 001 experienced reactions with fluids enriched in 18O, before ejection into space by an impact," the authors summarize in their paper.

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

#6498. Scientists Say This Medication Could Be the Next “Wonder Drug”

A diabetes medication may protect against heart attacks and strokes through an unexpected biological mechanism.

Two medications used in people with type 2 diabetes produced dramatically different results when scientists tested their ability to prevent dangerous blood clots. In mice with injured blood vessels, sotagliflozin reduced clot formation by approximately 60%, compared with just 5% to 10% for the widely prescribed drug empagliflozin.

Researchers at Michigan Medicine also found that sotagliflozin suppresses excessive platelet activity, a process that can block blood flow to the heart or brain. Published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation, the findings suggest a possible explanation for the drug’s ability to reduce heart attack and stroke risk beyond its effects on blood sugar.

Sotagliflozin, marketed as Inpefa, belongs to a group of medications called sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) inhibitors. These drugs interfere with proteins that transport glucose through the body. Common treatments such as empagliflozin (Jardiance) and dapagliflozin (Farxiga) primarily block SGLT2, a protein that helps the kidneys reabsorb glucose. Sotagliflozin acts on both SGLT2 and SGLT1, which is also present in other tissues.

Although SGLT2 inhibitors have established cardiovascular benefits, clinical trials have shown that sotagliflozin can also reduce ischemic events, including heart attacks and strokes. These occur when blood clots or other blockages restrict circulation. The researchers investigated whether the drug’s broader action on glucose transport proteins might help explain this protection.

“A drug that can both decrease the risk for diabetes along with the risk for having a heart attack or stroke could be a turning point in our ability safely treat this growing population in the US and abroad,” said Michael A. Holinstat, Ph.D., M.S., co-senior author and professor of pharmacology, internal medicine, and surgery at the University of Michigan Medical School.

Scientists compared sotagliflozin and empagliflozin using blood samples from healthy volunteers and people with type 2 diabetes. Sotagliflozin significantly reduced platelet activation and made platelets less likely to clump together. Empagliflozin produced little or no comparable effect.

Platelets normally help stop bleeding by gathering at damaged blood vessels. However, excessive activation can produce clots inside arteries, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke. Sotagliflozin’s ability to suppress this activity may contribute to its cardiovascular benefits.

“These experiments showed that sotagliflozin has a unique effect, and blocking SGLT2 alone is not enough to inhibit platelet aggregation,” said Eugene Chen, M.D., Ph.D., co-senior author and Frederick G. L. Huetwell Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.

“Sotagliflozin may offer additional protection against blood clots, potentially lowering the risk of heart attack and stroke.”

The researchers next investigated whether inhibiting SGLT1 alone could account for sotagliflozin’s effects. When they genetically removed SGLT1 from mouse platelets, blood clot formation decreased by approximately 40%. However, neither this genetic approach nor treatment with mizagliflozin, a drug that selectively blocks SGLT1, fully reproduced sotagliflozin’s results.

This suggests that other biological mechanisms contribute to the drug’s ability to prevent clot formation. One possibility involves SGLT1 in endothelial cells, which form the inner lining of blood vessels and interact with circulating platelets. Researchers have not yet established whether these cells contribute to sotagliflozin’s anti-clotting effects.

“Sotagliflozin appears to be in the sweet spot because compounds that have higher levels of SGLT1-selective inhibitors can cause gastrointestinal issues,” said Bertram Pitt, M.D., co-author and professor emeritus of internal medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.

“We think this could be a wonder drug with potential to offer benefit for many conditions.”

Sotagliflozin is FDA-approved to reduce certain cardiovascular risks in adults with heart failure and in adults with type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and additional cardiovascular risk factors. The researchers hope to investigate whether its effects on clotting could benefit patients with other conditions, including chronic kidney disease and atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm associated with increased stroke risk.

The laboratory and animal findings provide evidence that sotagliflozin affects clotting through mechanisms beyond conventional SGLT2 inhibition. However, further clinical research is needed to determine how much this platelet effect contributes to preventing cardiovascular events in humans and whether it can do so without increasing bleeding complications.

“The search for medications that reduce the risk of life-threatening blood clots without increasing the risk of bleeding has continued for decades,” Holinstat said.

“Sotagliflozin has now been demonstrated to serve both functions and may represent the next advancement in prevention of blood clots, heart failure and stroke in patients with and without diabetes.”

Reference: “SGLT1/2 inhibitor sotagliflozin, but not SGLT2-selective inhibitor empagliflozin, attenuates platelet activation and thrombosis” by Livia Stanger, Krista Goerger, Xu Zhang, Pooja Yalavarthi, Andrew Rickenberg, Adriana Yamaguchi, Mariane Flores Nascimento, Ashleigh Kilgore, Heeseo Kim, Xiaokang Wu, Yanhong Guo, Anna R. Dahlgren, Jifeng Zhang, Jordan A. Shavit, Bertram Pitt, Y. Eugene Chen and Michael Holinstat, 14 October 2026, The Journal of Clinical Investigation. DOI: 10.1172/JCI201899

This work was supported by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (F31HL179940, R35HL150784, R01HL109946), the National Institute of General Medical Sciences (T32GM140223, and the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences (T32TR004371) of National Institutes of Health. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the NIH

The work was also supported by the American Heart Association and Lexicon Pharmaceuticals.

Michael Holinstat is a consultant and receives research funding from Lexicon Pharmaceuticals. Bertram Pitt is a consultant for Lexicon Pharmaceuticals. The remaining authors declare no conflicts of interest.

#6496. The 38 Best Restaurants in Barcelona, According to a Local Food Guide

From local Catalan cuisine to a burgeoning global food scene, here are the best meals in Barcelona right now

From Barcelona’s towering churches and bustling avenues to the sun-drenched beaches and idyllic plazas, it’s obvious why this city captures visitors’ hearts. You can also eat incredibly well here, and often for not very much money — though Barcelona loves a tasting menu and the World’s 50 Best Restaurant list awarded Disfrutar the No. 1 spot last year. Despite Barcelona’s famed cuisine, it’s also easy to have a downright disappointing meal if you settle for any old paella-slinging bar along Les Rambles (known in Spanish as La Rambla) or La Barceloneta. (Tip: If a restaurant has to pay someone to stand outside and hassle pedestrians, the food isn’t worth it.)

Start with some classic tapas and paella (both great but neither entirely Catalan) and be sure to seek out local gems like bittersweet vermouth, seasonal seafood, and homestyle Catalan cuisine. But after writing and revising this list for nearly a decade, I have to insist you don’t overlook the city’s burgeoning global cuisines; save room for Calabrese paninis, Northeast Asian sharing plates with natural wines, towering fried chicken sandwiches, South Indian fish stews, and nose-to-tail yakitori.

We update this list quarterly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing Barcelona dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in euros), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in October 2026: Lluritu, a Mediterranean marisquería with three locations across the city; a parallel universe of Catalan culinary history in a former water bottling plant at Franca; and the trendy modern Catalan cuisine of Manda Huevos.

Sam Zucker is a freelance writer, photographer, filmmaker, travel Instagrammer, and gastronomic tour guide in Barcelona. He has contributed to Monocle, National Geographic’s “48 Hours” guides, Culture Trip, and Vice Travel, among others.

From local Catalan cuisine to a burgeoning global food scene, here are the best meals in Barcelona right now

From Barcelona’s towering churches and bustling avenues to the sun-drenched beaches and idyllic plazas, it’s obvious why this city captures visitors’ hearts. You can also eat incredibly well here, and often for not very much money — though Barcelona loves a tasting menu and the World’s 50 Best Restaurant list awarded Disfrutar the No. 1 spot last year. (Tip: If a restaurant has to pay someone to stand outside and hassle pedestrians, the food isn’t worth it.)

Start with some classic tapas and paella (both great but neither entirely Catalan) and be sure to seek out local gems like bittersweet vermouth, seasonal seafood, and homestyle Catalan cuisine. But after writing and revising this list for nearly a decade, I have to insist you don’t overlook the city’s burgeoning global cuisines; save room for Calabrese paninis, Northeast Asian sharing plates with natural wines, towering fried chicken sandwiches, South Indian fish stews, and nose-to-tail yakitori.
