The Defense Intelligence Agency's latest "Challenges to Security in Space" report included a declassified satellite photo of China's Shenlong, or "divine dragon," space plane, which has released at least nine mysterious payloads into low Earth orbit since 2022.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new U.S. intelligence agency report has seemingly released the first clear photograph of China's mysterious "dragon" space plane in orbit around Earth. The surprise snap reveals that the top-secret vehicle is very similar to its American counterpart and provides new clues about its capabilities.

The image is widely believed to show China's secretive Shenlong, or "divine dragon," space plane, which has been in action for just over six years. During this time, the reusable winged spacecraft has repeatedly made headlines after deploying various unidentified objects in low Earth orbit (LEO). As a result, government officials, private companies and individual researchers have closely monitored the vehicle using tools such as ground-based radar.

Until now, the only direct images of the space plane have been blurry snaps of light reflecting off the uncrewed vehicle toward Earth's surface — offering no clear clues to its specific design, capabilities or intended purpose. China has also never publicly shared any photos of the vehicle or revealed any key information about its design.

On Monday (Oct. 26), the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released the latest version of its "Challenges to Security in Space" report, which assesses the various factors that pose a risk to American space assets. Deep within the 130-page document (on page 53), the authors included a previously unseen image of a "PRC [People's Republic of China] Spaceplane." The image's brief caption revealed that the photo had been taken in 2024 by a satellite belonging to the private space company Maxar Technologies, now known as Vantor.

The surprise inclusion of the photo was spotted and shared on the social platform X by journalist Andrew Jones, who specializes in China's space program and has previously shared crucial information about other ongoing missions.

The new image suggests that Shenlong looks very similar to the U.S. Space Force's X-37B space plane, which is also currently orbiting Earth.

Neither the caption nor the related section of the report made any mention of the photo being the first of its kind or explained why it was previously classified, raising questions about whether the authors realized its significance.

There is one small caveat. The report notes that China has two active space plane designs — Shenlong and Tengyun, meaning "cloud rider" — and the image's caption does not specify which design we are looking at, according to The Aviationist.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, there have been no confirmed launches of Tengyun to date. Existing photos of a potential prototype also hint that this vehicle's design looks markedly different from what we can see in the new photo. Therefore, most experts agree that the spacecraft in the image is most likely Shenlong.

Until now, all we really knew about Shenlong is that it operates similarly to NASA's iconic space shuttles: It gets launched into space by a rocket and circles Earth before eventually gliding down to the planet's surface, where it can then be refueled and relaunched into LEO.

It is not the world's only active space plane. The U.S. Space Force has its own, the X-37B, which has already completed seven orbital missions since its first launch in 2010 and is currently in LEO experimenting with quantum navigation. Based on the new photos, Shenlong shares many similarities with its American counterpart.

Until now, the only direct images of Shenlong were blurry snaps of light reflecting off the spacecraft back to Earth's surface.

"The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays," technology news site ArsTechnica reported. "In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the U.S. Space Force."

However, the two spacecraft are not exactly the same: "The overall arrangement resembles the American vehicle, although differences in wing geometry show that the two spacecraft are not externally identical," according to specialist news site Global Defense News.

It is still unclear how large Shenlong is. The X-37B is 29 feet (8.8 meters) long and has a wingspan of 15 feet (4.5 m), according to Popular Science.

The new image also indicates that Shenlong is most likely not a military asset, Global Defense News reported, noting that "the image does not establish a weapons role."

Shenlong shares the same key design features as X-37B (right) but is not identical to its American counterpart.

However, China likely has other space-based weapons, similar to the mysterious "in-orbit" American weapons recently confirmed by U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink.

"China has developed and will continue to advance weapons for use against satellites in orbit to disrupt, damage, and destroy other nations' space capabilities," DIA representatives wrote in a separate section of the new report. "Beijing aims to become the preeminent leader in space," they added.

Since first launching into space on an initial two-day mission in September 2020, Shenlong has completed two feature-length missions: an eight-month stint in LEO between August 2022 and May 2023, and a nine-month spaceflight between December 2023 and September 2024. (The new image was taken during the latter mission).

The space plane is currently on its fourth mission, which launched Feb. 7 on board a Long March 2F rocket from China's Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Live Science's sister site Space.com previously reported. In total, Shenlong has racked up more than 800 days in orbit. However, it is unclear whether the same space plane was used on all four missions or if China has more than one space plane in use.

Shenlong was most recently launched into space on board a Long March 2F rocket on Feb. 7. (This image shows the same rocket during a different launch in 2011.)

So far, Shelong has released at least nine unidentified payloads around Earth. These objects are most likely small satellites, known as cubesats, but their purpose remains unclear.

The most recent object was deployed in June this year, although astronomer Jonathan McDowell, who specializes in tracking spacecraft in LEO, has since suggested that the spacecraft retrieved the object, potentially with a robotic arm, and rereleased it in late August.

The new report also mentions that the space plane "appeared to maneuver with a companion satellite" during its second mission in November 2022, coming within 330 feet (100 m) of the smaller spacecraft and potentially even capturing and re-releasing it.

This may support an existing theory that the main goal of Shenlong is to "conduct rendezvous and proximity operations" with other spacecraft, and that its payloads may be targets for it to practice flyby maneuvers in orbit.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Oct. 29 to correct a typo. A previous version of the article abbreviated the People's Republic of China as "PCR" rather than "PRC". This has been corrected.

#6474. Scientists Finally Identify Mysterious Creature Nearly 90 Years After It Was First Found

A millipede first collected nearly 90 years ago in South Australia has finally been identified as a new species, challenging assumptions about where its moisture-loving relatives can survive. Named Colobothrix deckeri, the species belongs to the family Dalodesmidae, which typically inhabits damp environments. Yet its original collection site receives just 400 to 500 millimeters (15.7 to 19.7 inches) of annual rainfall, making it the first member of its family recorded from such a dry region of Australia.

The new species also possesses an unusual microscopic feature. Mature males in Dalodesmidae and certain other millipede families have tiny, ball-shaped structures on their legs called sphaerotrichomes, normally topped by a long, pointed bristle known as a seta. In C. deckeri, that bristle is reduced to a short, blunt rod. This distinctive anatomy inspired the new genus name Colobothrix, meaning “stunted hair.”

The discovery began with a specimen collected in 1936 on South Australia’s lower Yorke Peninsula. It remained unidentified in the South Australian Museum (SAMA) until 2015, when German researcher Peter Decker encountered it while examining borrowed museum specimens for his doctoral research on a different millipede family, Paradoxosomatidae.

Recognizing that the animal belonged to Dalodesmidae, Decker sent photographs of its microscopic features to Australian millipede specialist Robert Mesibov. The specimen provided the first evidence that this family occurred in dry South Australia. Mesibov searched the original collection area in 2016 and 2017, but neither expedition located another specimen. He later named the species in Decker’s honor, publishing the description in the peer-reviewed, open-access journal ZooKeys.

Unknown to the researchers at the time, additional specimens had already been collected about 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the original location. In 2010, arachnologists Michael Rix and Danilo Harms were surveying spiders and leaf-litter invertebrates on Kangaroo Island when they discovered a remarkable new assassin spider species in the island’s relatively wet northwestern region. Their collections also included several unidentified millipedes, which were deposited in the Western Australian Museum (WAM).

The island’s devastating 2020 bushfires later destroyed the original collection site, raising fears that the rare assassin spider might be approaching extinction. During a follow-up survey in 2021, arachnologist Jessica Marsh found the spider at additional locations several kilometers (a few miles) away. Her collections of other invertebrates also contained specimens of the unidentified millipede.

In early 2026, Mesibov discovered the Western Australian Museum’s millipede record online and contacted curator Mark Harvey. Close-up photographs supplied by Harvey confirmed that the Kangaroo Island specimens belonged to the same species collected on the Yorke Peninsula in 1936.

Mesibov subsequently visited Kangaroo Island and successfully located living specimens near the earlier collection sites. “Third time lucky!” said Mesibov. “I found the new millipede alive and well this year at relatively wet sites not far from its 2010 and 2021 localities.”

He collected several specimens for the formal species description and future genetic research. The specimens collected in 1936, 2021, and 2026 are now housed at the South Australian Museum.

Although C. deckeri has been confirmed on Kangaroo Island, researchers still do not know whether it survives at its original Yorke Peninsula location. That mainland site receives considerably less rainfall than the species’ known habitats in northwestern Kangaroo Island.

Mesibov suspects that the peninsula’s underlying limestone could provide a possible explanation for how the millipede survives in such a dry environment.

“The 1936 locality is underlain by limestone,” said Mesibov, “and the rock is broken where it is exposed at the ground surface. I wonder if the species survives in small voids in this bedrock, as a relict from wetter periods in South Australia’s past. That might explain why I couldn’t find it in 2016 and 2017, and how it could persist in such a dry climate.”

Reference: “Two new millipede genera and species from Kangaroo Island, South Australia (Polydesmida, Dalodesmidae, Spirostreptida, Cambalidae)” by Robert Mesibov, 23 October 2026, ZooKeys. DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1295.214938

#6473. The 4 Best Nugget Ice Makers to Get Soft, Chewable Ice at Home

We tried out the best versions that sit on your countertop and churn out several pounds of ice per day.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’re a fan of soft, crunchy, chewable ice, a countertop nugget ice maker can bring that sought-after texture right to your kitchen. Also known as pellet or “Sonic” ice, nugget ice is made of compacted flakes that are soft, airy, and easy to munch on and slow to melt. It’s especially good for soaking up the flavor of whatever you’re drinking, making it a favorite for everything from sodas and cocktails to iced coffee and just plain, old water.

Nugget ice makers have become increasingly popular home appliances, but the machines themselves can be relatively advanced. They require more complex internal components than basic ice makers, and thus tend to cost more—often starting around $400 for a high-quality design. Depending on the appliance, you’ll also find features like large ice baskets, water reservoirs, self-cleaning cycles, and high daily production.

To help you find the right machine for your kitchen and budget, we researched, tested, and reviewed the best nugget ice makers from manufacturers such as GE, Euhomy, and Gevi. Whether you’re entertaining friends or just ready to retire the built-in ice maker on your fridge, these are the models we recommend.

The selection of countertop nugget ice makers available from trusted and reliable brands is limited, so we dug to find and test the best options by considering product specs, capabilities, and prices. During testing, we ran cleaning cycles to get the systems ready to go. We then timed how long it took for each machine to produce one batch of ice, and again for how long it took to fill the ice basket completely.

Throughout our setup and testing, we evaluated each model’s ease of use, reliability, and the quality of the ice they made. We took note of any cool or unique features like app compatibility, storage options, and more.

Our home appliance writer, Nick Hilden, also spoke with Jessica Randhawa, founder and head chef at the Forked Spoon, and Yu Jiang Zhao, mixologist, about what to keep in mind when choosing a nugget ice maker.

This was the nugget ice maker that made our tester throw out their ice trays once and for all. It takes everything we liked about the previous version, GE Profile Opal 2.0, and boosts the ice production speed, upgrades a smattering of components and functions to make it easier to clean and enhance its lifespan, and includes an external water tank and ice scoop to boot.

We’ve found that it churns out ice at a rapid enough pace to keep round after round of cold beverages for a sizable gathering. It has an easy-to-use app that offers smart functions such as scheduling alerts for maintenance. Additionally, its sleek design has a timeless vibe that won’t look dated two years from now.

It’s got a footprint nearly that of two shoeboxes side by side, which is a bit big for a smaller kitchen. It can also get somewhat noisy when it’s actively producing ice—about the volume of a loud refrigerator—though it’s basically silent when it’s just keeping it cool. But if you’re looking for reliable, convenient ice on demand, there’s none better.

Full GE Profile Opal 2.0 Ultra Nugget Ice Maker Review

This little unit packs a surprising amount of ice production power, churning out as much or more than any of the larger models on our list (40 pounds per day). Additionally, its compact size makes it perfect when you have less countertop real estate to spare, or if you want portable ice production for a backyard barbecue or camping in an RV.

Our testing found that it churns out ice fast, with the first batch in under ten minutes. Its operation is as straightforward as they come, and its cleaning is easier than most other machines, with an automatic cleaning mode that requires little effort on your part besides draining out the water that runs through the system.

All told, it’s a great ice maker for anyone who wants a no-fuss model that will look nice in the kitchen without taking up too much space. It also offers similar performance to larger, more expensive models, minus the roomy storage capacity.

Full Euhomy Smart Countertop Nugget Ice Maker Review

The Gevi 2.0 is the kind of ice maker you won’t mind taking up prime countertop real estate, given its polished design. The bin holds almost five pounds of ice (the largest capacity on our list), and the machine has thick insulation on all sides to keep cubes frozen for longer.

One of our favorite features is the door on the ice maker that opens to a 90-degree angle. To achieve this, the Gevi ditches the viewing window that’s present on other models, but this design choice allows you to pull the ice basket forward. This made it very simple to scoop our pellet ice once the container was full.

The instruction manual says that it takes about 15 to 30 minutes for the first cubes to form, but I noticed a couple of pellets had dropped around the 9-minute and 20-second mark. They were fairly wet to start but began forming more compactly over time and were the perfect, crunchy texture. However, it takes a few hours to get a full basket, which is tricky if you need ice immediately.

The water reservoir is kind of awkward to access with the door style, but the Gevi also comes with a hose that hooks up to your tap if you want it to fill automatically.

Ice makers require regular cleaning to ensure both quality ice and a long lifespan for the unit, and we found that the Silonn Nugget Ice Maker makes it easier than the rest. Most notable is its self-cleaning function, which is as effortless as it gets: Push a button to start the clean cycle, and let it do its thing. This is unlike other models that require removing a lot of parts or going through a complex series of steps. We also like that you can just toss its removable water reservoir and ice bin in the dishwasher, with no hoses or bottles to clean.

In terms of operation, it delivers most everything you want from a solid ice maker. It produces a hefty 44 pounds of ice a day, and its 2.6-pound bin holds plenty of ice for several rounds of drinks. It’s straightforward and intuitive to use—all you need to do is fill it with water—and is somewhere in the middle in terms of countertop footprint.

It does produce more noise than other popular models. Most nugget ice makers crank the volume up when actually producing ice, but this one has a noticeable hum even when on standby. For reliable ice with no-hassle cleaning, however, it’s hard to beat.

One of the key benefits to a good nugget ice maker is that it can churn out upward of 30 or even 40 pounds a day, making it ideal for hosting large, thirsty groups. The best models can have the first cubes ready within about 10 minutes, and will have a full bin within an hour or so.

A countertop machine, of course, can’t store three dozen pounds of ice. Most ice bins hold 1 to 3 pounds, which will replenish as depleted. It’s rare to go through a full bin, so unless you expect to host a particularly large number of people, this may not be the most pressing concern.

The vast majority of home nugget ice makers are equipped with a built-in water reservoir. These are great for at-home use as they don’t require installation and are highly portable, making it easy to pack them away for storage.

The larger the tank, the more ice the machine will produce. However, this also means that it will require more counter space. Models with smaller water reservoirs eat up less room, but require you to refill them frequently.

You can plug some models directly into your home plumbing system, which eliminates the need to fill a tank as it will draw water continuously. These, however, may require expert installation depending on your DIY skills, and will usually end up in a cabinet or closet rather than on your countertop.

The bigger the ice maker, the more countertop space it uses, so consider how much room you have in your kitchen. Our top pick, the GE Opal 2.0, is a great ice maker, but it has a pretty big footprint for a kitchen with limited counter real estate. When measuring dimensions, don’t forget about the inch or two of clearance that you’ll need for the fan, which keeps the motor from overheating.

If you have the space for it, Randhawa recommends placing the model in the pantry. This not only keeps your countertops open, but can muffle the operating noise.

“With most nugget ice machines you should expect some sound when operating on standby, but they can get pretty noisy when producing ice,” says Randhawa. “That might not matter in the din and clatter of cocktail hour, but could be more bothersome when things quiet down.”

It’s difficult to determine how loud a particular model will be without actually hearing it as there is no standardized noise rating. Your best bet is to check reviews for what previous buyers or reviewers have to say.

Nugget ice makers use a large metal cylinder with an auger inside that freezes as the machine runs. Water then pours into the cylinder and starts to freeze along the walls, producing a thin sheet of ice that the auger scrapes and pushes through the machine as ice flakes.

The machine then squeezes the flakes to push out excess water and compacts them into small, airy pieces so that what you end up with is a soft, porous nugget of ice that (probably) won’t crack your teeth when you chew it. They’re ideal for beverages because they take on the flavor of the drink, and there’s really nothing quite like that taste and texture.

Unfortunately, nugget ice makers aren’t ready to use right out of the box. Once you’ve gotten your unit, it’s best to let it sit upright on a level surface for at least two hours before plugging it in. This helps the refrigerant settle. The time may vary depending on the model you have, so it’s best to refer to the manual for the specific time.

You should also run the self-cleaning or sanitizing cycle before getting started. A combination of equal parts water and vinegar can get the job done. By doing this, you’re clearing the machine of any lingering residue or grime that could affect the clarity and taste of the ice. After completing a cycle with the solution, you can run another one with just water for a full wash-down.

Nugget ice makers are not a set-it-and-forget-it machine—they require regular cleaning and additional upkeep. One of the main concerns with these appliances is calcium buildup, or limescale, which accumulates if you have hard tap water.

To prevent this, it’s a good rule of thumb to occasionally descale your ice maker. You can make a 1:1 solution of distilled white vinegar and water, put it in the reservoir, and run it through the machine for a few cycles. Another tip is to use filtered water.

Self-cleaning modes should be run at least once a month, but if you’re a frequent party host, every other week couldn’t hurt. If you’re using a nugget ice maker that hooks up to a water line, you would benefit from an inline filter. Vacuuming the fan and blowing out the condenser also prevents clogs from dust and debris that may cause overheating.

Nugget ice makers make anywhere from 24 to 44 pounds of ice in a 24-hour period. They start up relatively quickly (as little as 10 minutes) but may take up to an hour to fully fill the ice bin.

Models with large capacity bins are best for big groups, while smaller ones are good for home bars and entertaining a couple of friends. Some options have ice bins that are insulated to keep ice from melting, while others just have an acrylic bucket in which ice melts faster.

For those that regularly host large gatherings or just don’t want to run out of nugget ice, we suggest running your nugget ice maker the day before and storing nugget ice in the freezer. Alternatively, you could stockpile extra nugget ice just in case you’re burning through more than expected the day of your event.

Most nugget ice machines are countertop units, so special installation isn’t necessary. We’ve specifically recommended models that don’t require you to install them, as the vast majority of owners will want something user-friendly and easy to store when not in use. Typically speaking, ice makers that require installation are heavy-duty, professional-grade units for serving large groups of people.

According to Randhawa, “Most nugget ice machines just use a standard outlet and require space around it to vent per the instructions.” Without proper ventilation space, your unit could overheat and break down.

“[Nugget ice makers] run compressors constantly and consume more power than people think it should for a countertop appliance,” says Zhao. “If energy consumption is a concern to you, look for those with an Energy Star rating, and factor in that it will likely be running a good portion of the day.”

Newer models tend to need about 0.05 to 1 kilowatt-hour per day, depending on your ice use. The more ice you make, the more power you’ll need. That’s roughly the equivalent of an energy-efficient fridge, which increases electric bills by about $10 to $15 a month.

If you always want ice at the ready, then you’ll have to run your nugget ice maker at all times, but it’ll likely shut off once the bin is full. “This is a normal operating procedure,” says Zhao. “Turning it off and on [manually] every day reduces its life and means you are waiting 15 to 20 minutes for your first batch every day.”

However, these machines don’t technically need to run year-round if you’re worried about possibly running up your electric bill. “You can turn them off and put them away when you don’t plan on using them,” says Randhawa. “We put ours away during vacations and over the winter, after the temperature drops, which is generally when we don’t want ice in our drinks.”

#6472. NYC’s Hottest New Wine Bar Started With a DM Slide

An interview with the team behind El Camarón Peludo.

Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings.

Giovanni Cervantes and Tania Apolinar spent the last five years slinging tacos at breakneck pace to keep up with the lines at Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez and rowdy World Cup crowds at Socceria. Now the duo is slowing things down a bit for their first full-service restaurant El Camarón Peludo, a playful wine and seafood spot in the West Village where guests linger over mariscos.

At the tiny, walk-in-only restaurant, the menu fuses Mexican seafood dishes with Spanish influences and excellent wine from around the world. For the project, Cervantes and Apolinar teamed up with chef Carlos Barrera, a Mexico City-born chef who has worked in Michelin-starred restaurants in Spain and hosted dozens of popular pop-ups around NYC. When I sat down with Cervantes and Apolinar, I planned to pick their brains about how and why they manage four wildly popular (and very different) New York City restaurants. Then I learned how much El Camarón Peludo was the result of fate: If it weren’t for space constraints, a tapas-fueled trip, and a social media superfan, the duo may have had an entirely different restaurant on their hands.

Pre Shift: Where did the idea for El Camarón Peludo come from?

Tania Apolinar: When we were looking at [the space], we considered making it a taqueria, but because of the [long shape of the restaurant], it wouldn’t have worked for that concept. We knew we wanted to do something different, focused on seafood and wine.

Giovanni Cervantes: I was in conversation with Carlos about this idea to serve mariscos in New York when we saw the space. We didn’t know [at the time], but we were setting up the basis of the menu because we were talking about what we like and what we miss a lot [from Mexico]. We also talked about [our past trips] to Europe. We were really interested in how to match [the style of European tapas and wine bars] with what we do, which is the Mexican approach.

How did you connect with Barrera for the project?

Cervantes: Carlos was one of the first clients that we ever had in Taqueria Ramírez. We met basically through that and through Instagram. He was always commenting a lot...

Cervantes: Exactly. Sending the flame emoji. Then soon enough, we find out that we were neighbors because he lives in Greenpoint, so we started seeing each other more often.

Apolinar: Then we did a pop-up with him serving his famous Trompo Negro, which is like al pastor with [a smoky black spice paste that is widely used in Yucatán and surrounding regions], and that was the first time we actually connected in a working setup. We’re really aligned and happy with the partnership.

Can you tell me about how you balance Mexican and Spanish influences on the menu?

Cervantes: When we found the space, we knew it was the perfect setup to try something different. Then we made a trip to Europe and a trip to Mexico. After we came back from Europe, I think I was feeling very “Europeanized.” I remember having a conversation with Tanya and Carlos about making it even more Spanish, and both of them were like, “What?” And I’m glad they [pushed back], because we definitely found the right balance.

Apolinar: We’re talking about Mexican and Spanish, but in the end, it’s about the seafood and the freshness, the product that we really want to stand out. That’s why [we serve a] very simple gambas a la plancha, and the carpaccio has that approach as well, but then other more Mexican classics [like tostadas topped with tuna or aguachile] have more sauces and all of that.

Cervantes: And it’s not just the food. The influence that we took from different parts of Europe is the setup, the vibe, the size of the plates, the type of space. We want the space to feel cozy and friendly.

How is the service different from your other spots?

Cervantes: At Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez, it’s all about efficiency. Making it right, as fast as you can, and getting people in and out of the place. It’s nonstop volume. The consistency is awesome over there, and that’s [how we] measure that we’re making it right. Here it’s different. It’s more about the experience of the space and the music and the wine. [Our staff are] with these people for an hour or two, so you try to make it personal in a way. It feels different when you have that much time to see how people are enjoying the experience and transporting people to that world through what we’re doing. That’s comforting to me.

Now that you have four different restaurants around the city, how do you balance your time between them?

Cervantes: For Taqueria Ramírez, the very first one, we can sleep very well because almost everybody on the staff has been there since we opened. I’m just mentioning that because it’s all about building the right team because you can only be in one place at a time. Then at Carnitas, our partners [Yvon de Tassigny and Kari Boden] are really great and the plan was for them to be the day to day operators from the beginning. So right now we’re between El Cameron Peludo and Socceria because they’re the new babies and there’s a lot of work to do there.

Tania: It’s tiring, but at the end of the day, I’ve been enjoying it a lot. It’s nonstop but it feels rewarding to see the point of view of customers and make people feel happy and connect to them.

#6471. Martian Polar Crater Ice Shifts with Seasonal Frost

The planet Mars shares many landforms and weather patterns with the Earth, including changing seasons, volcanoes, canyons, dust storms and dust devils, and water ice. But one feature that Earth and Mars share among the eight planets in our solar system are polar ice caps. Both are one of each planetâs striking features, but the major difference is while Earthâs polar ice caps are both comprised of water, Marsâ north polar ice cap is only comprised of water while its southern polar ice cap is carbon dioxide. The reasons for this are determined by altitude, but Marsâ northern polar ice cap is one of the most studied regions primarily due to its water ice composition. But how does the north polar ice cap water ice change with the seasons compared to Earth, and what can this teach scientists about Marsâ climate history?

Now, an international team of researchers might have shed new light on this conundrum. As discussed in a recent study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, the researchers challenged our understanding of ice deposits in Marsâ northern polar ice cap region. The primary motivation behind this study was to fill a longstanding knowledge gap regarding the seasonal changes in Martian polar ice deposits, specifically focusing on craters. The researchers note that better understanding seasonal changes in polar ice cap deposits could help gain insights into long-term climate changes on the Red Planet.

For the study, the researchers analyzed images of 36 craters within the northern polar ice cap region of Mars. The images were obtained from NASAâs Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera between 2006 and 2025. This time period is also referred to as Mars Years (MY) 28â38 since one year on Mars is 668 Earth days. The goal of the study was to identify how polar ice deposits on crater floors changed with seasons, specifically whether the deposits increased or decreased in size based on winter or summer months, respectively.

In the end, the researchers found that 32 of the 36 craters exhibited changes in bright deposits, broadly indicating ice deposits are expanding and shrinking with the seasons. Of the remaining four craters, the researchers didnât observe changes in brightness. The researchers note that seasonal frost deposits on the outside of each crater could be responsible for the changes in brightness.

âNot all craters exhibit changes in frost coverage from one Mars year to the next,â the study notes. âFor a given Mars year, only a subset of craters show altered frost conditions relative to previous years, while others maintain similar or nearly identical frost extents. This spatial heterogeneity suggests that seasonal frost cycles and interannual mass balance are localized processes rather than cap-wide phenomena. Local topography, crater geometry, and microclimatic conditions likely modulate energy balance and vapor transport, leading to crater-specific responses to broader climatic forcing.â

Essentially, the researchers found the changes in crater ice deposits are triggered by local climate changes, as opposed to being triggered by larger climate changes. The reason why understanding Marsâ climate changes is important is to help pin down specific triggers, whether itâs seasonal or related to other factors. For example, Mars experiences much larger climate changes on grander scales compared to Earth due to the Red Planetâs planetary tilt having much larger swings than Earth. However, as this study demonstrates, local climates are still capable of delivering their own changes disconnected from the larger climate picture. This study identifies seasonal changes in polar ice deposits while providing motivation for future modeling work that could help expand our understanding of localized climates on Mars.

What new insights into Mars polar crater ice will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6470. Scientists Discover That a Giant Bird Thought Extinct for Thousands of Years Never Actually Disappeared

Ancient DNA analysis has challenged a 150-year-old belief about a giant bird thought to have disappeared after the last Ice Age.

For more than 150 years, scientists believed that enormous crane bones found in European caves belonged to a giant bird species that disappeared after the last Ice Age. Now, ancient DNA has overturned that identification, revealing that the supposedly extinct bird was actually a larger version of a species still living in Europe today.

Researchers at Bournemouth University (BU) found that the fossils attributed to Grus primigenia belonged to the common crane. Their findings also raise questions about whether other prehistoric birds classified as extinct species were simply larger forms of birds that survive today.

The mystery began in the 19th century when French biologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards examined unusually large crane bones discovered in caves in southern France. Believing they represented a distinct species, he named the bird Grus primigenia. The remains dated to the end of the last Ice Age and were long considered evidence of an extinct giant crane.

To investigate the bird’s identity, a team led by Dr. John Stewart, Professor of Evolutionary Paleoecology at BU, analyzed ancient DNA from 18 crane bones recovered across England, Wales, France, Germany, and the Balearic Islands. Working with the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, Sweden, the researchers used genetic evidence to determine which species the bones belonged to.

“Previous studies had merely used the size and shape of the bones to attempt to understand these large birds. The use of DNA analysis has given us a more accurate picture of what they represent,” Stewart explained.

The genetic findings indicate that the oversized fossils belonged to common cranes rather than a separate extinct species. Stewart believes differences in body size between male and female cranes may have contributed to the original misidentification.

“We suspected that these large cranes were not extinct and instead represented larger, modern European common cranes. We believe that the reason for the mistaken identity was that cranes have large males and smaller females, and we think this contributed to previous speculation that there were two different species: the living, common crane we see today and the extinct, larger species,” Stewart said.

Although the DNA evidence clarifies the birds’ identity, it leaves another question unanswered: Why were some prehistoric common cranes considerably larger than those living today?

“The challenge going forward is to investigate the reason for the cranes decrease in size. Wetland drainage and human land use changes are what we suspect, but more work is needed to resolve that,” Stewart said.

The researchers plan to investigate whether changes in wetland habitats and human land use contributed to the reduction in crane body size. These remain possible explanations rather than established causes.

The findings suggest that some prehistoric bird species identified primarily through fossil measurements may need to be reconsidered. Differences in bone size do not necessarily indicate separate species, and ancient DNA could help determine whether other supposedly extinct birds were actually larger or smaller populations of surviving species.

“While it is true that many species of birds are vulnerable to human actions today, it may be that we have overestimated the number of extinctions in the past,” Stewart said.

“Some of these may instead represent size changes to living species,” he concluded.

Reference: “Ancient DNA study resolves the taxonomic status of the extinct large Palaearctic crane Grus primigenia Milne-Edwards, 1871 (Aves: Gruiformes: Gruidae)” by John R. Stewart, Rebecca Rickard, Sheila Hamilton-Dyer, Keith Dobney, Veronique Laroulandie, Josep Antoni Alcover, Joan Femenias-Gual, Nadja Pöllath, Erik Ersmark, Bodil Cronholm, Per G. P. Archaeologists found several ancient weapons, intact vases and a bronze razor in the volcanic crater lake.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have recovered a well-preserved bronze sword from a volcanic lake in Italy. The 3,300-year-old weapon may have been deposited in the lake as an offering to a deity or for a high-status warrior who lived long before the rise of the Etruscans or the Romans.

The sword was found in Lake Mezzano, which is located in the crater of an ancient volcano roughly 60 miles (100 kilometers) northwest of Rome, according to a translated statement from the Superintendence of Archaeology, Fine Arts and Landscape for the Province of Viterbo and Southern Etruria. Dating to the Late Bronze Age (14th to 13th centuries B.C.), the sword has maintained its sharp edge. It is the third such sword found in Lake Mezzano in the past 50 years.

Bronze Age people erected pile dwellings or stilt houses in what is now Lake Mezzano, and archaeologists recovered parts of the submerged settlement during their recent investigations. According to the statement, researchers also found numerous intact vases, axes, arrowheads, daggers, spearheads, pins and a bronze razor.

The bronze sword dates to the Late Bronze Age and may have been a symbol of power.

The sword and the razor were found near each other, suggesting the two artifacts may have been linked to a person of high social status, such as an elite warrior. But the placement of the metal weapons in a lake may also be related to a wider Bronze Age ritual practice where hoards of jewelry and bent or ritually "killed" artifacts were tossed into bodies of water. This practice continued through the centuries into Etruscan times, when wells were ritually "closed" with artifacts and human sacrifices.

During the 13th century B.C., people in central Italy engaged in trade networks that spanned the Mediterranean. "In this context, bronze weapons were not only instruments of combat, but also symbols of prestige, identity, and power," according to the statement.

The sword and other artifacts discovered in Lake Mezzano are giving archaeologists new information about the people who flourished in prehistoric Italy long before the Romans and Etruscans. Additional research is planned in the coming years, according to the statement.

#6468. New Research Resolves the Mystery Behind Van Gogh's The Starry Night

Starry Night, the iconic painting by legendary Impressionist Vincent Van Gogh, has inspired debate among art historians and astronomers for decades. Was the painting something that Van Gogh was spontaneously inspired to create in the early morning hours in July 1889, or did it present a realistic depiction of the night sky over Saint-RÃ©my (where he painted it)? According to a recent study conducted jointly by South Korean telescope manufacturer SLLAB and the School of Space Research at Kyung Hee University, it's the latter.

For over a century and a half, scholars focused primarily on religious and symbolic interpretations of the painting. It was not until the mid-1980s that studies were presented that analyzed its astronomical aspects. These were conducted by UCLA art historian Albert Boime (1984) and Harvard astronomer Charles Whitney (1986), who examined celestial correspondences and proposed constellation identifications based on a mid-June date. However, the two reached conflicting conclusions, and no studies since have examined the painting using observational geometry.

The study, presented in Scientific Reports (a Nature journal), instead narrows the dates on which a crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades star cluster (which appear closely together in the painting) fell within Van Gogh's field of view. The study's first author, Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, CEO of SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, has spent years building telescopes and observing the night sky and was inspired to weigh in on the debate.

(a)The stars in The Starry Night (1889) overlaid by the real stars after matching for size, orientation, and position; red dashed lines show the residual differences. (b) The stars in CafÃ© Terrace at Night (1888), left, and the stars around the Summer Triangle. Credit: Kim et al., Scientific Reports

"To an observational astronomer, the cluster of stars in The Starry Night is the Hyades in Taurus," he said. "But the moment I read the earlier studies explaining it as Aries, I heard the painting calling to me." The research builds on Kim's previous book (released in 2025) and began with two field trips to France in 2019 to gather additional evidence and add quantitative data. Traditionally, the painting was dated to June 18th, 1889, based on a letter Van Gogh wrote to his brother, Leo.

However, on that date, the Moon was in its waning gibbous phase, which does not match the slender crescent in the painting. On July 22nd, the Moon was a crescent, and the Hyades cluster would have been seen rising in the east alongside Venus (placing it in the Taurus constellation). In the past, that date was thought to be one when Van Gogh experienced one of his seizures, but cross-analysis of the original French and Dutch letters and the details mentioned in both suggests his seizure began in late July.

Using on-site photographs taken in Arles, the team verified Van Gogh's field of view overlooking the RhÃ´ne River. Afterward, they traveled to Saint-RÃ©my, where they located the spot where Van Gogh drew the landscape in preparation for his painting. They then conducted a statistical shape analysis to confirm that the five central stars in the painting corresponded to the Hyades cluster, which matched even more closely in the pen drawing Van Gogh made after he finished the painting.

These results suggest that the sky in the painting was based on actual observation rather than pure impressionist feeling. The methods employed could also be extended to other historical night paintings, leading to collaborative efforts between astronomers and art historians. The team has already used the same method on another of Van Gogh's famous creations that features stars in the sky - CafÃ© Terrace at Night (painted in 1888) - and found a possible match to the Summer Triangle asterism.

"I hope this work prompts a renewed, multidisciplinary look at the sequence and working methods of the Saint-RÃ©my paintings, and at Van Gogh's movements that summer," Kim said. "Our conversation with Van Gogh's other skies is still ongoing. We plan to tell those stories one by one."

#6467. Beyond the Iconic Potato Dish at New NYC Restaurant Somssi

There’s plenty of creative dishes coming out of this West Village kitchen

You’ve probably heard of the Potato Potato Potato dish at Somssi, the newest restaurant from Na:eun Hospitality. The triple-layered potato dish is the most labor-intensive dish on the menu but has also become the most popular order, with the kitchen going through up to 100 pounds of potatoes each week. The whimsical, caviar-topped dish really encapsulates what the restaurant is trying to achieve: “We should have serious food, serious hospitality, but we shouldn’t take ourselves too seriously,” says managing partner Ahris Kim. Here’s how the Somssi kitchen preps to create the newly famous potato and plenty of other dishes before a night of service.

Yukon gold potatoes are put through a ricer to become a cream and butter-heavy puree that is set in molds in the freezer. After being toasted in breadcrumbs, the logs of potato are wrapped in russet potato ribbons before being fried up to order.

Next is the ox tongue, which is brined for just over 16 hours before being slow-cooked in herbs, aromatics, and beef tallow for four hours. Huge cuts of tongue are carefully scored so they will get a great sear when they hit the grill. It’s served on a romesco sauce with just a bit of wasabi on the side.

Finally, pork loin is coated in ground shrimp for a creative schnitzel that is reminiscent of shrimp toast. The schnitzel is topped with a sweet-and-sour plum sauce that balances out the thick, crispy fried exterior. Scallop crudo is made up of pressed scallops surrounded with a strawberry sauce and topped off with gooseberries and peppers.

#6466. Human Bodies Are Producing Two Billion Tons of CO2 a Year

A new study reveals that the amount of carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism has increased dramatically over three decades.

The carbon dioxide produced by human bodies as they convert food into energy increased by 74% over three decades, according to a University of Bath-led study. By 2015, the global total had reached an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons (2.26 billion U.S. tons) annually, highlighting a substantial component of the Earth’s carbon cycle that scientists had not previously quantified on this scale.

Unlike emissions from burning fossil fuels, the CO2 humans exhale largely comes from carbon recently absorbed from the atmosphere by plants and transferred through food. Burning coal, oil, and natural gas releases carbon that has been stored underground for millions of years, adding it to the active carbon cycle.

Published in The Lancet Planetary Health, the study found that annual CO2 production from human metabolism rose from 1.18 billion metric tons (1.30 billion U.S. tons) in 1985 to 2.05 billion metric tons (2.26 billion U.S. tons) in 2015. More than 60% of that increase was attributable to population growth rather than a substantial rise in the amount produced by each individual.

To estimate global emissions from metabolism, the researchers analyzed thousands of real-world measurements of CO2 production in people ranging from infants to older adults. They combined these findings with worldwide population and body weight data to calculate how human metabolic activity changed over time.

Professor Javier Gonzalez, who led the research at the University of Bath’s Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism, explained:

“We all produce carbon dioxide simply by turning food into energy, but until now we haven’t had a good idea how much that adds up to worldwide.

“What we’ve found is that the increase is mainly because there are more of us. This gives scientists one more piece of the puzzle when working out where carbon comes from and where it goes. Ultimately, this information can help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be.”

Human metabolism contributes to the continuous movement of carbon through the environment, particularly in densely populated cities. Accounting for that activity could help researchers develop more accurate carbon budgets and better assess the effects of strategies designed to reduce emissions.

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not suggest people should exercise less, change their diets, or attempt to reduce the carbon dioxide they breathe out. The purpose is to improve scientific measurements of carbon movement, not identify respiration as a contributor to fossil fuel emissions.

Gonzalez stressed the distinction: “The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels. We’re not saying that breathing is driving climate change.

“What this study does is give us a much clearer picture of how much CO2 people produce around the world, and how that is changing as the population grows. This understanding can help improve the accuracy predictions of carbon reduction programs.”

Reference: “Accounting for global carbon dioxide production from human metabolism between 1985 and 2015: a modelling study” by Javier T Gonzalez, Lorenzo Lolli, Bruno Spellanzon, Greg Atkinson, Ed Maunder, Alfonso Moreno-Cabañas, Jariya Buniam, Dylan Thompson, James Betts, Philip N Ainslie, Heliodoro Alemán-Mateo, Linda Bandini, Ellen E Blaak, Carlijn V C Bouten, Pascal Bovet, Soren Brage, Regina Casper, Prasangi Dabare, Barry W Fudge, Melanie Gillingham, Annalies H Goris, Michael Gurven, Hinke Haisma, Marije B Hoos, Noorjehan Joonas, Peter Katzmarzyk, Misaka Kimura, Sai Krupa Das, Pulani Lanerolle, Christel L Larsson, Marie Löf, Aviva Must, Marian Neuhouser, Theresa A Nicklas, Robert M Ojiambo, Kirsi H Pietilainen, Susan B Racette, Eric Ravussin, Leanne M Redman, John J Reilly, Susan Roberts, Luis B Sardinha, Analiza M Silva, Srishti Sinha, Anders M Sjödin, Eric Stice, Samuel S Urlacher, Edgar A Van Mil, Jeanine A Verbunt, Jonathan C K Wells, Tsukasa Yoshida, Xueying Zhang, Alexia Murphy-Alford, Cornelia U Loechl, Amy Luke, Michele Novaes Ravelli, Herman Pontzer, Jennifer Rood, Hiroyuki Sagayama, Dale A Schoeller, Klaas R Westerterp, William W Wong, Yosuke Yamada and John Speakman, 26 October 2026, The Lancet Planetary Health. DOI: 10.1016/j.lanplh.2026.101546

#6465. The Best Dehumidifiers for Keeping Basements, Bedrooms, and Bathrooms Dry

These top-rated dehumidifiers remove excess moisture and reduce musty odors.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Towels that don’t dry, a basement with a lingering musty smell, air that feels heavy no matter what temperature you set your smart thermostat to—if any of this sounds familiar, it may be time to invest in a dehumidifier.

Unlike an air conditioner, a dehumidifier’s primary job is removing excess moisture, rather than cooling the room itself. By pulling moisture from the air, dehumidifiers not only improve how your home smells, but they also help to prevent mold and improve overall air quality.

Dehumidifiers often come with a variety of features, like adjustable humidity settings, automatic shutoff, and energy-efficient operation. Some models have additional user-friendly features like continuous drain hookups and built-in Wi-Fi, while others stand out more for their power and reliability.

I researched models from trusted brands like Midea, Costway, and GE and incorporated insights from Popular Mechanics testers to help you find the best dehumidifier for your needs. Below, I also share tips and tricks to keep in mind when shopping for a dehumidifier.

For this guide, I researched dozens of dehumidifiers, reviewed expert and consumer feedback, and incorporated hands-on testing from Popular Mechanics reviews editor Tom Price. I’ll update this guide as more testing is completed. I also spoke with Michael Rubino, a mold and air quality expert and founder of HomeCleanse, for tips on what to look for in a dehumidifier and information on how these appliances can impact indoor air quality.

To test each model, we placed every dehumidifier in a room within its coverage and capacity range. It was difficult to maintain equal humidity for each option, given the wide range of rooms where testing occurred (including bathrooms, living rooms, and laundry rooms—all places where you really notice a change in humidity), so success was measured based on the dehumidifier’s ability to lower humidity levels over one hour, as well as the amount of water collected. The goal was to use each device in everyday settings where excess moisture and humidity tend to become most noticeable.

This dehumidifier from Homelabs has the best balance of features and usability that I came across in my research. Designed for spaces up to 4,500 square feet, it’s a flexible option for medium- to large-sized rooms or those living in humid climates. It's designed to remove 35 pints of water per day, with a listed maximum of 80 pints under ideal conditions.

It has a removable and washable air filter, auto shutoff when the tank is full, and turbo mode for optimal moisture removal. The dehumidifier is also Energy Star-rated, which means it meets the EPA’s energy-efficiency standard. It has a washable air filter and sits on rotating wheels so you can easily move it around your home.

Regardless of the room you’re in, you can monitor and control the dehumidifier's readings and settings via Wi-Fi. This appliance also has an auto-defrost feature and a filter quality indicator light that alerts you when it’s time to clean the filter.

The Costway 32-Pint Dehumidifier is an updated version of the Costway 30-Pint Dehumidifier, which Price previously tested. Based on his experience and my own research, I think Costway offers one of the most affordable dehumidifiers on the market, especially given its size and capacity.

What stands out most with this model is the variety of operating modes. There’s an auto mode that turns the device on or off based on your selected humidity level, a continuous dry mode for persistently damp spaces, and a sleep mode that dims the display lights and lowers operating noise to around 33 decibels.

The Costway also includes a 24-hour timer and two fan speeds for additional customization. Its relatively compact size makes it easy to move between rooms, though Price noted that you’ll probably want to keep it near a drain if possible. He also observed that the half-gallon tank fills surprisingly quickly in humid conditions, especially when running continuously.

For ultra-clammy crawl spaces or damp attics, the Alorair dehumidifier excels. It’s compact and portable, and the lack of an attached tank greatly reduces its size. It’s also quite powerful: This particular model is capable of removing up to 70 pints of moisture from the air over the course of a day.

Because it lacks a holding tank for all the moisture it collects, you’ll need to provide your own holding container or have a drain nearby. The Alorair has two draining options: gravity draining, or you can use the water pump. Gravity draining, as the name suggests, means that the dehumidifier can expel water through the attached tube, though this also means that the unit must be higher than the draining point. You’ll also want a bucket or other receptacle to catch all that water.

The water pump, on the other hand, pushes the collected water out and upward. This feature is especially useful for spaces with a window, sink, or drain that can collect that excess water. Once you’re done using the water pump cycle, the Alorair pushes any remaining water out of the unit in order to prevent any lingering moisture that could cause mold or mildew within the device itself.

Price was particularly impressed by the built-in pump, which he found made it much easier to drain water upward into a sink rather than relying on gravity. That, combined with its custom humidity settings and continuous operation capabilities, makes the Alorair a smart pick for attics and basements.

If you're looking for a dehumidifier with more precise controls, the Frigidaire is one of the more customizable options out there. You can adjust humidity settings directly on the unit, through Frigidaire’s app, or via compatible smart home devices. Once it reaches your selected humidity level, it automatically shuts off; this is especially useful if you live in a humid climate but don’t want your air to feel overly dry.

Another standout feature is the 1.7-gallon water bucket, which is fairly generous for a 35-pint model and allows it to run longer between emptying sessions. There’s also a continuous drainage option if you’d rather not deal with the tank at all. As an added bonus, the Frigidaire can double as an air purifier with the purchase of an attachable filter that helps capture dust and allergens.

Designed for much smaller spaces, this dehumidifier from Pro Breeze is best suited for bathrooms, closets, laundry rooms, or bedrooms up to around 250 square feet. During testing, Price was impressed by how simple and unobtrusive it felt. Unlike most larger dehumidifiers, it doesn’t use a compressor, so it runs very quietly, enough that he barely noticed it while getting ready or working nearby.

Its compact size makes it easy to tuck the Pro Breeze away on a shelf or a countertop. Price used it in his bathroom and found it helped to prevent his towels from feeling like “perpetually damp rags between showers.”

There isn’t a continuous drainage option, though, with its size, it’s relatively easy to empty it out. Once the 52-ounce reservoir is full, an indicator light turns on and the unit automatically shuts off to help prevent overflow. Just keep in mind that while this model works well for small-scale humidity issues, it doesn’t have the power needed for large rooms or damp basements.

If you’re dealing with a damp basement or large living space that always seems humid in the summer, the Midea Cube is one of the more practical high-capacity options we’ve found. The holding tank has an enormous capacity—4.2 gallons—and can pull up to 50 pints of moisture from the air within 24 hours. That extra-large tank also means less frequent emptying, which can be a huge plus if you often find yourself forgetting to check your dehumidifier (or just find constantly emptying a tank tedious and time-consuming). Of course, that large tank also means it can be quite heavy when full, which is something to consider before purchasing (though it does come with a hose for continuous draining).

For all its power, the Midea Cube 50-Pint is surprisingly energy-efficient; it’s Energy Star Certified, which is nice to know, especially if your dehumidifier tends to run frequently. It’s compatible with Alexa and allows remote humidity monitoring, which can be helpful if you’re stashing it in a room you don’t frequent very often. I also think its design is quite clever: The unit twists open for use and collapses into a more compact shape when it's time to store it for the season.

For smaller spaces, such as an apartment, bedroom, or laundry room, a 50-pint dehumidifier may be excessive. You need something smaller, quieter, and more compact, which is where I think the GE 22 Pint Portable Dehumidifier really shines. Its relatively petite size makes it easy to move from room to room, and it features a Smart Dry mode that automatically adjusts the fan speed based on room conditions. It’s also considered a fairly quiet option, which is a plus when working with a small space.

That said, its smaller footprint also means a smaller tank size; at only 8.5 pints, some report having to empty the GE every 12 hours. It’s also not powerful enough to dry out extremely damp spaces. However, if you need a small, unobtrusive dehumidifier, I think this is a solid pick.

If noise is a consideration (think bedrooms, shared spaces), then you’ll want to pay attention to a dehumidifier’s decibel level. Forty decibels is comparable to a library or a quiet suburban street; not silent, but not enough to be disruptive to most people. That’s what sets the Waykar CTH30A apart from other models; it runs at about 34 decibels, making it quiet enough for a bedroom or shared space, while still efficiently pulling unwanted moisture from the air.

Besides its exceptionally quiet operation, this model can cover approximately 2,000 square feet, has four operating modes (including a turbo mode for when you need to dehumidify a space quickly), and has a washable, reusable filter. The wheeled base makes it easy to move from room to room, and it comes with a 3.3-foot hose (which you can extend with a garden hose for better reach) for continuous drainage. This is important, as the 0.4-gallon holding tank fills quickly, especially in very damp areas; the continuous drain option will save you multiple trips to the sink.

“Choosing the right machine for the size of the space is massively important for reaping the benefits of using a dehumidifier,” Rubino explains. “If the dehumidifier’s capacity is insufficient for the square footage or moisture load, it may run constantly without ever effectively lowering humidity levels.” Conversely, a bigger model may be unnecessarily powerful and bulky for everyday use.

Capacity is something you’ll often see referenced when shopping for a dehumidifier, and this is measured by how many pints of moisture the unit can remove from the air over a 24-hour period. For mildly humid bedrooms, bathrooms, or laundry rooms, smaller 20- to 30-pint models are often enough. But if you’re dealing with a damp basement, stale air, condensation on windows, or towels that never seem to dry completely, it’s usually worth sizing up.

A room’s temperature also plays a factor. Warm air holds more moisture than cool air, so a dehumidifier will work more efficiently. As a result, cool but humid basements might require larger units.

You may also notice that newer dehumidifiers sometimes list lower pint capacities than older models with similar performance. That’s because the Department of Energy updated its testing standards in recent years to better reflect real-world home conditions, resulting in lower (but generally more realistic) capacity ratings.

You essentially have two options for disposing of all that collected moisture: manually emptying the tank or setting up continuous drainage with a hose.

Manual tanks have their advantages. For one, you have a lot more flexibility in where you place your dehumidifier: it can be set up anywhere there is an outlet, and you can let it run until the tank is full. The installation process is not complex and can be more cost-effective, as well. However, manually dumping a tank of water can get old, fast, especially if the bucket fills quickly.

“Continuous drainage is always a great option for rooms that are consistently humid,” Rubino says. “That way, the machine can run steadily without frequent monitoring or the need to constantly empty the reservoir.”

For basements, crawl spaces, or rooms with persistent moisture problems, continuous drainage is usually the more practical long-term solution. “This is also a great option for seasonal or vacation homes that aren’t lived in year-round,” Rubino adds. Many models include a hose adapter that allows water to drain automatically into a floor drain, utility sink, or nearby window. Some higher-end models (like our HomeLabs pick) also include built-in pumps, which allow water to travel upward instead of relying on gravity alone.

While your dehumidifier is hardly the noisiest appliance you own, noise levels can make a difference. Most compressor-style models produce a steady fan and compressor hum while running, which may not matter much in a basement but can become a lot more noticeable in bedrooms, home offices, or shared living spaces.

As a rule of thumb, larger-capacity models tend to be louder because they move more air and work harder to remove moisture quickly. Smaller thermoelectric units (like the Pro Breeze) are usually quieter, though they’re also significantly less powerful and best suited for very small spaces.

If you’re planning to run a dehumidifier overnight or in a room where you spend a lot of time, it’s worth paying attention to fan settings, sleep modes, and overall size. A louder, more powerful unit may dry the room faster, but it can also become annoying if it’s running constantly nearby.

Many dehumidifiers now include extra smart features like Wi-Fi connectivity, app controls, and voice assistant compatibility. While these aren’t strictly necessary, they can be useful in certain situations.

For example, remote monitoring allows you to check humidity levels or adjust settings without walking down to the basement every few hours. Scheduling features can also help reduce energy use by running the unit only during certain times of day, such as when you’re at work.

That said, not everyone needs app integration or smart-home compatibility. For many people, features like auto shutoff, automatic restart after power outages, and built-in humidistats (like the GE) are going to be far more useful than voice controls or smartphone notifications.

Energy efficiency is especially important because dehumidifiers often run for hours at a time. That means energy efficiency can make a noticeable difference over time, especially if you live in a particularly damp climate or plan to run the unit continuously in a basement.

Energy Star-certified models are generally worth prioritizing because they remove moisture more efficiently while using less electricity. In some cases, a slightly more expensive model may actually save money long-term if it runs more efficiently and doesn’t need to operate as often.

Choosing the right humidifier size for your needs really depends on two things: the square footage of the space, and the amount of moisture you’re trying to remove. We usually recommend 30- to 35-pint models for larger spaces like basements. Smaller units in the 20- to 30-pint range generally work well for bedrooms and offices.

Sometimes, but it all depends on your home’s layout. Your dehumidifier will work best in an open space where air can circulate freely, so if rooms are separated by closed doors or by hallways, a single unit may not work as effectively. For enclosed rooms or rooms on different floors, you’ll have more success by either using multiple dehumidifiers or moving your dehumidifier between spaces as needed.

Since humidifiers use both a fan and a compressor to remove moisture from the air, they all produce some level of noise. Most will produce an amount of noise similar to what you’d get from a window air conditioner or box fan. If noise is a concern, look for models that list decibel ratings or have a quiet mode for bedrooms or living areas.

#6464. Researchers May Have Solved a Puzzling Contradiction in the Ryugu Sample

The Solar System's asteroids are sometimes referred to as fossils because they preserve evidence of the conditions when the Solar System formed. Asteroids are critically different than their planetary counterparts. On the rocky planets, the rock itself has been subjected to billions of years of change. On Earth, tectonic plates have melted rocks, exposure to water has altered its mineral content, and pressure deep inside the Earth has transformed its crystalline structure. Cosmic and solar radiation has also driven fundamental changes on some worlds, and across Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, a mixture of these factors have altered the rock.

But asteroids and the parent bodies they came from haven't been subjected to all of these forces. In many ways, they remain unchanged from the early days of the Solar System, 4.5 billion years ago. They haven't remained completely unchanged; that would be next to impossible. But their ancient state and what it can teach us about the Solar System's history is why we've sent missions to collect samples and return them to Earth.

In 2020, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA)Hayabusa 2 successfully completed its sampling mission to asteroid Ryugu and returned its precious sample to Earth. Almost six years after its arrival on Earth, the Ryugu sample is still generating valuable scientific results, as researchers examine its mineralogical and chemical composition.

The newest results are in research titled "Pervasive poorly crystalline Mg-rich hydrous silicate material in C-type asteroid matrices." It's published in Nature Communications Earth and Environment, and the lead author is Reon Okumura from the Division of Geosciences and Civil Engineering at Kanazawa University, Japan.

Ryugu and other carbonaceous chondrites present an apparent contradiction. It involves aqueous alteration, where contact with water creates mineralogical and chemical changes in rocks and minerals. Aqueous alteration isn't a rare action that happens only in space environments; it's common on Earth. The best-known example is how clay forms from common silicate rocks in Earth's crust, from exposure to water. It's basically how soil is created.

A JAXA official successfully retrieving the 16 kg capsule that it contained a sample from the asteroid Ryugu. (Courtesy: JAXA)

There's obviously no soil on Ryugu, but there is aqueous alteration. "C-type asteroid-derived samples, including Ryugu and carbonaceous chondrites, consist primarily of fine-grained matrices of magnesium-rich hydrous silicates formed by aqueous alteration," the paper states.

The contradiction stems from the matrix of minerals in the asteroid. There seems to be two components, each altered under a different set of aqueous conditions. That implies that Ryugu's interior matrix is patchy, which is highly improbable. An asteroid can be clumpy on a macroscale, but how can it have two components in the same mineral matrix? That's been a nagging question in cosmochemistry: how can aqueous alteration happen to some of the matrix while leaving some of it more intact?

The authors write that Ryugu's matrix is "commonly interpreted as mixtures of serpentine- and saponite-like phyllosilicates..." Serpentine and saponite are both found on Earth, where they're created when rock is aqueously altered. But despite the fact that they're generally interpreted to be these substances, "their mineralogical characteristics do not fully correspond to these well-crystalline terrestrial layered silicates."

To dig into this apparent contradiction, the researchers used the SPring-8 synchrotron radiation facility and the Photon Factory High Energy Accelerator, both in Japan. Both of these research facilities use powerful x-rays to look deeply into the Ryugu sample.

They found the expected serpentine and saponite, but they also identified something else: poorly crystalline magnesium silicate hydrate (M-S-H).

âWhat makes M-S-H particularly interesting is that it can accommodate a wide range of magnesium-to-silicon ratios,â said study corresponding author Keisuke Fukushi of Kanazawa University. âThis flexibility may be key to understanding how water-rock interactions proceeded without erasing pre-existing chemical differences within their parent asteroids.â

The composition of most materials remains stable when subjected to the same aqueous conditions. But previous research and lab work shows that M-S-H is a bit of an oddball: it can exist in the same aqueous conditions and have different magnesium to silicon ratios. So this work suggests that M-S-H is the initial starting point, and that if it formed into serpentine and saponite phases, the presence of M-S-H can explain the two different outcomes without necessarily requiring a different aqueous alteration for each one.

This illustration helps explain the findings. The previous interpretation on the left shows tighly packed grains of serpentine and saponite, with the parallel lines representing their orderly crystal structure. The alternating blue and green lines in some grains represent interleaves of serpentine and saponite layers in the same crystal. There's almost no empty space between grains. The image on the right shows the new model, with a background of poorly crystalline M-S-H, making up the bulk of the matrix. In this model, serpentine and saponite are a minor part of the matrix, and are poorly-formed intrusions. Image Credit: Keisuke FUKUSHI, Kanazawa University (2026)

The study says something not only about Ryugu, but about carbonaceous chondrites. Much of their matrices could be poorly crystalline M-S-H. If this material precipitated first and then was transformed later, the different compositions of clay-like minerals found in the matrix could have arisen without a separate, distinct water environment for different regions of the parent asteroid.

"Assuming its initial precipitation and subsequent mineralogical transformations, a wide range of compositional variation can be produced without requiring separate aqueous conditions for each local composition," the authors write. "This framework provides a physicochemical basis for explaining the compositional variability and associated phyllosilicate diversity of C-type chondritic matrices within a parent-body alteration scenario."

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) is developing a reputation for successful sampling missions, one of the most difficult type of missions to complete. The original Hayabusa mission, though plagued with difficulties, still managed to return a small sample from asteroid Itokawa in 2010. Hayabusa 2 was a complete success, as this research shows. And at this moment, JAXA's Martian Moons eXplorer mission is on its way to collect a sample from Phobos, the largest of Mars' two moons.

That sample should be on Earth five years from now. What questions will it answer?
